[Peah 1:4.1] MISHNAH: They established a principle for peah : Everything that is food, is treated as private property, grows from the earth, is harvested at one time, and is stored, is subject to peah . Grain and legumes are included. And among trees sumac and carob, walnut and almond, vine and pomegranate, olive and date palm are subject to peah .
[Peah 1:4.2] HALAKHAH: ( Lev . 19:9 ) “And at your reaping,”not only reaping; from where do we add plucking? The verse says “to harvest.” From where do we add uprooting? The verse says “your harvest.” Not only grain, from where do we add legumes? The verse says “in your land.” From where do we add trees, the verse says “your field.”
[Peah 1:4.3] It was stated: One may sow vegetable seeds and tree seeds together. But he who sows with grape kernels is whipped 40 times. {NAME} said, it is written ( Deut . 22:9 ): “Do not sow your vineyard with two kinds;” the main produce of your vineyard you should not sow with two kinds. {NAME} asked before {NAME}: There they say that tree seeds are called seeds but here you say that tree seeds are not called seeds. He said to him: There the verse excluded them since usually people do not call them “seeds,” but here the verse added ( Lev . 11:37 ) “any sown seed that may be sown.”
[Peah 1:4.4] Some would understand it from here: ( Deut . 24:21 ) “When you harvest your vineyard.” How do you understand this? {NAME} said, do not be punctilious, as you say ( Lament . 1:22 ) “to punish them repeatedly.” ( Deut . 24:21 ) “When you shake your olive tree.” How do you understand this? {NAME} said ( Lev . 19:27 ): “Do not round off the peah of your head.” Since olive and vineyard are special in that they are harvested at one time for storage, so also everything that is harvested at one time for storage is obligated. But olive and vineyard are special in that they are subject to first fruits and subject to peah , so only that which is subject to first fruits should be subject to peah . The verse says ( Lev . 19:9 ): “Your harvest,” even the harvest of rice and millet.
[Peah 1:4.5] It should mention the olive tree but not the vineyard. If it would mention olive tree but not vineyard, I would say that the olive tree, which is not subject to the rule of isolated berries, is subject to peah , but that vines, which are subject to the rule of isolated berries, are not subject to peah . Lo, the mention of the vineyard is needed. Or if it would mention vineyard but not olive tree, I would say that vines which are subject to the rule of isolated berries are subject to peah , but that the olive tree which is not subject to the rule of isolated berries is not subject to peah . Lo, the mention of the olive tree and of the vineyard is needed.
[Peah 1:4.6] From the olive tree one may infer peah for all trees. From the vineyard one should infer the rule of isolated berries for all trees. (Just as from the olive tree one infers peah for all trees so one should infer the rule of isolated berries for all trees from the vineyard.) {NAME} said, any property that is common to both yields an inference but any property that is [not] common to both yields no inference.
[Peah 1:4.7] It is fine according to the opinion of {NAME}. Since {NAME} established: Everything that was in a set and left the set to be applied to a new rule, is removed from the set and forms a new one; it is necessary that peah should be mentioned for the vineyard. But for the rabbis who say, it remains in its set and keeps its special status, why is peah mentioned for the vineyard? {NAME} said, if only the vineyard were singled out, the question would be valid. But now that vineyard and olive tree are singled out, if it would mention olive tree but not vineyard, I would say that the olive tree, which is not subject to the rule of isolated berries, is subject to peah , but that vines, which are subject to the rule of isolated berries, are not subject to peah .
[Peah 1:4.8] Just as you say for the harvest that its collection must be at one time in order to qualify for peah , should one say that the same is true for the laborer? {NAME} said, there is a difference since it says ( Deut. 23:26 ): “You may pluck rubbed ears,” even of something that is not stored.
[Peah 1:4.9] It was stated ( Tosephta Peah 1:7 ): “{NAME} says, moist dates are free from peah because the first among them does not wait for the last one. “{NAME} seems to say what is correct, what is the reason of the rabbis? {NAME} said, because they all need moisture at the same time.
[Peah 1:4.10] {NAME} and {NAME} both say taro is like a vegetable for tithes, the sabbatical year, peah , and first fruits. For vows it is questionable.
[Peah 1:5.1] MISHNAH: Forever he gives as peah and it is free from tithes until he smoothes. He may take from the threshing floor and sow and it is free from tithes until he smoothes. And he feeds domestic animals, wild animals, and fowl and is free from tithes until he smoothes, the words of {NAME}. If a Cohen or a Levite bought all the grain of a threshing floor, the tithes belong to them until it was smoothed. He who dedicates to the Temple and then redeems is obligated for tithes unless it was smoothed by the Temple administrator.
[Peah 1:5.2] HALAKHAH: {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of {NAME}, {NAME} turned it in the name of {NAME}: If someone separated first fruits from a smoothed heap, it is free from the great terumah . {NAME} said before {NAME}: Does not the Mishnah say so: “Forever he gives peah and it is free from tithes until he smoothes.” Hence, if he smoothed he is obligated, but this does not apply to terumah ? It should say that he also is obligated for first fruits even though he did not smooth yet! But he is the one who said this: “Why are they called firstlings? Because they are first before everything else.” And anything which precedes something else, the latter is obligated for it.
[Peah 1:5.3] Our Mishnah is from the House of Shammai, since the House of Shammai say (Mishnah 6:1): “Property abandoned to the poor is ownerless property.”
[Peah 1:5.4] It turns out that {NAME} is like the stores of Bene Ḥanun as it has been stated: Why were the stores of Bene Hanun destroyed three years before the destruction of the Temple? Because they eliminated produce from the duty of tithes since they were inferring ( Deut . 14:22 ) “ You should certainly give tithes,” that excludes the buyer, ( Deut. 14:23 ) “You should eat,” that excludes the vendor.
[Peah 1:5.5] {NAME} said, they fined them so that they should not run after wine presses and threshing floors.
[Peah 1:5.6] A butcher who is a Cohen. The colleagues in the name of {NAME}: One frees him for one week. {NAME} said, I went to the South and I heard {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of Rebbi (Simeon) [Joshua] {NAME}: One frees him for one week. {NAME} compares it to the statement of {NAME}, they fined them. {NAME} said to him, if it is because of a fine, even one week should not be free for him. A grocer who is a Cohen, {NAME} said, one frees him for one week. {NAME} said, one does not free him for one week. According to {NAME}, what is the difference between the grocer and the butcher? The grocer may cheat, the butcher cannot cheat.
[Peah 1:5.7] It was stated: Rebbi and {NAME} did not disagree about produce bought on the field from a Gentile that it is subject to tithes because the Jew takes his place, nor about harvested produce bought from the Gentile that it is free from tithes. What did they disagree about? About him who buys harvested produce from his fellow in a year of tithes for the poor. {NAME} said, one takes it from him whether he be poor or rich. But Rebbi said, one takes it from the rich, one does not take it from the poor. What is the reason of {NAME}? Just as nobody has any rights on the single stalks, the forgotten sheaves, and the peah of his own field, so he should have no right to his tithe for the poor. What is the reason of Rebbi? Single stalks, the forgotten sheaves, and peah do not cause tebel , but the tithe for the poor creates ṭebel . It became ṭebel already in the possession of the first owner! What is the reason of {NAME}? Because of a fine! What is the reason of Rebbi? Only the rich person has the power to buy ; it is not in the power of the poor to buy. As {NAME} says, he may take a loan; but Rebbi says that he will not be able to borrow.
[Peah 2:1.1] MISHNAH: The following separate regarding peah : The river, the water canal, a private road, a public road, a private path or a public path open both summer and winter, a fallow field, a ploughed field and [another kind of] seed. He who cuts for animal feed makes a separation, the words of {NAME}; but the sages say it does not create a separation unless he ploughed.
[Peah 2:1.2] HALAKHAH: “The following separate regarding peah .” Because it has been said ( Lev . 19:9 , 23:22 ): “Your field,” that he should not give from one field for another.
[Peah 2:1.3] It cannot be connected. If you would say that it is connected, it should separate even a field of trees, but we have stated there (Mishnah 3): “Everything separates for seeds but only a fence separates for trees.” Hence, by a fence it is connected and not connected! If you say it is connected, even hair pressing down does not separate, since we have stated: “Hair pressing down does not separate but he gives one peah for all!” That means that it is not connected. If you say it is connected then it should separate if it is one-sided, as we have stated: “If the hair was pressing down from both sides it does not separate.” Hence, from one side only it separates
[Peah 2:1.4] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If someone gave peah from one field for another one, it does not acquire holiness.
[Peah 2:1.5] {NAME} asked before {NAME}: If he intended to let them acquire from the boundary strip? He avoided answering him. The opinions of {NAME} are contradictory since we have stated there (Mishnah 3:2): “The sages agree with {NAME} about someone who sowed dill or mustard in three places.” (The Mishnah means: dill in three places or mustard in three places.) {NAME} said, because the first of them does not wait for the last. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Because they are usually sown in separate beds. And here he says so? It is obvious for him that it separates. What he could not decide is whether it does become sanctified as peah or maybe it does not become sanctified! {NAME} stated: If someone gave peah from one field for another one, it does not acquire holiness. One understands that this means even the boundary strip.
[Peah 2:1.6] {NAME} said, rue separates for peah . {NAME} investigated whether they were used by Joshua to divide the Land. {NAME} asserted in the name of {NAME}: they were used by Joshua to fix the boundaries of the Land.
[Peah 2:1.7] A water canal, whenever it is flowing. A river even though it does not flow.
[Peah 2:1.8] If it is correct that we have stated “a private road,” what is the need for “a public road?” I tell you, even a public road does not separate for trees, only a fence does. Since we have stated “a private path,” what is the need for “a public path?” To exclude one that is permanent in summer but is not permanent in winter.
[Peah 2:1.9] Rav said: Fallow land and ploughed land of a bet rova‘ , other produce even the tiniest amount. {NAME} said: Fallow land, ploughed land, and other produce at three preliminary furrows. Do they disagree? What Rav said refers to produce subject to peah , what {NAME} said refers to produce not subject to peah . But did we not state that fallow or ploughed land is subject to peah ? What Rav said refers to an average field, what {NAME} said refers to a plot 50 by 2.
[Peah 2:1.10] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Both {NAME} and {NAME} said the same. Just as {NAME} said that he who cuts for fodder separates, so {NAME} will say that he who cuts for fodder separates. Just as {NAME} said that an obligation for peah separates, so {NAME} will say that an obligation for peah separates. But we find that {NAME} says that an obligation for peah separates since we have stated: “If locusts ate it, ants undermined it, or a storm or animals broke it, it is free; everybody agrees that if he ploughed it separates, if he did not plough it does not interrupt.” Who is “everybody”? Does not {NAME} say, if it is free from peah , but if it were obligated it would interrupt even if he did not plough. Parallel to what we stated there: “{NAME} said, when? If he started before it was one-third ripe, but if it is one-third ripe one is forbidden to cut.” If he cuts he is obligated for peah . And anything that is obligated for peah separates.
[Peah 2:1.11] {NAME} questioned: Just as {NAME} said, if he started before it was one-third ripe, even if he continued after it was one-third ripe he will be freed from collecting, forgotten sheaves, and peah , would {NAME} say that if he started before it was one-third ripe, even if he continued after it is one-third ripe he will be freed from collecting, forgotten sheaves, and peah ?
[Peah 2:2.1] MISHNAH: An irrigation canal that cannot be harvested together, {NAME} says it separates. For all hills subject to weeding, even if cattle can not pass by with their implements, he gives one peah for everything.
[Peah 2:2.2] HALAKHAH: They wanted to say that there is no disagreement. It was found stated: “A permanent irrigation canal separates”
[Peah 2:2.3] They wanted to say: What {NAME} talks about is one who stands on one bank and cannot cut on the other bank, but if he stands in the middle and cuts on both banks it does not separate. It was found stated in disagreement: “If he was standing in the middle and harvesting on both banks, it separates; on one bank it does not separate.”
[Peah 2:2.4] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If there was a rock along the length of his entire field, if he has to lift the plough from one side and transport it to the other side, it separates, from the other side it does not separate. But did we not state: “For terraces which are each ten hand-breadths higher than the other, he must give peah for each one separately. Less than that he gives one peah for all of them.” But for less than that, does he not have to lift the plough from one (terrace) and transport it to the other? Even for less than that he has to lift it. We had to state “ten” only because of the concluding statement: “If the heads of the terraces are connected, he gives one peah for all.”
[Peah 2:3.1] MISHNAH: Everything separates for seeds but only a fence separates for trees. But if hair was pressing down it does not separate and he gives one peah for all. : But for carob trees all that see one another. {NAME} said, in my father’s house they used to give one peah for the olive trees they had in every direction and for all carobs that saw one another. {NAME} said in the former’s name: also for all carob trees they had in the entire town.
[Peah 2:3.2] HALAKHAH: “Everything separates for seeds.” What is pressing down? It rises while pressing as in a mortar or must it press down on the fence? From the text “hair was pressing down,” the fence does not press. That means it presses down on the fence.
[Peah 2:3.3] {NAME} said: Sometimes they need to be inside four cubits and sometimes they need to be inside ten handbreadths if they are planted ten to a bet se‘ah . How do you understand this? They need to be within four cubits of the fence; the crowns have to be within ten handbreadths of one another if they are planted ten to a bet se‘ah .
[Peah 2:3.4] “But for carob trees all that see.” What defines the directions for them? The town defines the directions for them. {NAME} said, the family of Rebbi had four oil presses in the four directions of the town and their used to give for each oil press according to its direction.
[Peah 2:3.5] If there were three (groups of) trees, the outer ones see the middle ones, the middle ones see the outer ones, but the outer ones do not see one another, then one may give from the outer ones for the middle ones and from the middle ones for the outer ones but one may not give from the outer ones for the outer ones.
[Peah 2:4.1] MISHNAH: He who sows one species on his field gives one peah even though he works at two different threshing floors. If he sows two species, he gives two peot even though he threshes them together. He who sows two different kinds of wheat on his field gives one peah if he processes them together, two peot if he threshes them separately. It happened that {NAME} sowed before {NAME}; they ascended to the stone hall and asked. Naḥum the scribe said: I have the tradition from {NAME}, who received it from my father, who received it from the pairs, who received if from the prophets, a practice going back to Moses on Sinai, that he who sows two different kinds of wheat on his field gives one peah if he stores them together, two peot if he stores them separately.
[Peah 2:4.2] HALAKHAH: If he cut half the fine wheat and half the coarse wheat to process them together and then he changed his mind and processed them separately he cannot give from the fine wheat for the coarse either the first time or at the end. If he cut half the fine wheat and half the coarse wheat to process them separately and then he changed his mind and processed them together, he may give from the fine wheat at the end for the coarse wheat at the end, from the fine wheat the first time for the coarse wheat the first time. He gives from fine wheat for fine wheat if he finished harvesting his field, but if he did not finish harvesting, he may not give even from fine wheat for fine wheat. If he cut half the fine wheat and all the coarse wheat to process them together and he changed his mind and processed them separately then he gives from the fine wheat for the fine wheat and all the coarse wheat is exempted.
[Peah 2:4.3] {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: If you come to notice a practice of which you do not know the reason, do not push it aside as something alien since many practices were shown to Moses on Sinai and all of them were absorbed into the Mishnah. {NAME} said, that is correct! If Naḥum had not come and explained it to us about the two kinds of wheat, could we have known?
[Peah 2:4.4] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: ( Hos . 8:12 ) “I wrote down for him most of My teaching.” But was most of the Torah written down? Rather, more things are derived from what is written than what is (only) oral tradition. Is that so? But so it is: Things derived from what is transmitted orally are preferred over those written.
[Peah 2:4.5] {NAME} says: “I wrote down for him most of My teaching,” these are the admonitions. Nevertheless, is it not that ( Hos . 8:12 ) “they were considered foreign”.
[Peah 2:4.6] {NAME} said: If I had written down for you most of my teaching, would it not be considered Gentile? What is the difference between us and the Gentiles? These produce their books and those produce their books. These produce their parchments and those produce their parchments.
[Peah 2:4.7] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Things have been said orally and things have been said in writing, and we do not know which ones are preferred. From what is written ( Ex . 34:27 ): “By the mouth of these words I concluded a covenant with you and Israel;” it follows that the oral traditions are preferred.
[Peah 2:4.8] {NAME} and {NAME}. One said that if you kept what is oral tradition and kept what is written I will conclude a covenant with you, otherwise I shall not conclude a covenant with you. The other one said, if you watched all that is oral tradition and kept all that is written you will receive your reward, otherwise you will not receive any reward.
[Peah 2:4.9] {NAME} said: On them, and on them; all, like all; words, the words; Bible, Mishnah, Talmud, and Aggadah. Even what a competent student will discover before his teacher was said to Moses on Sinai. What is the reason? ( Eccl . 1:10 ) “There is something about which one would say, look, this is new!” His colleague will answer, “it already has been forever.”
[Peah 2:4.10] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: One makes inferences neither from practices, nor from homiletics, nor from extraneous sources, but only from study. {NAME} stated: The case of two kinds of wheat is the same as the case of two kinds of barley. {NAME} said, that was part of the original practice and it was forgotten: The case of two kinds of wheat is the same as the case of two kinds of barley. But did we not state ( Mishnah 3:3): “He who strips moist onions for the market and stores dry ones;” can you say about market and storage that this was of the original practice and was forgotten?
[Peah 2:4.11] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: One makes no inferences from a ruling. Everybody agrees that one makes no inferences from an action. {NAME} said to him, that means somebody who does not understand, but he who understands may act. He said to him, whether one understands or one does not understand, if there is a disagreement. But if there is no disagreement, whether one understands or one does not understand.
[Peah 2:5.1] MISHNAH: A field harvested by Gentiles or robbers, undermined by ants, ruined by a storm or animals, is free. If he harvested half of it and robbers harvested the other half, it is free since the obligation of produce is when it is standing. If robbers cut half of it and he harvested the other half, he must give peah from what he cut. If he harvested half and sold half, the buyer gives peah for everything. If he cut half and dedicated half, he who redeemed it from the treasurer gives peah for everything.
[Peah 2:5.2] HALAKHAH: The Mishnah, if they cut for themselves, but if they cut for a Jew it is obligated. And we have formulated regarding this: One does not hire Gentile workers because they do not know about gleanings.
[Peah 2:5.3] The Mishnah, if they cut to destroy it. But if they do not cut to destroy it, it is obligated. {NAME} said, even if you say that they do not cut to destroy it, it is free since peah is given from standing produce and real estate cannot be robbed.
[Peah 2:5.4] Because he separates from cut grain for standing grain and from standing grain for cut grain but he does not separate from cut grain for either cut or standing grain. Sometimes he has to separate from cut grain for standing grain. How can this be? If he finished his field and left something standing on it for peah , at the moment he cuts the first stalk from this, peah returns to the sheaves; he has to give from cut grain. Not only if he finished his field but even if he cut some and said: “From here and further on I give for peah ,” at the moment he cuts the first stalk from this, peah returns to the sheaves and he separates from cut grain for standing grain.
[Peah 2:5.5] May the seller get the peah which permits the sheaves? Let us hear it from the following (Mishnah 5:4): “ {NAME} said: When is this, if he received it for a half, a third, or a quarter.” What is the difference between this and the first case? It must be, “if you cut it, a third will be yours.” {NAME} said, this implies that the seller may get the peah which permits the sheaves. {NAME} said, there the obligation of the field did not come during his ownership, but here the obligation of the field started during his ownership. It is correct that if he cut half of the field and sold what he cut, the buyer is allowed gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and peah . May the buyer get the peah which permits the sheaves of the seller? That is the disagreement of Rebbi and {NAME}.
[Peah 2:5.6] {NAME} asked: Can a harvest outside of the Land become subject to peah ? Could you not say that a dedicated crop is exempt and (a crop) outside the Land is exempt; just as a dedicated crop may become obligated, so from outside the Land it may become obligated? He found it stated: ( Lev . 19:9 , 23:22 ) “When you harvest the harvest of your Land,” and not the harvest outside of the Land.
[Peah 2:5.7] If the treasurer cut half of the half but did not finish to harvest the rest before somebody redeemed everything, he gives from the harvest for what was harvested but all that was harvested in the possession of the Temple is already exempted.
[Peah 3:1.1] MISHNAH: Rectangles of grain between olive trees: The House of Shammai say, peah from each single one, the House of Hillel say, from one for all of them. They agree that one gives one peah for all of them if the edges of the rows are touching. If someone harvests his field in spots and leaves moist stalks, {NAME} says, peah from each spot, but the Sages say, from one for all of them. The Sages agree with {NAME} that he who sows dill or mustard at three different places gives peah from each spot.
[Peah 3:1.2] HALAKHAH: We have stated: “between olive trees.” In the House of Rebbi they stated “between fruit trees.” Our Mishnah needs the one of the House of Rebbi and that of the House of Rebbi needs our Mishnah. If we had stated, but not the House of Rebbi, we would say that it said only “between olive trees”, which in themselves are subject to peah , but for those which are free from the obligation of peah even the House of Shammai will agree that he gives one peah for all of them. Hence, our Mishnah needs that of Rebbi. Or if there were the declaration of the House of Rebbi but we had not stated ours, we would say that it refers only to those which are between trees free from the obligation of peah , but for trees which in themselves are subject to peah even the House of Hillel will agree that he gives peah from each single one. Hence, both our Mishnah and the baraita of the House of Rebbi are needed.
[Peah 3:1.3] What are we dealing with? If they are widely spaced, even the House of Shammai will agree that he gives one peah for all of them. If they are densely planted, the House of Hillel will agree that he gives peah from each single one. But we deal with the case of 10 plants on a bet se’ah . The House of Shammai compare it to widely spaced, the House of Hillel compare it to densely planted ones.
[Peah 3:1.4] What is the reason of the House of Shammai? People do not usually introduce seeds between trees. Does it turn out that the House of Shammai are like {NAME}? Just as {NAME} said that people do not usually introduce onions between vegetables, so the House of Shammai say that people do not usually introduce seeds between trees! It is reasonable to say that the House of Shammai will agree with {NAME} but {NAME} will not agree with the House of Shammai. The House of Shammai will agree with {NAME} that people do not usually introduce onions between vegetables. {NAME} will not agree with the House of Shammai because people usually introduce seeds between trees.
[Peah 3:1.5] If there was a fence there, it is like a tree. How about two?
[Peah 3:1.6] So far if they are combined from one side and the other. If they were combined only on one side, either by three coarse furrows or at any place?
[Peah 3:1.7] “He who harvests his field in spots,” etc. Like a spotted field; the place where fertilizer makes plants grow early is called “spotted.”
[Peah 3:1.8] So far if it was dry on both sides and moist in the middle. How about being moist on both sides and dry in the middle?
[Peah 3:1.9] {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: “{NAME} follows the argument of his teacher {NAME}. Just as {NAME} says that moist and dry are two different kinds, so {NAME} says that moist and dry are two different kinds.” The colleagues said before {NAME}: Why should he argue like {NAME}? He could argue even like the Rabbis since we have stated there ( Mishnah 3:3): “He who rips out moist onions for the market and keeps dry ones for storage!” {NAME} answered: We understand that market and storage make two kinds, are moist and dry two kinds?
[Peah 3:1.10] Two kinds, half moist and half dry, even {NAME} will agree. But did we not state: “The Sages agree with {NAME} that he who sows dill and mustard at three different places …” It is so: Either dill at three places or mustard at three places. {NAME} says, because the first one does not wait for the last one. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Because they usually are being sown bed by bed. According to {NAME}, he has to give from each stalk; according to {NAME} he has to give from each bed.
[Peah 3:2.1] MISHNAH: He who rips out moist onions for the market and keeps dry ones for storage gives peah for each batch separately; the same applies to peas and vineyards. He who thins out gives peah for what is left. He who rips out with one hand gives from the remainder for everything.
[Peah 3:2.2] HALAKHAH: It is stated: “In patches it is obligated at the beginning and at the end.” What is “in patches?” {NAME} said, just as we have stated: “He who rips out moist onions for the market and keeps dry ones for storage.” {NAME} said, for example nigella: If one sows it, it produces thin bulbs; if one plants seedlings, it produces large bulbs. For if it were not so, we would say because it is for sowing it should be freed from peah . But are wheat grains not also for sowing? Wheat is mostly for eating, that one is mostly for sowing. According to {NAME}, are vegetables subject to peah ? Its kind is collected for storage. How does {NAME} deal with it? It is finished and needs only to dry out.
[Peah 3:2.3] It was stated: ( Lev . 19:9 ) “The gathering of your harvest,” not the gathering of your plucking. {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: He who collects ears for his dough in any quantity is free from peah . {NAME} says, even with a sickle. {NAME} said, only if he left some standing. Did we not state ( Tosephta Peah 1:10 ): “If he had five vines and he harvested them and brought them into his house, he is free from fallen berries, from orlah , from the fourth year , but he is obligated for gleanings. {NAME} said, one for those which are fully ripe, one for those which are not fully ripe. {NAME} said, you may even say that both deal with the case that they are fully ripe, or both deal with the case that they are not fully ripe. There if he wanted to eat them as grapes, here if he wanted to make them into wine, he may do so. This is informed from that and that is informed from this. This is informed from that, if he wants to eat them as rubbed ears [he may do so] even if he did not leave a remainder. That is informed from this, if he wants to drink them as wine [he may do so] only if he left a remainder.
[Peah 3:2.4] “He who thins out gives peah for what is left.” It was stated ( Tosephta Peah 1:10 ): {NAME} said: When has this been said? If he thins for sale, but if he thins for his own use he gives from the remnant for everything. {NAME} said, that means, if he sowed thickly in order to thin later. But if he sowed thickly without intention to thin later, not only if he uses it for himself but even for the market he gives from the remnant for everything.

He said to them: When he reacquired them one by one. But did we not state: Even though one with a large harvest will not store the mother-onions, one with only a small harvest will. [Peah 3:4.1] MISHNAH: Brothers who split give two peot . When they later form a cooperative, they give one peah . Two people who together bought a tree give one peah . If one bought the North side and the other the South side, each gives peah for himself.
[Peah 3:4.2] HALAKHAH: If he harvested half a field in company [with his brother] and then they split up, he does not give from his own part either for the initial harvest or for the final one. When they changed their minds and after splitting formed a company and harvested half a field, and then separated again, he can give from his part at the end for his partner’s part at the end, but not from his part at the start for his partner’s part at the start.
[Peah 3:4.3] {NAME} said: If he wanted to cut half of his field and actually cut half of this half, but when he came to cut the other half he finished off his entire field, then he may give from the first cut on the intermediate ones and from the intermediate ones on the first but not from the first on the first. {NAME} said: If he had a field where half of it was one third ripe, the other half was not yet one third ripe, and by the time he finished harvesting half of the first half, the entire field also was one third ripe, he gives from the first cut on the intermediate ones and from the intermediate ones on the first but not from the first on the first.
[Peah 3:5.1] MISHNAH: He who sells tree trunks in his field gives peah from each single one. {NAME} says, when? If the owner of the field did not retain anything, but if he retained his field, he gives peah for all of them.
[Peah 3:5.2] HALAKHAH: So far when he started harvesting beforehand; even if he did not start to harvest? Let us understand it from the following ( Mishnah Ḥulin 11:2 ): “If he bought the shearings of another man’s sheep, if the seller retained anything, the seller is liable, otherwise the buyer is liable.” {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: This is {NAME}. Is there a difference? There, both if he started to shear or if he did not start to shear, and here there will be no difference whether he started harvesting beforehand or did not start beforehand.
[Peah 3:5.3] What is the reason of {NAME}? Because the obligation of the harvest falls on the standing grain? Or because he sold to him, excluding his obligation? Let us understand it from the following: “If he bought the shearings of another man’s sheep, if the seller retained anything, the seller is liable, otherwise the buyer is liable.” {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: This is {NAME}. Could you say there that the obligation of the harvest falls on the standing grain? No, it is because he sold to him, excluding his obligation! And here also it is because he sold to him, excluding his obligation.
[Peah 3:5.4] What is the difference between them? If the buyer transgressed and separated peah . If you say, it is because the obligation of the harvest falls on the standing grain, what he gave he gave. But if you say that because he sold to him, excluding his obligation, he gave and may collect money from him. If the part of the seller burned, if it is because the obligation of the harvest falls on the standing grain, if it is burned it is burned. But if you say that because he sold to him, excluding his obligation, if it is burned he may collect money from him.
[Peah 3:6.1] MISHNAH: {NAME} says, a plot of a bet rova ‘ is obligated for peah . {NAME} says, if its yield is two seah . {NAME} says, six by six hand-breadths 109 . {NAME} said, if it is enough to cut and cut a second time; practice follows his words.
[Peah 3:6.2] HALAKHAH: What is the reason of {NAME}? It says here “your field” and it says about kilaim “your field”. Just as “your field” mentioned there means a bet rova ‘, so here it means bet rova ‘. What is the reason of {NAME}? It says here “your field” and it says further on ( Deut . 24:19 ): “You might forget a sheaf on the field.” Just as the field mentioned there means two, so here also two. What is the reason of {NAME}? Six by six from a vegetable patch. “{NAME} says, if it is enough to cut and cut a second time, and practice follows his words.” Does “harvesting” mean following the technique of harvesters, or is it any amount? Since it is written ( Ps . 129:7 ): “The harvester did not fill his palm with it, nor the binder of sheaves his bosom,” that means that one follows the technique of harvesters.
[Peah 3:7.1] MISHNAH: {NAME} says: Any real estate is subject to peah and first fruits, to write a prozbol based on it, and to acquire simultaneously non-guaranteed property with money or contract or possession. If someone signs over his properties when bedridden and reserved for himself any real estate, his gift is permanent; if he did not reserve any real estate for himself, his gift is not permanent. If he signs over his properties to his sons and signs over some real estate for his wife, she lost her ketubah . {NAME} says, if she accepted it, even if it was not in a written document, she lost her ketubah .
[Peah 3:7.2] HALAKHAH: {NAME} asked in the name of {NAME}: Think of it, if there were only one ear! Before he cut, there was no obligation; after he cut, there will be nothing left! {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Explain it if there was one stalk with five ears!
[Peah 3:7.3] {NAME} asked: Why does he not say: “Any crop is subject to peah ?” But because he has to enunciate first fruits he formulates it as “real estate.”
[Peah 3:7.4] It was stated: “And the appearance.” {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: He who owns no real estate is freed from the appearance. {NAME} asked: And why do we not say: He who has no real estate is freed from the declaration, since it is written ( Deut . 26:15 ): “From the land that You gave us.” {NAME} taught a tradition in the name of {NAME}: “He who has no real estate is freed from the declaration, since it is written: From the land that You gave us.”
[Peah 3:7.5] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: He who has no real estate is free from the appearance since it is said ( Ex . 34:24 ): “Nobody will illegally desire your land.” It happened that one person left his grain heap; when he returned, he found lions surrounding it. It happened that one left a chicken coop; when he returned, he found torn cats before it. One man left his house open; when he came, he found a snake rolled up on its tail. {NAME} told the following story: Two brothers in Askalon had Gentile neighbors. These said, if those Jews go up to Jerusalem, we will take all they have. When they went up, the Holy One, praise to Him, alotted to them two angels who came and went in their likeness. When they returned, they sent them valuable presents. They said to them: where have you been? They said to them, in Jerusalem. They said to them: Whom did you leave in your house? They said, nobody. They said: Praised be the God of the Jews Who did not let us act and did not abandon them!
[Peah 3:7.6] From where that non-guaranteed property may be acquired with guaranteed property, by money, document, or possession? {NAME} in the name of {NAME}; {NAME}, {NAME} Tortaya in the name of {NAME}, it is written ( 2Chr . 21:3 ): “Their father gave them many gifts, silver and gold and delicacies, with fortified cities in Jehudah.” So far real estate and movables were at the same place. If real estate was at one place and movables elsewhere? {NAME} said, let us hear from the following: {NAME} said to them, it happened that a man from Madon was in Jerusalem, rich in movables. He wanted to distribute them, to give them as gifts. They said to him, you cannot do that except if you acquire real estate. What did he do? He went and bought a rock near Jerusalem and said: The Northern part I give to X with a hundred amphoras of wine, the Southern part I give to Y with a hundred amphoras of oil. The matter came before the Sages and they upheld his words. {NAME} said before {NAME}: But was he not bedridden? For in general a person might give property rights only in writing, and here even orally. In general, a person might give only if real estate and movables are at the same place, but here the real estate even was at one place and the movables elsewhere. He said to him: But is there a difference for {NAME}? The sick person for {NAME} is like the healthy person for the rabbis.
[Peah 3:7.7] There, we have stated: “Any real estate is subject to peah and first fruits.” What is the use of “any” real estate? {NAME} said, explain it if it had space for one stalk but a pearl was hidden in it.
[Peah 3:7.8] Who is bedridden? Anyone who did not get sick suddenly. It is customary for the relatives to visit him immediately; unrelated persons visit him after three days. If he falls ill suddenly, everybody visits him immediately. A clarification: {NAME}, {NAME}, and {NAME} went to visit {NAME} after three days. He said to them: Do you want to sustain the baraita in my case?
[Peah 3:7.9] “If he reserved any real estate for himself, his gift is permanent,” even if he did not recover. “If he did not reserve any real estate for himself, his gift is not permanent” if he did recover.
[Peah 3:7.10] {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of Rav: They declared oral instructions by a bedridden person equal to written and delivered ones by a healthy person, on condition that he had died from that particular sickness and that he describes the property and says, give field X to Y. If he says, half of the field to X and half to Y, is that designated? Or only if he says: the Northern half, the Southern half?

Why did he write it with an obligation of acquisition, in order to give it the status of a gift by a healthy person.

Everybody agrees that if his first master was an Israel, he may not eat terumah ; maybe the giver will recuperate.
[Peah 3:7.14] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}, a baraita supports {NAME} and {NAME}: “ A healthy person who wrote a will and a bedridden one who wrote a gift document may change their minds.” A healthy person who wrote a will may change his mind, even as long as he is healthy. Similarly, a bedridden person who wrote a gift document may change his mind, even while he still is bedridden.
[Peah 3:7.15] What is a will? “It should be granted to me to live and get up from bed, but if I should die, my properties should be given to X.” What is a gift? “All my properties are given as a gift to X from now on,” or it must be written: “as of today.”

[Peah 4:1.1] MISHNAH: Peah is given connected to the ground. From a climbing vine and a date palm, the owner brings it down and divides it up among the poor. {NAME} says, also for smooth nut trees. Even if 99 poor people say to distribute and one says to grab, one listens to him whose request is in keeping with practice. But for a climbing vine and a date palm it is not so; even if 99 say to grab and one says to distribute, one listens to him whose request is in keeping with practice.
[Peah 4:1.2] HALAKHAH: ( Lev . 23:22 ) “Do not finish off the corner of your field during your harvest.” This shows that peah is given standing on the ground. One might think this also includes climbing vine and date palms, but the verse says “harvest.” Harvest is special in that a small person can do it as well as a tall person; this excludes climbing vine and date palm where a small person cannot do it as well as a tall person.
[Peah 4:1.3] Some want to understand it from the verse ( Lev . 19:10 , 23:22 ) “abandon,” put before them grain in its straw, fenugreek in bundles, dates in brooms. I might think that this also includes climbing vine and date palms, but the verse says “them.” What argument do you have to include these and to exclude those? After the verse included, it excluded. I include those that are not dangerous and exclude those that are dangerous.
[Peah 4:1.4] Is it not connected? He calls it by the name peah when it is on the tree. If you say not from standing produce, he calls it by the name peah when it is taken down. If you say he calls it by the name peah when it is on the tree, the removal is charged to the poor. If you say he calls it by the name peah when it is taken down, the removal is the obligation of the owner. But even if you say that he calls it by the name peah when it is on the tree, they charge the owner with taking it down because of the danger.
[Peah 4:1.5] It was stated in the name of {NAME}: All trees are dangerous. Does {NAME} not infer from “harvest” while the rabbis likewise infer from “harvest?” Everybody infers from “harvest”, except that {NAME} says that all trees are dangerous and the rabbis say only the climbing vine and the date palm are dangerous. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: It has happened that five brothers died climbing five smooth nut trees.
[Peah 4:1.6] If the owner called it peah and nevertheless finished harvesting the entire field, I read for him: “Do not finish off the corner of your field during your harvest.” If he did not call it peah and finished harvesting the entire field, I read for him: “Do not finish off the corner of your field during your harvest.”
[Peah 4:1.7] If they agreed among themselves, even so one does not listen to him.

[Peah 4:3.6] It was stated in the name of {NAME}: For five reasons one should give peah only at the end of one’s field, because of robbing the poor, because of idling the poor, because of cheats, because of bad impression, and because the Torah said ( Lev . 19:9 ): “Do not finish off the corner of your field.” Because of robbing the poor, that no man should see a free hour and say to his poor relative: Come, and take this peah for yourself. Because of idling the poor, that the poor should not sit around, watch the entire day, and say: Now he is giving peah , now he is giving peah , but rather they should go, collect on another field, and come at the moment of finishing. Because of the cheats, that one should not say: I already gave, and then he chooses the good and brings out the bad. Because of bad impression, that the passers-by should not say: Look, this man harvested his field and did not leave peah for the poor. And because the Torah said: “Do not finish off the corner of your field.”

[Peah 5:2.1] MISHNAH: : A single ear on the field to be harvested and its head reaches to the grain that is still standing, if it can be cut together with standing grain, it belongs to the owner, otherwise it is for the poor. An ear of gleanings that was mixed up in a stack of grain, he gives tithes for one ear and gives it to him. {NAME} said, how can the poor man exchange something that never was in his possession? But he has to give the poor rights to the entire stack; then he gives tithes for one ear and gives it to him.
[Peah 5:2.2] HALAKHAH: What is standing grain that saves standing grain? {NAME} said, the same as we have stated: a single ear on the field to be harvested and its head reaches to the standing grain. {NAME} said, only if the harvested field surrounds it, and only if its head reaches the standing grain, and only if it can be cut together with standing grain. If it can be cut together with standing grain but standing grain cannot be cut with it, it is saved. If there were two, the inner one can be cut together with the outermost standing grain, but the outer one cannot be cut with the standing grain; the inner one is saved and saves.
[Peah 5:2.3] {NAME} said, when I was mashing olives with {NAME}, he said to me: Any olive that you can reach when stretching out your hand is not forgotten. {NAME} said, if he passed it over and forgot it, it is forgotten. The Mishnah disagrees with {NAME}: A single ear on the field to be harvested and its head reaches to the grain. Can you not stretch out your hand and take a single ear on the harvested field? {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: They said that about the second row.
[Peah 5:2.4] Can something that is apt to be saved but was forgotten become legally forgotten? Let us hear from the following: “When he removed the first, second, and third sheaves but forgot the fourth, some state: If he took away the fifth one, it (the fourth) becomes legally forgotten, but some state: If he waited long enough that he could have taken away the fifth one, it becomes legally forgotten.” {NAME} said, he who says, “if he removed the fifth one,” (speaks of the case) where there is a sixth one, but he who says, “if he waited long enough that he could have removed the fifth one,” (speaks of the case) where there is no sixth one. Before he took away the fifth one, would not the fourth one be apt to be considered starting a row? That means that something that is apt to be saved but was forgotten can become legally forgotten.
[Peah 5:2.5] Can something that is apt to save but was forgotten become legally forgotten? Let us hear from the following: “One seah of cut grain and one seah of uncut grain.” Here the cut grain should save the uncut grain. That means that something that is apt to save, but was forgotten, can become legally forgotten. {NAME} said, explain it if he was cutting and removing the sheaves row by row. He already forgot the standing grain before he might forget the sheaves.
[Peah 5:2.6] How does he do it? He brings two ears and says: If this one is gleanings, all is fine; but if not, then its tithes are contained in the other one, and he gives him the first one. Do we not have to worry that the one used to contain tithes in it was gleanings? {NAME} said, he brings two ears and says: If this one is gleanings, all is fine; but if not, then its tithes are contained in the other one, and he gives him one of them.
[Peah 5:2.7] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}, this follows {NAME}, as we have stated there: “For {NAME} says that everything whose replacement is in the hand of the Cohen is freed from the obligatory gifts, but {NAME} obligates him.” {NAME} said, the words of {NAME} imply that he has to empower the priest. {NAME} said, the statement of {NAME} contradicts {NAME} since we have stated here: “He has to give the poor rights to the entire stack; then he gives tithes for one ear and gives to him.” {NAME} said, the words of {NAME} imply that he has to empower the priest, hence this is not from the words of {NAME}. {NAME} said, the Mishnah itself testifies that it is by {NAME}. The first Tanna wants to say that he transfers as property to the poor not the entire stack but only one ear. The other Tanna wants to say that he transfers the entire stack as property to the poor. The first Tanna wants to say that this is like the transfer of property from one’s right hand to his left hand; it is no transfer. The other Tanna wants to say that it is not transferring property from one’s right hand to his left hand; it is transfer.
[Peah 5:2.8] {NAME} stated: {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: The reasoning of {NAME} is inverted! There he makes him acquire, and here he says thus? He answered “according to your reasoning,” in your reasoning that you say it is by exchange. “How can the poor man exchange something that never was in his possession? But he has to give the poor man rights to the entire stack; then he gives tithes for one ear and gives to him.”
[Peah 5:3.1] MISHNAH: One does not use a waterwheel with buckets, the words of {NAME}. But the Sages do permit it, because it is impossible. A householder wandering from one place to another who was in need of taking gleanings, forgotten sheaves, peah , and tithes of the poor should repay them once he comes home, the words of {NAME}. But the Sages say, he was poor at that moment.
[Peah 5:3.2] HALAKHAH: It was stated: He who waters his field before a poor person had entered it, if his potential loss is greater than the poor man’s, it is permitted, but if the poor man’s loss is greater than his, it is prohibited. {NAME} says, in both cases he deposits them on the fence and the poor man comes and takes what is his.
[Peah 5:3.3] The reasoning of {NAME} is inverted: There, he says that just as he prunes for himself, so he prunes for the poor; but here he says thus! There, they caused it for themselves since they did not come, but here they came.
[Peah 5:3.4] The reasoning of the rabbis is inverted: There, they say if his potential loss is greater than the poor’s, and here they say thus! There, it is possible, but here it is impossible.
[Peah 5:3.5] Now {NAME} says, one does not use the water wheel, and one estimates the loss to the owner. Now the rabbis say, one uses the water wheel and estimates the loss to the poor. To whom does he pay? {NAME} said, to the poor of his place, because otherwise, what could we say? {NAME} said, it is needed for the measure of justice.
[Peah 5:4.1] MISHNAH: If he switches with the poor, what he receives is exempt but what the poor get is obligated. If two persons received a field as sharecroppers, one gives his part and his tithes of the poor to the other one, and vice-versa. He who receives a field to harvest is barred from its gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and peah . {NAME} said, when is this so? When he received it for one-half, one third, or one quarter; but if he told him, one third of what you will harvest will be yours, he may take gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and peah but not the tithes of the poor.
[Peah 5:4.2] HALAKHAH: It is stated: A father and his son, a man and his relative, two brothers, two associates redeem Second Tithe for one another and give tithe of the poor to one another. {NAME} said, a curse should come upon him who gives tithe of the poor to his father. He said, why? If they were both poor!
[Peah 5:4.3] What is the difference between this and the first case? It must be “if you cut it, a third will be yours.” {NAME} said, that implies that the seller may get the peah which permits the sheaves. {NAME} said, there the obligation of the field did come during his ownership, but here the obligation of the field did not come during his ownership.
[Peah 5:4.4] {NAME} said, there is a difference for gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and peah because they have to be abandoned.
[Peah 5:5.1] MISHNAH: If someone sells his field, the seller is permitted but the buyer is barred. Nobody should hire a worker on condition that his son may collect gleanings after him. He who does not let the poor collect gleanings, or who lets one person collect but not the other, or helps one of them, robs the poor. On him it was said ( Prov. 22:28 , 23:10 ): “Do not displace an eternal boundary.”
[Peah 5:5.2] HALAKHAH: Our Mishnah is about someone who sold the field with the standing crop. But if someone sold the standing crop and retained the field for himself, for him I read “your field”, for the other one I read “your harvest.”
[Peah 5:5.3] “By doing so, he robs the poor.” The owner who does that robs the poor. The worker who does that robs the owner and the poor, and about him it was said: “Do not displace an eternal boundary.”
[Peah 5:5.4] {NAME} and {NAME}, one said these are the ones who came up from Egypt, the other said these are the ones who lost their property; a blind man is called “plenty of light.” {NAME} said, ( Is. 58:7 ) “degraded poor you shall bring to your house.” {NAME} said, if you do this, I will credit it to you as if you had presented First Fruits in the Temple. It says here, “you shall bring,” and it says there ( Ex. 23:19 ): “The first fruits of your land you shall bring to the Eternal’s Temple.”
[Peah 5:6.1] MISHNAH: A sheaf forgotten by the workers but not by the owner, by the owner but not by the workers, or the poor stood before it or covered it with straw, is not a forgotten sheaf.
[Peah 5:6.2] HALAKHAH: A sheaf forgotten by the workers but not by the owner is not a forgotten sheaf since it is written ( Deut. 24:19 ): “When you harvest and you forget.” If the owner forgot but the workers did not, it is not a forgotten sheaf since it is written: “When you are harvesting and you forget.” {NAME} says in the name of {NAME}: Even if donkey drivers passing by on the road saw a sheaf forgotten by the workers but not by the owner, it is not a forgotten sheaf unless everybody forgot it.
[Peah 5:6.3] If he stood in town and said: I know that the workers are forgetting sheaves at place X; if they forgot it is not a forgotten sheaf. If he stood on the field and said: I know that the workers are forgetting sheaves at place X; [if they forgot] it is a forgotten sheaf, since it says ( Deut. 24:19 ): “On your field and you forget a sheaf.” On the field you forget, but in town you do not forget. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: The same holds in regard to found objects. Where are we holding? If he may touch it, in the city, even inside his field. {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Only if he can touch them, even inside his field.
[Peah 5:6.4] If it was completely covered by straw? Let us hear from the following: “The blind who forgot makes a forgotten sheaf.” Is a blind person not like a sheaf completely covered by straw? {NAME} said, if he remembered the straw. {NAME} position is parallel to {NAME}; just as {NAME} said, if he remembers the upper one, so {NAME} said, if he remembered the straw.
[Peah 5:7.1] MISHNAH: He who makes sheaves as helmets, round bundles, wheels, and small sheaves is not subject to the law of forgotten sheaves. If he takes them from there to the threshing-floor, the rules on forgotten sheaves apply. If he makes sheaves for a stack, it is subject to the rules on forgotten sheaves. If he takes them from there to the threshing-floor, the rules on forgotten sheaves do not apply. This is the principle: Everybody who makes sheaves for a place that is the end of his work is subject to the rule on forgotten sheaves, from there to the threshing-floor is not subject to the rule on forgotten sheaves. To a place that is not the end of his work it is not subject to the rule on forgotten sheaves, from there to the threshing-floor is subject to the rule on forgotten sheaves.
[Peah 5:7.2] HALAKHAH: {NAME} says, from the top, as you say ( 1Sam. 17:5 ): “A brass helmet on his head.” Round bundles, {NAME} said, from the bottom, as you say ( Deut. 32:34 ): “It is hidden with me.” חֲרָרָה a wheel. Small sheaves, {NAME} said ( Deut. 24:19 ): “When you will be harvesting the harvest of your field and you forget a sheaf on the field,” just as harvest has no other harvest after it, so too a sheaf, which has no other sheaf-making after it.
[Peah 6:1.1] MISHNAH: The House of Shammai say, property abandoned to the poor is abandoned, but the House of Hillel say, it is not abandoned unless it is abandoned also to the rich, as in a Sabbatical year. If all sheaves of a field are of one qab each, except one which is of four qab and they forgot about that one, the House of Shammai say, it cannot be a forgotten sheaf, but the House of Hillel say, it can be a forgotten sheaf.
[Peah 6:1.2] HALAKHAH: {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: The reason of the House of Shammai ( Lev. 19:10 , 23:22 ) “for the poor and the sojourner.” Why does the verse say, “relinquish them”? There is another relinquishing like this one. Just as this one is for the poor and not the rich, also what is spoken of elsewhere is for the poor and not for the rich.
[Peah 6:1.3] {NAME} said, the reason of the House of Hillel, ( Ex. 23:11 ) “let drop,” why does the verse say, “and abandon it”? There is another abandoning like this one. Just as this one is for poor and rich alike, also what is spoken of elsewhere is for poor and rich alike.
[Peah 6:1.4] How do the House of Hillel deal with the reason of the House of Shammai? “Relinquish them ” is a restriction, these are for the poor, not for the rich, but what is spoken of elsewhere is for poor and rich alike. How do the House of Shammai deal with the reason of the House of Hillel? “Let it drop and abandon it ” is a restriction, this abandoning is for poor and rich alike, but what is spoken of elsewhere is for the poor but not for the rich. {NAME} said, the Mishnah supports {NAME}: “Abandoned also to the rich, as in the Sabbatical year.”
[Peah 6:1.5] Property abandoned to animals but not to humans, to Gentiles but not to Jews, to rich but not to poor, everybody agrees that it does not have the status of abandoned property. For humans but not for animals, for Jews but not for Gentiles, for the poor of one town but not for the poor of any other town is a disagreement between {NAME} and {NAME}. In the opinion of {NAME}, this abandoning is legal abandoning. In the opinion of {NAME}, this abandoning is not legal abandoning. {NAME} said, they disagree explicitly: {NAME} said, this abandoning is legal abandoning. {NAME} said, this abandoning is not legal abandoning.
[Peah 6:1.6] {NAME} said, that which was said, if it was abandoned to the poor but grabbed by the rich is a difference between {NAME} and {NAME}. According to {NAME}, who asserts that [it is legally abandoned] as soon as a person abandons anything from his property, [in our case] it is legally abandoned. According to {NAME}, who says that nothing may leave the hands of its owners except if it is taken up [by another person, in our case] it is not legally abandoned.
[Peah 6:1.7] So far, if he abandoned it for a longer period of time. But if he abandoned only for a short time? Let us hear from the following: “If he abandoned his field, he may cancel his action during two or three days.” {NAME} Dima stated before {NAME}: Even after three he may cancel his action. He said to him, since you say after three days, is it the same after three or after many? The language of a baraitha supports {NAME}: “About when is this said? If he abandoned in an unspecified way. But if he said: My field shall be abandoned one day, one week, one month, one year, a sabbatical period, as long as nobody took it over, either he or another person, he may cancel. But after somebody acquired it, either he or somebody else, he cannot cancel.” This means that short or long periods are the same. It also means that they were not worried about dishonesty. That obviously answers {NAME} question, since {NAME} had said, are short and long times the same?
[Peah 6:1.8] What are we discussing? If it should be recognizable, two would be enough. If for a row, three would be enough. One scholar quoted this statement by {NAME} before {NAME}: Anything he can split and make into a row following the House of Shammai. {NAME}: That goes by proportionality; “if all sheaves of a field are of one qab each, except one which is of four qab and they forgot about that one,” if all sheaves of a field are of two qab each, except one which is of eight qab .
[Peah 6:2.1] MISHNAH: A sheaf that was near a closure, a stack, cattle, or vessels, if it was forgotten, the House of Shammai say, it is not a forgotten sheaf, but the House of Hillel say, it is a forgotten sheaf.
[Peah 6:2.2] HALAKHAH: It is difficult about the House of Shammai; closure and stack are definite things, and they say it is not a forgotten sheaf. It is difficult about the House of Hillel; cattle and vessels are not definite things, and they say it is a forgotten sheaf.
[Peah 6:2.3] “By its place, if it was standing beside the wine press or beside a breach in the fence.” This Mishnah follows the House of Shammai, since the House of Shammai say, it is not a forgotten sheaf. {NAME} said, it is everybody’s opinion. There a stationary object is beside a stationary one, but here a movable object is beside a stationary one.
[Peah 6:2.4] {NAME} said: I asked {NAME}, about which sheaves do the Houses of Shammai and Hillel disagree? He said to me, this is the teaching: The sheaf which was near a closure, a stack, cattle, or vessels, if it was forgotten, the House of Shammai say it is a forgotten sheaf, but the House of Hillel say it is not a forgotten sheaf. But when I came to {NAME}, he told me that the Houses of Shammai and Hillel did not disagree that a sheaf near a closure, a stack, cattle, or vessels, if it was forgotten, was a forgotten sheaf. What did they disagree about? About a sheaf he took up and put beside a closure, beside a stack, beside cattle, beside vessels, and forgot about it; in that case the House of Shammai say it is not a forgotten sheaf because he already acquired rights to it. But the House of Hillel say it is a forgotten sheaf. And when I came and lectured about these things before {NAME}, he said to me, by the Covenant, these are the words that had been spoken to Moses on Horeb.
[Peah 6:2.5] There we have stated: “A woman who inherited property before she was betrothed, the Houses of Shammai and Hillel both are of the opinion that she may sell or give away and her actions are valid. If she inherited after she was betrothed, the House of Shammai say, she may sell, but the House of Hillel say, she may not sell.” {NAME} asked before {NAME}, why did we not state it with the leniencies of the House of Shammai and the stringencies of the House of Hillel? He said to him, the Mishnaiot come only for circumstances that are either stringent on both sides or lenient on both sides. But here it is a stringency on one side and a leniency on the other side. But did we not state: “The House of Shammai say, property abandoned to the poor is abandoned?” Is this not lenient for the poor and stringent for the householder, and it was stated! It is lenient for the poor and not stringent for the householder, since it was abandoned by his intent. He said to him, did we not state: “The sheaf that was near a closure, a stack, cattle, or vessels, if it was forgotten,” is this not lenient for the householder and stringent for the poor, and it was stated! He said to him, it is lenient for the householder but not stringent for the poor, because they did not acquire it yet. You may also say here, it is lenient for the woman and not stringent for the husband since he did not yet acquire property rights to it. He said to him, since he became betrothed to her, the inheritance fell to both of them.
[Peah 6:2.6] {NAME} said, they argued before {NAME}: Because betrothed she is his wife and married she is his wife; just as the sale by the latter is void, the sale by the former also should be void. He said to them, we are ashamed of the new ones, now you want to roll old ones over us! The new ones, after nissuïn , the old ones before nissuïn , when she was married in the second ceremony.
[Peah 6:3.1] MISHNAH: Heads of rows, the sheaf next to it proves, and a sheaf that was taken up to be brought to town and then was forgotten, they all agree that they never are forgotten sheaves. The following describe heads of rows: Two who started in the middle of the row, one turned North and the other turned South, and they forgot before them or after them. The one before them is a forgotten sheaf, the one after them is not a forgotten sheaf. A single person who started at the head of a row and forgot before and after himself. The one before him is not a forgotten sheaf, but the one after him is a forgotten sheaf because it falls under ( Deut . 24:19 ) “do not return to take it.” This is the principle: Anything that falls under “do not return to take it,” is a forgotten sheaf, but anything that does not fall under “do not return to take it,” is not a forgotten sheaf.
[Peah 6:3.2] HALAKHAH: From where about heads of rows? {NAME} said, it is written ( Deut. 24:19 ): “When you are harvesting your harvest on your field and you forget,” what you harvest you can forget. That refers to the start of rows of standing grain. End of rows of standing grain? {NAME} said, “do not return to take it.” From the place you came from you should not return to take it. So far, about starts of rows of sheaves, ends of rows of sheaves? {NAME} said, we learn starts of rows of sheaves from starts of rows of standing grain and ends of rows of standing grain from ends of rows of sheaves.
[Peah 6:3.3] “The sheaf next to it proves.” How is that? ( Tosephta Peah 3:4 ): “If he had ten rows of ten sheaves each and he removed one row of them in a North-South direction; when he forgot one of them it is not forgotten because it is considered East-West.” When he then removed the sheaves East-West and forgot one of them, let us hear from the following: When he removed the first, second, and third sheaves but forgot the fourth, some state: If he removed the fifth, it becomes legally forgotten, but some state: If he waited long enough that he could have removed the fifth, it becomes legally forgotten. {NAME} said, he who says, “if he removed the fifth” if there is a sixth, but he who says, “if he waited long enough that he could have removed the fifth” if there is no sixth. Before he took away the fifth, would not the fourth be apt to be considered starting a row? If this is named “forgotten,” then also in our case it is “forgotten.”
[Peah 6:3.4] If there was an oversize sheaf and he removed a sheaf from the outside next to the inside, it is considered a row. If he removed from the inside next to the outside, may it be considered a row? If he removed from the top beside the bottom it is considered a row. If he removed from the bottom beside the top, is it considered a row?
[Peah 6:3.5] When Rav descended there, he declared: I am this place’s {NAME}. There came an old man and asked him, two slain people, one on top of the other? Rav was of the opinion that one breaks the neck. He told him, one does not break the neck. He asked him, why? He said to him, not the lower one for he is hidden, not the upper one because he floats. When he ascended here, he came to Rebbi, who told him: He told you correctly, “if he is found,” and not “if they are found.”
[Peah 6:3.6] The great {NAME} said: If a water canal crossed the entire field, if he has to lift the plough on one side and put it on the other side, it is not considered one row, otherwise it is considered one row. If he cut half a row and came back the next day it is considered a row, when he sat down to eat, when he sat down to sleep, when his friend called him, when it got dark.
[Peah 6:3.7] “ A sheaf he took to bring to town, put it on another one, and forgot about both, the lower one is a forgotten sheaf but the upper one is not a forgotten sheaf. {NAME} said, neither of them is a forgotten sheaf; not the lower one because it is covered and not the upper one because he already had acquired it.” {NAME} said, if he remembers. {NAME} parallels {NAME}, just as {NAME} said, if he remembers the straws, so {NAME} said, if he remembers the upper one.
[Peah 6:3.8] ( Tosephta Peah 3:4 ) “A field whose sheaves are mixed up, if one was forgotten it is not a forgotten sheaf until he removes all around it.”
[Peah 6:4.1] MISHNAH: Two sheaves may qualify as forgotten sheaves, three may not. Two heaps of olives or carob may qualify as “forgotten sheaves”, three may not. Two plants of hemp may qualify as “forgotten sheaves”, three may not. Two berries may qualify as dropped berries, three may not. Two stalks may be gleanings, three may not, following the House of Hillel. About all of these, the House of Shammai say three are for the poor and four for the proprietor.
[Peah 6:4.2] HALAKHAH: {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If he made them like a Gamma (Γ).
[Peah 6:4.3] He said only “heaps”, not olives. What is the difference between heaps and olives? Heaps are the end of the harvest, single olives are not the end of the harvest.
[Peah 6:4.4] {NAME} said, when I was mashing olives with {NAME}, he said to me: Any olive you can reach when stretching out your hand is not forgotten. {NAME} said, if he passed it over and forgot it, it is forgotten.
[Peah 6:4.5] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Half a bunch of grapes are dropped berries. {NAME} stated: Half a bunch of grapes or an entire bunch are dropped berries. But did we not state: “Two berries are dropped berries?” {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If he cuts and deposits them under the vine.
[Peah 6:4.6] If they are made like a shepherd’s flute? Menahem in the name of {NAME}: Only if he cuts them equally.
[Peah 6:4.7] {NAME} said, the reason of the House of Shammai ( Deut. 24:19 , 20 , 21 ): “It shall belong to the stranger, the orphan, and the widow.” The reason of the House of Hillel ( Lev. 19:10 ): “For the poor and the stranger.” {NAME} said, both of them explained the same verse, “it shall belong to the stranger, the orphan, and the widow.” The House of Shammai say, for the poor, and the House of Hillel say, for the proprietor.
[Peah 6:5.1] MISHNAH: A sheaf containing two seah that was forgotten is not a “forgotten sheaf.” Two sheaves that together are two seah , {NAME} says, they are for the proprietor, but the Sages say, they are for the poor. {NAME} said to them: Does large size of the sheaves increase or decrease the power of the proprietor? They said to him, it increases it. He said to them: Since a sheaf containing two seah that was forgotten is not “forgotten sheaf,” it is only logical that two sheaves that together are two seah should not be “forgotten sheaf” either. They said to him, if they said that about one sheaf that is like a stack, do you want to say the same about two sheaves that are like bundles? Standing produce of two seah which was forgotten is not “forgotten sheaf.” If it does not have two seah but it might bring two seah , even if it were oats it is considered like barley grains.
[Peah 6:5.2] HALAKHAH: {NAME} said, it is written ( Deut. 24:19 ): “When you are harvesting your harvest on your field and you forget a sheaf on the field,” a sheaf to which you may stretch out your hand and take it. Some Tannaïm stated: “And you forget a sheaf,” but not a stack.
[Peah 6:5.3] How does it work out? If he forgot one sheaf next to it, if you make it a sheaf, everybody agrees that it is “forgotten sheaf.” If you make it a stack, a difference between Shammai and Hillel. If he forgot two sheaves, if you make it sheaves, a difference between the Houses of Shammai and Hillel; if you make it a stack it will not be considered a row.
[Peah 6:5.4] {NAME} said ( Deut. 24:19 ): “When you are harvesting your harvest on your field and you forget a sheaf on the field ,” a sheaf containing two seah that was forgotten is not “forgotten sheaf.” Standing produce containing two seah that was forgotten is not “forgotten sheaf.” {NAME} said, considering only the ears. If they were thin, one looks at them as if they were long, if they were scorched, one looks at them as if they were full.
[Peah 6:6.1] MISHNAH: Standing produce saves sheaves and standing produce. But a sheaf saves neither sheaves nor standing produce. What is standing produce that saves sheaves? Everything that is not forgotten, even if it is only one stalk. A seah of uprooted grain and a seah of not uprooted grain, also trees, garlic and onions do not combine. {NAME} says, if a poor man’s right comes in the middle, they do not combine, otherwise they do combine.
[Peah 6:6.2] HALAKHAH: {NAME} said, it is written ( Deut. 24:19 ): “When you are harvesting your harvest on your field and you forget a sheaf on the field ,” a sheaf surrounded by harvest and not a sheaf surrounded by standing produce. And why a sheaf surrounded by harvest and not a sheaf surrounded by standing produce? Under a sheaf surrounded by harvest is the field, under a sheaf surrounded by standing produce is straw.
[Peah 6:6.3] It was stated: “The standing produce of his neighbor saves his own, the standing produce of a Gentile saves that of a Jew, the standing wheat saves barley, the words of Rebbi. But the Sages say, only his own produce saves and only its own kind.”
[Peah 6:6.4] {NAME} stated: Just as standing produce saves the sheaf, so the sheaf saves the standing produce. This is logical: If standing produce, on which the power of the poor is enhanced, saves if any of it was forgotten, it is only logical that the sheaf should save, since on it the power of the poor is reduced. Rebbi answered him: If standing produce, on which the power of the poor is enhanced, saves if any of it was forgotten, is it logical that the sheaf, on which the power of the poor is reduced, if any of it was forgotten should save? From the words of both of them we infer that sheaf is saved by sheaf, but standing produce is not saved by standing produce.
[Peah 6:6.5] Hence, if he forgot, is it “forgotten sheaf”? Explain it if he forgot the standing produce first.
[Peah 6:6.6] Hence, if all is cut it is for the proprietor. Our Mishnah follows {NAME}.
[Peah 6:6.7] Then the cut grain should save the uncut grain. This means that something that is apt to save, but was forgotten, can become legally forgotten. {NAME} said, explain it if he was cutting and removing the sheaves row by row. He already forgot the standing grain before he might forget the sheaves.
[Peah 6:6.8] Does it mean that it really comes, or only that it is able to come? Let us hear from the following: “For example grain and vineyard.” And is the vineyard on the spot? That means, even if it is able to come!
[Peah 6:7.1] MISHNAH: Grain cut for animal feed or to bind sheaves, and similarly garlic used to bind as well as bundles of garlic and onions are not subject to “forgotten sheaves.” Anything hidden in the ground, such as luf , garlic, and onions, {NAME} says, they are not subject to “forgotten sheaves”, but the Sages say, they are subject to “forgotten sheaves.”
[Peah 6:7.2] HALAKHAH: {NAME} said, not only if he gave it but even if he took it with the intention of giving it.
[Peah 6:7.3] There we have stated: “If someone sets fire to a stack in which were hidden vessels, {NAME} says, he pays for all that was in it. But the Sages say, he only pays for a stack of wheat or barley.” The argument of {NAME} is inverted; there he says to include the hidden things, but here he says to exclude the hidden things. There ( Ex. 22:5 ) “and a stack or standing grain was consumed.” I understand that since it says “standing grain” it includes a stack. Why does the verse add “a stack?” In order to include the hidden things. But here ( Deut. 24:10 ) “your field,” in the open, to exclude anything hidden. The argument of the rabbis is inverted; there they say to exclude the hidden things, but here they say to include the hidden things. There, “or standing grain or a field,” just as a field is in the open, so all must be in the open. But here, “your field,” in the open, to exclude that which is hidden; “your harvest,” in the open, to exclude that which is hidden. That is a restriction after a restriction and every restriction after a restriction is only to add the hidden things.
[Peah 6:8.1] MISHNAH: He who harvests at night or removes the stacks, or a blind person, are subject to the law of forgotten sheaves. But if he intended only to take the large pieces, he is not subject to the law of forgotten sheaves. If he said: “I harvest on the understanding that I shall take what I might forget,” he is subject to the law of forgotten sheaves.
[Peah 6:8.2] HALAKHAH: So is the Mishnah: He who harvests at night or removes the stacks at night, or a blind person day or night.
[Peah 6:8.3] {NAME} said, not only for the large pieces, but also for the thin pieces. Since he is going to check for the large ones, the thin ones likewise are not subject to the law of forgotten sheaves.
[Peah 6:8.4] If he said: “I harvest on the undertanding that I shall take what I might forget,” he is subject to the law of forgotten sheaves, since he made a condition against what is written in the Torah, and if anybody makes a condition against what is written in the Torah, his condition is invalid.
[Peah 7:1.1] MISHNAH: Every olive tree that has a special name on the field, for example “a dripping olive tree” in its time, if it was forgotten, is not subject to the law of the forgotten sheaf. When does this apply? For its name, its production, and its place. By its name, if it was dripping or from Beth Shean. By its production, if it produced much. By its place, if it stood next to the wine-press or near a hole in the wall. For all other olive trees, two are subject to the law of the forgotten sheaf, three are not. {NAME} says, there is no law of the forgotten sheaf for olive trees.
[Peah 7:1.2] HALAKHAH: {NAME} said, it is written ( Deut . 24:19 ): “You will forget a sheaf on the field,” a sheaf you forget forever; this excludes one you certainly will remember after some time.
[Peah 7:1.3] {NAME} asked: If it was marked in his mind, is it as if it were marked? If it stood in the shadow of a date palm, the date palm marks it. If two of them were dripping, each of them marks the other. If the entire field was of dripping olive trees?
