[Ketubot 7:6.7] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If they saw her putting on her underpants and the pedlar leaves her house, the thing is ugly, she should leave. There is slime on her bed, the thing is ugly, she should leave. There is slime on his bed, the thing is ugly, she should leave. His sandal is in front of her bed, the thing is ugly, she should leave. Her sandal is in front of his bed, the thing is ugly, she should leave. Both leave the same dark place, the thing is ugly, she should leave. They lift one another from the cistern, the thing is ugly, she should leave. Both of them clap on her thighs in the bathhouse, the thing is ugly, she should leave. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}, in all these cases, if she brings an explanation for her behavior she is believed. {NAME} in the name of Rav: A case came before Rebbi and he said, what of it? They asked before him: Even if they saw him putting his mouth on her mouth? He said, this did happen, that they saw a man putting his mouth on her mouth. The case came befote {NAME}, who said that she should leave without ketubah. Her relatives appealed the case and said, if she is deviant, she should leave without ketubah. If she is not deviant, she should take the entire ketubah. {NAME} said to them, bring the ketubah that we may read it. They brought the ketubah and found written in it: If this X marries this Y as her husband and should no longer desire his company, she shall take half the ketubah sum. {NAME} said, since she agreed that he should put his mouth on her mouth it is as if she hated him; she has only half the ketubah. She lies in his bosom or he lies in her bosom, she is deviant. If they embrace, she is deviant. If they kiss, she is deviant. If the door is locked, she is deviant. If it is blocked, that is a problem.
[Ketubot 7:7.1] MISHNAH: If somebody performed the preliminary marriage with a woman on condition that she had no obligation of vows on her and it turned out that she had vows to fulfill, she is not preliminarily married. If he married her definitively without inquiry and she had vows to fulfill, she should leave without ketubah . If somebody performed the preliminary marriage with a woman on condition that she had no bodily defects and it turned out that she had bodily defects, she is not preliminarily married. If he married her definitively without inquiry and she had bodily defects, she should leave without ketubah ; and all defects which disqualify a priest disqualify a woman. If she had bodily defects, as long as she is in her father’s house, the father has to prove that the defects developed after she was preliminarily married and his field was swamped; once she entered her husband’s domain, the husband has to prove that she had the defects before the preliminary wedding so that his acquisition was in error, the words of {NAME}. But the Sages say, when was this said? For hidden defects, but he has no claim about visible defects, and if there is a public bathhouse in his town he has no claim for hidden defects since he checks her out through his female relatives.
[Ketubot 7:7.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody performed the preliminary marriage with a woman on condition that she had no obligation of vows on her,” etc. “If she had bodily defects, as long as she is in her father’s house,” etc. We have stated defects. Which vows? {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: If she vowed not to eat, or not to drink wine, or not to wear dyed garments. {NAME} said, the fine linen garments which come from Bet She‘an have the status of dyed garments. {NAME} said, the Mishnah deals with the case that he said to her, “on condition that you have no obligation of vows on you.” But if he said, “on condition that you have no obligation of any vow on you,” then even if she made a vow not to eat carob fruit it is a vow.
[Ketubot 7:7.3] “If she went to an Elder and her dissolved her vow, she is preliminarily married. To a doctor and he healed her, she is not preliminarily married.” What is the difference between the Elder and the doctor? The elder uproots the vow from its start; the doctor heals only for the future. Some Tannaïm state: Even if she went to an Elder and her dissolved her vow, she is not preliminarily married. The baraita follows {NAME}, as we have stated there: “{NAME} said, they forbade this only because of the other.” What is the reason of {NAME}? It would have been logical about a vow which has to be investigated by a Sage … because a vow which does not have to be investigated by a Sage. Some Tannaïm state: She is allowed to marry without a bill of divorce. Some Tannaïm state: She is forbidden to marry without a bill of divorce. They wanted to say that he who says, she is allowed to marry without a bill of divorce, is {NAME}, and he who says, she is forbidden to marry without a bill of divorce, are the rabbis. Everything follows the rabbis. He who says, she is allowed to marry without a bill of divorce: Since she knows that if she went to an Elder, he would dissolve her vow, since she does not go therefore she can be married without a bill of divorce. But he who says, she is forbidden to marry without a bill of divorce, that she should not go to an Elder who would dissolve her vow, then the preliminary marriage would become retroactively valid for her and it would turn out that her children become bastards. Therefore she is forbidden to marry without a bill of divorce.
[Ketubot 7:7.4] {NAME} said, the Mishnah deals with the case that he married her preliminarily conditionally but definitively silently. But if he married her preliminarily silently and definitively silently, she can claim her ketubah . {NAME} said, even if he married her preliminarily silently and definitively silently, she has no ketubah . {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: But she needs a bill of divorce from him even if he married her preliminarily conditionally but definitively silently. {NAME} asked before {NAME}: In case he married her preliminarily silently and divorced her after the preliminary marriage, what does {NAME} say? Let us hear from the following: “If she had bodily defects, as long as she is in her father’s house, the father has to prove.” This implies that if the father proved his case, she can claim her ketubah. What do you see to say, if he married her preliminarily silently and divorced her after the preliminary marriage! Where do we hold? Since afterwards [it is stated]: “When was this said? For hidden defects, but he has no claim about visible defects.” If he [made it conditional], could he not also claim for visible ones? But did not the colleagues say before {NAME}: Should we say that the following statement disagrees with {NAME}? “Once she entered her husband’s domain, the husband has to prove.” This implies that if the husband proved his case, she has no claim to ketubah. But by the statement of {NAME} ban Laqish, she has a claim to ketubah. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: The Mishnah deals with the case that he definitively married her but did not sleep with her; {NAME} speaks about the case that he definitively married her and slept with her; I am saying that she was acceptable to him since he took her to bed.
[Ketubot 7:7.5] “And all defects which disqualify a priest disqualify a woman. They added to them for women mouth odor, sweat odor, and a hairless mole.” {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: They taught this about the skin of the face. But did we not state: “When was this said? For hidden defects, but he has no claim about visible defects,” and this is of the visible defects! Explain it if she hid it under her headgear. It was stated: “A mole with hairs is a defect, whether it be large or small, whether it be on the body or on the face. Without a hair it is a defect on the face but not on the body. When has this been said? If it is small. But if it is large, it is a defect whether it be on the body or on the face. How big is large? {NAME} says, up to an Italic as .” {NAME} said, for example such a Gordianic denar his measure is half an ubiquitous gold piece. {NAME}, {NAME}: {NAME} asked: A bald woman with a row of hair going from one ear to the other? They wanted to understand it from the following: “They added to them for women mouth odor, sweat odor, and a hairless mole.” They did not mention baldness. They wanted to conclude that it is not a defect. There came {NAME}: {NAME} said, it is a defect. It is listed only if it is ugly for both sexes. But something which is beautiful in one sex but ugly in the other, like a bald pate, even though it is a defect it was not listed. You should know that this is so because a beard is beautiful for a man and a defect for a woman, and we did not state: In addition, for a woman a beard. There are breasts which are beautyiful for a woman and a defect for men, and we did not state: In addtion, for a man women’s breasts.
[Ketubot 7:7.6] The Mishnah deals with defects which do not spontaneously appear. But about defects which spontaneously appear, the husband has to bring proof and say that he stipulated about them.
[Ketubot 7:8.1] MISHNAH: If a man developed defects, one does not force him to divorce. {NAME} said, when has this been said? For minor defects. But for major defects one forces him to divorce.
[Ketubot 7:8.2] HALAKHAH: “If a man developed defects,” etc. {NAME} in the name of Rav: So is the Mishnah, “if he had.” But if they developed newly, one forces him to divorce. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Practice follows {NAME}. There came a case before {NAME} about a kopeaḥ , and he forced him. It turns out that following Rav if he did not become so, following {NAME} if he became so. {NAME} said, {NAME} follows {NAME}. Which [statement of] {NAME}? The former or the later? If the former, until she made a condition. If the later, even if he made a condition it is nothing. But this Mishnah turns out following {NAME}; does “the following one forces to divorce” [follows] the rabbis? Let us hear from the following: “{NAME} says, if it was a major defect, e. g., blind in one eye, amputated of one of his hands, lame in one of his legs, immediately he shall divorce and pay the ketubah. ” This Mishnah turns out following {NAME}; “the following one forces to divorce” [follows] the rabbis.
[Ketubot 7:9.1] MISHNAH: The following one forces to divorce: Those smitten with boils, the one afflicted with a polyp, the dung collector, the brass refiner, and the tanner, whether they were in this before they married or they came to it after they married. For all of these says {NAME} that, even if he contracted with her, she can say “I thought that I could stand it, now I cannot stand it.” But the Sages say, she is forced to stand it except for the one smitten with boils because she causes him consumption. It happened in Sidon that a tanner died who had a brother tanner; there the Sages said, she can say: “I could stand that in your brother, I cannot stand it in you.”
[Ketubot 7:9.2] HALAKHAH: “The following one forces to divorce: Those smitten with boils,” etc. “The meqammeṣ. ” This is the dung collector; but some say it is the tanner. {NAME} said, the Mishnah implies that this is the dung collector since we have stated: “The meqammeṣ and the tanner.” “The brass refiner.” {NAME} said, that is the one who smelts brass from its ore.
[Ketubot 7:9.3] It was stated: “{NAME} said, I met an old man, smitten with boils, from Sepphoris. He told me, there are 24 kinds of boils; the worst one, and the one for which a woman is bad, is flowing boils. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: With the latter kind, the evil Pharao was smitten; that is what is written: “The Eternal smote Pharao and his house with great plagues,” etc. {NAME} said: Because he dared to touch the matron’s body. There are 24 kinds of cedar, and from all of them the verse mentioned only seven. That is what is written: “I shall give in the desert cedar, acacia, myrtle, and oil wood; I put in the prairie beroš, tidhar, and teaššur together. Beroš is cypress; tidhar is idra ; teasššur is the box-tree. They added to them ’allonim, ‘armonim, and ’almogim. ’Allonim are oaks, ‘armonim plane trees, ’almuggim aloës.
[Ketubot 8:1.1] MISHNAH: If a woman inherited property before she became preliminarily married, the Houses of Shammai and Hillel agree that if she sells or gives it away it is valid. If she inherited after she became preliminarily married, the House of Shammai say she may sell, the House of Hillel say she should not sell, but both of them agree that if she sold or gave it away it is valid. {NAME} said: They said before {NAME}: If he obtained the right to the woman, should he not also acquire the right to the property? He said to them, are we not ashamed about the new [properties] and you want to burden us with the old ones?
[Ketubot 8:1.2] HALAKHAH: “If a woman inherited property,” etc. So is the Mishnah: Before she was preliminarily married. What is the difference between before she was preliminarily married and after she was preliminarily married? Before she was preliminarily married, it fell to her; after she was preliminarily married it fell to her and him.
[Ketubot 8:1.3] {NAME} asked before {NAME}, why did we not state it with the leniencies of the House of Shammai and the stringencies of the House of Hillel? He said to him, the Mishnaiot apply only to circumstances that are either stringent on both sides or lenient on both sides. But here it is a stringency on one side and a leniency on the other side. But did we not state: “The House of Shammai say, property abandoned to the poor [is abandoned]?” Is this not lenient for the poor and stringent for the householder, and it was stated! He said to him, it is lenient for the poor and not stringent for the householder, since he intentionally abandoned it. He said to him, did we not state: “If the sheaf that was near a closure, a stack, cattle, or vessels was forgotten,” is this not lenient for the householder and stringent for the poor, and it was stated! He said to him, it is lenient for the householder but not stringent for the poor, because they did not acquire it yet. You may also say here, it is lenient for the woman and not stringent for the husband since he did not yet acquire property rights to it. He said to him, since he became betrothed to her, the inheritance fell to both of them.
[Ketubot 8:1.4] {NAME} said, they argued before {NAME}: Because preliminarily married she is his wife and definitively married she is his wife; just as the sale by the latter is void, the sale by the former also should be void. He said to them, we are ashamed of the new ones, now you want to roll the new on over the old ones! The new ones, after the definitive marriage; the old ones before the definitive marriage, when she was married in the second ceremony.
[Ketubot 8:2.1] MISHNAH: If she inherited property after she was definitively married, both agree that if she sold or gave away the husband retrieves from the hand of the buyers. [If she interited] before she was definitively married and [sold] after she was definitively married, {NAME} said if she sold or gave away it is valid. {NAME} said, they said before {NAME}: If he obtained the right to the woman, did he not also acquire the right to the property? He said to them, are we not ashamed about the new [properties], and you want to burden us with the old ones?
[Ketubot 8:2.2] HALAKHAH: “If she inherited after she was definitively married,” etc. We did state: She may sell or give away and it is valid. {NAME} stated: She should not sell or give away, but if she sold or gave away it is valid. ”{NAME} said, that is not what {NAME} gave as answer, but the following was his argument: No, if you have an argument about a preliminarily married one, where he has rights neither to what she finds, nor to her handiwork, nor to dissolve her vows, what can you say about a definitively married one where he has rights to what she finds, to her handiwork, and to dissolve her vows? Let the proof be the case of one who [inherited] before the definitive marriage and then was definitively married, in which case he has rights to what she finds, to her handiwork, and to dissolve her vows, and you admit to us that she should not sell or give away. He said to them, I agree that she should not sell or give away, but if she sold or gave away it is valid..” There came a case before {NAME}. He said, is not {NAME} an isolated opinion? One cannot rely on it. A baraita supports him and disagrees with him: ”Our teachers took up the case again, voted, and instructed about property which she inherited before the definitive marriage and then was definitively married, that she should not sell or give away, and if she sold or gave away it is invalid.” It disagrees that the sale is invalid. It agrees that our teachers took up the case again, instructed, and voted. Before they voted, they did not disagree with him.
[Ketubot 8:3.1] MISHNAH: {NAME} differentiates between properties: Properties known to the husband she shall not sell and if she sold or gave away it is invalid. Those unknown to the husband she shall not sell but if she sold or gave away it is valid.
[Ketubot 8:3.2] HALAKHAH: “{NAME} differentiates between properties,” etc. {NAME} said, properties known to the husband are real estate, those not known to the husband are movables. {NAME} said, properties known to the husband are those she inherited in the presence of the husband, those not known to the husband are those she inherited while her husband was overseas. A baraita supports {NAME}: The following are properties not known to the husband, what she inherited while her husband was overseas.
[Ketubot 8:4.1] MISHNAH: If she inherited money; real estate should be bought with it and he eats its yield. For produce cut from the ground, real estate should be bought and he eats its yield; with produce connected to the ground, {NAME} says one has to estimate how much the property is worth with produce and how much without, for the difference real estate should be bought and he eats its yield. But the Sages say, standing produce is his, cut it is hers; real estate should be bought from it and he eats its yield.
[Ketubot 8:4.2] HALAKHAH: “If she inherited money; real estate should be bought,” etc. {NAME} said, this is {NAME} opinion since {NAME} considers standing [produce] as if it were cut. {NAME} said, he did not hear that {NAME} said, {NAME} said this only for standing grain ready to be harvested and grapes ready to be harvested; therefore not unripe produce. But here, even unripe produce. {NAME} asked, are not the arguments of {NAME} contradictory? There, he did not consider standing [produce] as if it were cut, but here he considers standing [produce] as if it were cut. {NAME} said, {NAME} does not consider standing [produce] as if it were cut. But if you see cut grain, you empower the woman; if you see an unseeded field, you empower the man. In case of doubt you estimate how much it is worth unseeded and how much seeded. If before it was seeded it was worth (two denars) and when it was seeded (one denar), with that denar real estate should be bought and he reaps its yield.
[Ketubot 8:5.1] MISHNAH: {NAME} says, in the circumstances where he was empowered at her entrance he was disabled at her exit, and in the circumstances where he was disabled at her entrance he was empowered at her exit. What was connected to the ground at her entrance is his and at her exit is hers, what was cut from the ground at her entrance is hers and at her exit is his.
[Ketubot 8:5.2] HALAKHAH: “{NAME} says, in the circumstances where he was empowered,” etc. You say, at her entrance they are his: If she sold them they are not sold, if she gave them to a sharecropper he has the reward from it, if she dedicated them as First Fruits they are not dedicated You say, at her exit they are hers, if he sold them they are not sold, if he gave them to a sharecropper she has the reward from it, if he dedicated them as First Fruits, this is the disagreement of {NAME} and {NAME}, since they disagreed: ( Deut . 26:11 ): ‘You shall enjoy all the good things that the Eternal, your God, gave to you and your house.’ This teaches that a person brings First Fruits from his wife’s property.” {NAME} said, after her death but not during her lifetime. {NAME} said, there is no difference, during her lifetime and after her death. {NAME} follows his own opinion since he said, a person does not inherit from his wife as a biblical rule. In the opinion of {NAME} it never was dedicated. In the opinion of {NAME} it is dedicated and the holiness is removed.
[Ketubot 8:6.1] MISHNAH: If she inherited old male and female slaves, they should be sold and real estate bought with the proceeds, of which he eats the yield. {NAME} says, she does not have to sell because they are the glory of her father’s house.
[Ketubot 8:6.2] HALAKHAH: “If she inherited male and female slaves,” etc. The Mishnah speaks of those who do not work enough for their upkeep. But if they work enough for their upkeep, she does not have to sell because the glory of her father’s house still exists.
[Ketubot 8:7.1] MISHNAH: If she inherited old vines or olive trees, they should be sold for their wood and real estate bought with the proceeds, of which he eats the yield. {NAME} says, she does not have to sell because they are the glory of her father’s house.
[Ketubot 8:7.2] HALAKHAH: “If she inherited old vines or olive trees,” etc. {NAME} in the name of the rabbis there: The Mishnah deals with the case that she inherited olive trees but not their ground, vines but not their ground. But if she inherited olive trees with their ground, vines with their ground, she does not have to sell since her father’s house’s glory still exists. But the rabbis here say, even if she inherited olive trees with their ground, vines with their ground, did she not inherit the value of the olive grove, did she not inherit the value of the vineyard? A baraita supports the rabbis there: “ ‘I am selling you the vineyard’, this is a valid sale even if there are no vines since he sells him [the real estate] by description. ‘I am selling you the grove’, this is a valid sale even if there are no trees since he sells him [the real estate] by description.”
[Ketubot 8:8.1] MISHNAH: If somebody invests in his wife’s properties, if he invested much but it yielded little, or he invested little but it yielded much, what he invested he invested and what it yielded it yielded. If he invested and had no yield, he shall swear how much he invested and get repaid.
[Ketubot 8:8.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody invests in his wife’s properties,” etc. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Even if he ate only one basket of dates. {NAME} said, that is, if the investment is greater than the increase in value. But if the increase in value is greater than the investment, one gives him the increase in value. A baraita disagrees with {NAME}: “In all cases one evaluates it as for a sharecropper.” The baraita disagrees about planting; what {NAME} said was about a building. The baraita disagrees about planting, is that what {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: Even if he ate only one basket of dates. He said to him, in one case if he ate, in the other if he did not eat.
[Ketubot 8:9.1] MISHNAH: If a woman waiting for her levir inherited property, the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel agree that if she sells or gives away it is valid. If she died, what shall be done with her ketubah and the properties which enter and leave with her? The House of Shammai say, the husband’s and the father’s heirs shall split it. But the House of Hillel say, the properties are in the hands of the holders; the ketubah in the hands of the husband’s heirs and the properties which enter and leave with her in the hands of the father’s heirs.
[Ketubot 8:9.2] HALAKHAH: “If property came to a woman waiting for her levir,” etc. Here, you say “she may sell or give away and it is valid.” And you also say “the husband’s heirs should split with her father’s heirs!” {NAME} said, when do you say “she may sell or give away and it is valid”? If they came to her before she became a woman waiting for her levir. When do you say “the husband’s heirs should split with her father’s heirs”? If they came to her after she became a woman waiting for her levir. If they came to her before she became a woman waiting for her levir and produced revenue after she became a woman waiting for her levir, [that revenue is as if] they came to her after she became a woman waiting for her levir. {NAME} said, the levir in this situation is a problem for the House of Shammai. If he is a husband, he inherits everything. If he is not a husband, he inherits nothing. Because of the doubt, “the husband’s heirs should split with her father’s heirs.” For the House of Hillel it is obvious that he is a husband and inherits everything. For even his brother had only the usufruct.
[Ketubot 8:9.3] {NAME} stated: Her heirs, those who inherit her ketubah are obliged to bury her. {NAME} said, if {NAME} had not stated this, we would have had a problem. If she had no ketubah, do they not have to bury her? This is difficult. If a woman has no ketubah, does she not have to be buried? A wife, even if she has no ketubah, must be buried. This one, if she has a ketubah, is entitled to burial costs. But here, if she does not have a ketubah, she is not entitled to burial costs.
[Ketubot 8:10.1] MISHNAH: If his brother left money, real estate should be bought with it and he eats its yield. For produce cut from the ground, real estate should be bought and he eats its yield; connected to the ground, {NAME} says one has to estimate how much it is worth with produce and how much without, for the difference real estate should be bought and he eats its yield. But the Sages say, standing produce is his, cut it is up for grabs. If he took possession first, it is his; if she took possession first, real estate should be bought for the proceeds and he eats its yield. If he married her, she is his wife in every respect except that her ketubah is a lien on the property of her first husband.
[Ketubot 8:10.2] HALAKHAH: “If his brother left money,” etc. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: It is necessary, if the money was deposited with him, that you would not let him say, since I am the heir it is mine.
[Ketubot 8:10.3] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: One does not say “his” but [ ]. In which respect? In case the heir took it, one removes it from his hand. Does one have the same rule for the creditor? Was it not stated: If either the heir or the creditor took it, one takes it from their hands? {NAME} said, let us hear from the following: “If he dedicated 90 minas but his debt was 100 minas, [the creditor] adds another denar and redeems these properties.” Not necessarily a denar, but anything, that a dedication should not be seen to be profanated without redemption. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: One would be guilty of complete larceny. That is difficult. If one would be guilty of complete larceny, should if not be redeemed for its full value? If it can be redeemed for less than its full value, one should not be guilty of complete larceny! What are we talking about? If it is connected to the ground, can there be larceny about real estate? But we talk about standing grain. Since if the administrator misbehaved and took it, one does not take it from his hand; the administrator and the heir follow the same rule. Also if the heir misbehaved and took it, one does not take it from his hand. {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: The same rule holds for an ox. Can you say that an ox is real estate? {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: They made the rules for an ox parallel those of dedications that lost their value. Here, you say one takes it from his hand, but there you say, one does not take it from his hand. Since you diminished the woman’s power in that her ketubah is a lien only on the properties of her first husband, you strengthened her power in this matter that if the heir came and took it, one removes it from his hand. It was stated thus: Trees and cutting, old or young, one removes from their hands.
[Ketubot 8:11.1] MISHNAH: He should not say to her “here your ketubah is lying on the table” but “all my properties are pledged for your ketubah. ” If he divorced her, she has no ketubah- lien. If he took her back, she is like all women who have a ketubah .
[Ketubot 8:11.2] HALAKHAH: “He should not say to her ‘here is your ketubah ’”, etc. What does he do? “He marries her, he may divorce her and take her back, and she writes him a receipt for her ketubah. ” {NAME} said, the baraita has two possibilities. “Or she writes him a receipt for her ketubah. ” {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If he married her, divorced her, and took her back, if he wrote her a new ketubah , the lien is on his property; otherwise, it is on the property of her first husband. {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}, a Mishnah said so: “For he who takes back his wife, takes her back under the terms of her first ketubah .” In the end, if he married her, divorced her, and took her back? He tells you something new. Even if he married her, divorced her, and took her back, if he wrote her a new ketubah , the lien is on his property; otherwise, it is on the property of her first husband.
[Ketubot 8:11.3] {NAME} in the name of {NAME} said: A betrothed woman who died does not have a ketubah since she was not permitted to marry outside. That you should not say [the case] should be considered as if he divorced her and she should have a ketubah ; therefore it was necessary to say that she does not have a ketubah.
[Ketubot 8:11.4] In earlier times, her ketubah was deposited with her family; then it was easy for him to divorce her. They then instituted that her ketubah had to be deposited with her husband; even so it was easy for him to divorce her. Then they instituted that a man should buy with his wife’s ketubah cups, plates, and bowls; that is what we did state: “He should not say to her ‘here your ketubah is lying on the table’ but all his properties are pledged for her ketubah. ” Finally they instituted that a person should use his wife’s ketubah in business, then because he uses his wife’s ketubah in his business dealings he loses track of it and it becomes difficult for him to divorce her.
[Ketubot 8:11.5] {NAME} decreed three things: That a person should use his wife’s ketubah in his business dealings. And that children have to go to school. Also, he decreed impurity for glass ware. But did not {NAME}, {NAME} say in the name of {NAME}: {NAME} and {NAME} decreed impurity for Gentile lands and glass ware; {NAME} said, {NAME}? {NAME} said, {NAME} and {NAME} decreed on metal vessels; Hillel and Shammai decreed on the purity of hands. {NAME} in the name of Levi: That was the current practice; they forgot it, but the later ones got up and agreed to the opinion of the earlier ones to teach you that everything the Court insists on will come to be in the end just as Moses was told on Sinai; as {NAME} said ( Deut. 32:47 ): “For it is not an empty word, from you,” if it is empty it is from you because you do not exert yourself about it. “Because it is your life,” when is it your life? At the time that you exert yourself!
[Ketubot 9:1.1] MISHNAH: If somebody writes to his wife: “I shall have nothing to do with your properties,” he receives their revenues and if she should die, he inherits from her. In this case, why did he write “I shall have nothing to do with your properties”? If she sold or gave away, it is valid. If he wrote to her: “I shall have nothing to do with your properties, nor with their revenues,” he does not receive their revenues during her lifetime but if she should die, he inherits from her. {NAME} says, he continues to receive the investment results of her revenues unless he writes: “I shall have nothing to do with your properties, nor with their revenues, nor with revenues derived from revenues, without limits.” If he wrote “I shall have nothing to do with your properties, nor with their revenues, nor with revenues derived from revenues during your lifetime and after your death,” he does not receive the revenues during her lifetime and does not inherit from her after her death. {NAME} says, if she dies, he should inherit from her since he made a condition contradicting what is written in the Torah, and anybody’s condition contradicting what is written in the Torah is invalid.
[Ketubot 9:1.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody writes to his wife: “I shall have nothing to do with your properties,” etc. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If he did not take her in. But if he took her in, nobody can lose his rights by these expressions. {NAME} said, this is the word of {NAME}: He who says that “my hands are removed from this field, my feet are removed from this field,” did not say anything. {NAME} asked before {NAME}: Does a Mishnah imply that nobody can lose his rights by these expressions? Did we not state there: “If somebody was married to two wives when he sold a field and the first one wrote for the buyer: I have no claims on you, the second one can take it away from the buyer’s hands,” this implies, not the first one. He said to him, that text itself implies that nobody can lose his rights by these expressions, but here the second wife cannot take anything away from the first, and why can the first one not take it away from the buyer’s hands? For she writes to him: For any complaint I shall have regarding this field, I shall have nothing against you.
[Ketubot 9:1.3] If he wrote for her and she wrote for him. Just as he did not lose his rights so she did not lose her rights. If he wrote to her “from preliminary and definitive marriage”, that is the disagreement between the Houses of Shammai and Hillel. In the opinion of the House of Shammai she shall sell; in the opinion of the House of Hillel she should not sell.
[Ketubot 9:1.4] {NAME} asked before {NAME}: If he wrote to her: “I shall have nothing to do with your properties,” and she inherited properties afterwards, what is the rule? Can a person put a condition on something not in existence? {NAME} said before {NAME}: From his rights you can infer his obligations. If he had not written to her, would it make any difference, would he not receive its yield? That means, from his rights you can infer his obligations. {NAME} asked: If he wrote to her: “I shall have nothing to do with your properties which you shall inherit in the future,” what is the rule? Can a person put a condition on something not in existence?
[Ketubot 9:1.5] If she sold produce connected to the ground: {NAME} said, as if she sold harvested [produce]; {NAME} said, as if she sold a tenth of the ground. {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of Rav: If somebody writes a field over to his wife, she cannot sell the produce. {NAME} said, a baraita says so “What are revenues derived from revenues? He sells the produce, buys real estate, and eats its revenue.” {NAME} asked: If another person had written [real estate] over to her, would he not receive the revenue? If he himself wrote, not so much more! He said only “wrote over”, but not “sold”. What is the difference between one who writes and one who sells? He tried to find a reason to hide food from the wife.
[Ketubot 9:1.6] It is reasonable according to {NAME}, if he wrote: “I shall have nothing to do with your properties and the revenues,” that he cannot take the revenues. Even if he wrote: “I shall have nothing to do with this field and its yield,” he cannot eat its yield. It is reasonable according to the rabbis; if he wrote: “I shall have nothing to do with this field and its yield,” can he eat its yield? Even if he wrote, “I shall have nothing to do with your properties and its yields,” can he eat its yield? Let us hear from the following, as {NAME}, {NAME} said in the name of Rav: If somebody writes a field over to his wife, he has no right to its yield. {NAME} said, a baraita says so “What are revenues derived from revenues? He sells the produce, buys real estate, and eats its revenue.” Since he wrote, “I shall have nothing to do with your properties and their yields,” is that not as if he wrote a field over to his wife, and you say, he has neither revenue nor revenue from revenue! That means, there is no difference in the opinion of {NAME} whether he wrote “I shall have nothing to do with this field and its yield,” or he wrote “I shall have nothing to do with your properties and their revenues,” he cannot take any revenue. Similarly, for the rabbis it makes no difference whether he wrote “I shall have nothing to do with your properties and their revenues,” or he wrote “I shall have nothing to do with this field and its yield,” he can take its yield.
[Ketubot 9:1.7] {NAME} in the name of Rav: Practice follows {NAME}, but not in the matter of words. Practice follows {NAME} for he said, if she dies he inherits from her, but in matters of words, “since he made a condition contradicting what is written in the Torah, and anybody’s condition contradicting what is written in the Torah is invalid,” in personal matters. But in money matters, one’s stipulations are valid and that is a money matter! Why did we say that the condition is invalid? Because in the end he acquired it. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: The law should have been that if she sold or gave it away it should be valid, for [the buyer] acquired it. Why did they say it is invalid? That a wife should not sell her husband’s property and say, it is mine.
[Ketubot 9:1.8] {NAME} had a case and he asked the rabbis who told him, leave you properties. He asked {NAME}, who told him, enter your properties. {NAME} asked before {NAME}: Who are those rabbis? What about Rav, {NAME}, and {NAME}? He said to him, {NAME} rabbis.
[Ketubot 9:1.9] They asked before {NAME}: Following the Sages, if she died who inherits from her? Those, her brothers, inherit from her.
[Ketubot 9:1.10] {NAME} asked before {NAME}: If the brothers divided [the inheritance], the widow is supported by them. For you should not say, they should be considered as if they had sold the properties and the widow would not be supported by these, since it is obvious that if they sold, they sold their own property.
[Ketubot 9:1.11] {NAME} asked before {NAME}: It is written: “If the Jubilee will happen for the Children of Israel.” If the institution of the Jubilee exists, inheritances return; if the institution of the Jubilee does not exist, inheritances do not return. It is the opposite way, it comes to tell you that even if the institution of the Jubilee exists and inheritances return, inheritance by biblical law does not return!
[Ketubot 9:1.12] {NAME} asked before {NAME}: If he sold and then she died? He said to him, his sale is invalid; it is as if a son sold during his father’s lifetime and then the father died. If she sold and then he died? He said to him, her sale is valid; it is as if a father sold during his son’s lifetime and then the son died. {NAME} asked before {NAME}: What is the situation if she sold to her husband? He said, since {NAME} said, practice follows {NAME}, this implies that her sale is a sale. It was stated: “If somebody says, my property should be given to X, if X died to Y, [if Y died to Z]. If the first one died the properties should be given to the second, if the second died they should be given to the third. If the second one died during the first’s lifetime; since the second never acquired them, the third cannot acquire them.” He said to him, so did {NAME}, the father of the Mishnah, explain: After him to X, after him to Y; it is as if stated: if the third died during the second’s lifetime, since the second one did not acquire his heirs cannot acquire, one really could say: After him to X, after him to Y. It was stated: “Rebbi says, the first one may sell the real estate and buy movables. {NAME} says, he has only the usufruct.” {NAME} said, practice follows Rebbi. {NAME} said, since {NAME} said, practice follows Rebbi, that implies that he cannot dispose of it by a death-bed will. So said {NAME} before {NAME}: Since this woman’s upkeep is her husband’s responsibility, is it not like a gift of sick persons? He said to him, her upkeep is what is necessary for her: food, oil, and salt. But she wants to sell and buy chickens. This means that if the first one wanted to sell and buy chickens, he may sell. {NAME} said, her burial is equal to her upkeep. Since you said there, he may sell real estate and buy food, so he may sell real estate and buy a burial.
[Ketubot 9:1.13] {NAME} said: Those who write “if she should die childless, her property should return to her father’s family” write a monetary condition which is a valid condition.
[Ketubot 9:2.1] MISHNAH: If somebody died and left his wife, a creditor, and heirs, and he was owed a deposit or a debt by a third party, {NAME} says, these should be given to the weakest among them. {NAME} says, one does not show mercy in law! But these should be given to the heirs for all others have to swear, only the heirs do not have to swear.
[Ketubot 9:2.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody died and left a wife,” etc. {NAME} said, the weakest in his claim. For example, one lent before witnesses, the other lent on a mortgage document; it should be given to the one who lent before witnesses. {NAME} said, the weakest in his body. Think about it, if he is rich, like those of the family Andreas. {NAME} said, the weakest in his body and poor. As the following: They gave to a relative of {NAME} as the weakest. {NAME} brought slaves of {NAME} and took it away from her. {NAME} was leaning on {NAME} and said, what was done with that poor woman? He said to him, {NAME} brought slaves of {NAME} and took it away from her. Was he justified in doing this? {NAME} asked before {NAME}: Should we say that {NAME} follows his doctrine and {NAME} his own? Since they disagree: Everybody agrees that if they err in arguments, one does not reverse. In the words of the Torah, one reverses. Where do they disagree? If one errs in a Mishnah, for {NAME} says, an error in Mishnah is like an error in arguments, but {NAME} says, an error in Mishnah is like an error in words of the Torah. What is said of the Mishnah is also said of words of the Elders.
[Ketubot 9:2.3] Think of it, if they were exempt from swearing? One is biblical, the other is not biblical.
[Ketubot 9:3.1] MISHNAH: If he left produce taken from the ground, the one who takes them first acquires them. If the widow acquired more than her ketubah sum, or the creditor more than his claim, the remainder, {NAME} says, should be given to the weakest among them. {NAME} says, one does not show mercy in law! But it should be given to the heirs since all others have to swear, only the heirs do not have to swear.
[Ketubot 9:3.2] HALAKHAH: “If he left produce taken,” etc. Both Rav and {NAME} say, if they were collected at a trading place. But if somebody collected it in his house, his house acquired for him. {NAME} said, even if he collected it in his house, his house did not acquire for him. For he thinks that they are his but they are not his. Does from this follow how the owner acquires his produce in a Sabbatical year? {NAME} wanted to say, from the moment he put them into his vessel. {NAME} said, even if he put them into his vessel he did not acquire, for he thinks that they are his but they are not his.
[Ketubot 9:3.3] That widow took a slave girl. The case came before {NAME} who said, what she took, she took. {NAME} took her away, for she thought that she was hers but she was not hers. A similar case: The father of the sons of Shammai died and bequeathed a goat to them. The creditor came and took it. The case came before {NAME} who said, he took his own property. Did we not state that if either an heir or a creditor came and took, one does [not] remove from his hand; for they thought they were theirs but they were not theirs. {NAME} said, {NAME} agrees that if they sold it, or gave it as a pledge, or moved it to another place, if then the creditor came and took it one removes it from his possession.
[Ketubot 9:3.4] Think of it, if they were exempt from swearing? One is biblical, the other is not biblical.
[Ketubot 9:4.1] MISHNAH: If somebody engages his wife as grocer or appoints her as steward, he can make her swear any time he wants. {NAME} says, even about her distaff and her dough.
[Ketubot 9:4.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody engages his wife as grocer,” etc. Is {NAME} not correct? What is the rabbis’ reason? If you say so, there never would be peace in his house. If she broke vessels, is she responsible as an unpaid or a paid trustee? It would be reasonable to consider her a paid trustee. They said, she is not even an unpaid trustee, for if you say so, there never would be peace in his house.
[Ketubot 9:5.1] MISHNAH: If he wrote to her: “I have no vow or oath against you,” he cannot make her swear, but he can ask an oath from the heirs or her business associates. “I have no oath against you, or your heirs, or your business associates,” he cannot ask an oath from her, or her heirs, or her business associates, but the heirs can ask an oath from her, or her heirs, or her business associates.
[Ketubot 9:5.2] HALAKHAH: “If he wrote to her: “I have no vow or oath against you,” etc. {NAME} and {NAME} both say, not only about properties over which she exercised control during her husband’s lifetime but even about properties over which she exercised control after her husband’s death are the heirs prevented from making her swear.
[Ketubot 9:5.3] There, we have stated: “If somebody leases a cow from another person and lends it to a third party; if it died naturally, the lessee has to swear that it died naturally and the borrower has to pay to the lessee.” {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Only if he gave permission to lend to others. Also {NAME} stated thus: “The borrower cannot lend, nor the lessee lease, nor the borrower lease, nor the lessee lend, nor the trustee give to another unless they received permission from the owners. And all who changed the titles without the owners’ knowledge are liable. But the borrower is liable even if he did not change.” But it is because we stated: “An unpaid watchman can stipulate to be exempt from an oath and the borrower may stipulate that he not have to pay.” This means that even if he stipulated to be exempt that he is obligated. What if he wanted to let the borrower swear? Let us hear from the following: “If he wrote to her: ‘I have no vow or oath against you,’ he cannot make her swear, but he can ask an oath from the heirs or her business associates.” This implies that if he wanted to make the borrower swear, he can force him to swear. The first case teaches about the second and the second about the first. The first case teaches about the second, that if he wanted to make the borrower swear, he can force him to swear. The second case teaches about the first, that if he wants to force the wife to swear, that he can make her swear. {NAME} said, it is not necessary to derive the first case from the second, and what does one learn for the second case from the first? Following what {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: Only if he gave permission to lend to others. And here, only if he gave permission to let her sons be stewards. {NAME} said, he has to pay the lease all the time it is leased to him. {NAME} asked {NAME}: If the owners borrowed it and it died? He said to him, in that case we say, they ate it. {NAME} said, if they ate it, they ate their own property. {NAME} asked before {NAME}: How does one act? He said to him, there are two against four; one does not act following the argument. He said to him, they are two against two! {NAME} is the elder {NAME} student; {NAME} is {NAME} student.
[Ketubot 9:6.1] MISHNAH: “I have no vow or oath against you, neither I, nor my heirs, nor my business associates, against you, or your heirs, or your business associates,” he cannot ask an oath from her, neither he, nor the heirs, nor the business associates, from her, or her heirs, or her business associates. If she went from her husband’s grave to her family, or she remained in her in-law’s family but was not appointed as steward, the heirs cannot make her swear. But if she was appointed as steward, the heirs can make her swear for the future, but they cannot make her swear about the past.
[Ketubot 9:6.2] HALAKHAH: ““I have no vow or oath against you,” etc. {NAME} said, only if she was made a steward during her husband’s lifetime. But if she was appointed as a steward after her husband’s death, the heirs can(not) make her swear. That is the Mishnah: if she was not appointed a steward, the heirs cannot make her swear. If she was appointed a steward, the heirs can make her swear for the future, but they cannot make her swear about the past. What is “about the past”? From the time of death to the time of burial. And {NAME} said, even if he appointed her as steward after her husband’s death, the heirs can make her swear. But did we not state: “If he did not appoint her as steward, the heirs cannot make her swear. If he appointed her as steward, the heirs can make her swear for the future but cannot make her swear for the past.” He explains it about the first case. But if it is about the first case, {NAME} and {NAME} both say, not only about property over which she had control during her husband’s lifetime but even about property over which she acquired control after her husband’s death the heirs cannot make her swear. Explain it, from the time of death to the time of burial. For {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: The heirs cannot make her swear from the time of death to the time of burial. {NAME} stated: That she should not abandon him and leave for her family.
[Ketubot 9:7.1] MISHNAH: If she had compromised her ketubah , she shall not be able to collect without an oath. If one witness testifies that [the ketubah ] was paid, she shall not be able to collect without an oath. From orphans’ property, or from encumbered property, in his absence she shall not be able to collect without an oath.
[Ketubot 9:7.2] HALAKHAH: “If she went from her husband’s grave to her family,” etc. {NAME} said, this came down in the manner of a biblical oath. The ketubah is acknowledged in her hand for collection; it is as if collected. But since with the document of 200 there is an acknowledment of payment and she says, one mina [is due to her], she cannot be paid without an oath.
[Ketubot 9:7.3] It was stated “compromised”. Not that she reduced her ketubah . If her ketubah was 200 but she claims a mina, she is paid without an oath. What is the difference between one who compromises and one who claims less? {NAME} said, if she compromises there was a transaction between them; if she claims less there was no transaction between them.
[Ketubot 9:7.4] {NAME} asked: Since we stated there: “If one witness testifies that [the ketubah ] was paid, she shall not be able to collect without an oath,” should it be similar that if one witness testifies that [the ketubah ] was reduced, she shall not be able to collect the reduced sum without an oath? {NAME} said, at the moment that one witness testifies that the amount should be reduced, he is like a single witness who contradicts the testimony of two [witnesses] but no single witness can contradict the testimony of two.
[Ketubot 9:7.5] It was stated: If an heir’s father held a compromised promissory note, the son collects without swearing. In that the son’s power is greater than the father’s, since the son collects without swearing while the father can collect only by swearing. {NAME} said, nevertheless he has to execute an heir’s oath, “that our father did not charge us, that our father did not tell us, that we did not find a document among our father’s documents that this note was paid.” {NAME} asked, does the baraita follow the House of Shammai? For the House of Shammai say, “she collects her ketubah and does not drink.” {NAME} said, there the reason of the House of Shammai is: Bring my husband and I shall drink! But here, it would be in order that even his father would not have to swear. They instituted a rule that he has to swear. They instituted that for him, but not for his son. When he died, you put his son on the biblical rule.
[Ketubot 9:7.6] If a father became obligated to swear in court and died, his son cannot collect. If it were otherwise, what could we say? Can a man let his son inherit an obligation to swear? {NAME} said, you mean, if a man compromised his document in court, his son cannot collect. {NAME} asked: Because he walked those two steps, he loses? If he compromised it outside the court, he collects. Because he compromised it in court, he cannot collect?
[Ketubot 9:7.7] “If she had compromised her ketubah, she shall not be able to collect without an oath,” etc. {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: One pays from an orphan’s property only a document on which interest is due, and some say, also a woman’s ketubah. {NAME} said, because of her sustenance. {NAME} said, who is worried about sustenance? {NAME}! Since {NAME} said, it depends on the collection. What about it? For attraction, that everybody should jump to marry her. Some say, also for robbery and torts. {NAME} said, we stated both of these. Robbery from the following: “If it was mortgageable, he has to pay.” For torts from the following: “One pays from an orphan’s property only from the least valuable.” So is the Mishnah: One pays for torts from an orphan’s property only from the least valuable. But was it not stated: If the son took his father’s place, one estimates torts from the most valuable land, creditors from average quality, and a woman’s ketubah from the least valuable. {NAME} said, here about an adult orphan, there about an underage orphan.
[Ketubot 9:8.1] MISHNAH: If she had compromised her ketubah, how is that? If her ketubah was 1‘000 zuz and he said to her, you received your ketubah, but she says, I received only one mina, she shall not be able to collect without an oath. If one witness testifies that [the ketubah ] was paid, how is that? If her ketubah was 1‘000 zuz and he said to her, you received your ketubah, but she says, I received nothing, and one witness testifies that [the ketubah ] was paid, she shall not be able to collect without an oath. From encumbered property, how is that? If he sold his real estate to others and she collects from the buyers, she shall not be able to collect without an oath. From orphans’ property, how is that? If he died and left his estate to the orphans, if she is paid out by the orphans she shall not be able to collect without an oath. Not in his presence, how is that? If he went overseas and she collects in his absence, she shall not be able to collect without an oath. {NAME} says, any time she asks for her ketubah, the heirs can require an oath from her. If she does not ask for her ketubah , the heirs cannot require an oath from her.
[Ketubot 9:8.2] HALAKHAH: “If she had compromised her ketubah, how is that? If her ketubah was l‘000 zuz,” etc. “If one witness testifies that [the ketubah ] was paid,” etc. So is the Mishnah: “If she collects in his absence, she shall not be able to collect without an oath.”
[Ketubot 9:8.3] “If she collects in his absence, she shall not be able to collect without an oath.” Can one collect from a person in his absence? {NAME} says, explain it about a contract for which interest is due. Would the court collect interest? Explain it that it was guaranteed for a Gentile.
[Ketubot 9:8.4] Alexis said before {NAME}: We act much better than you do. We send edicts. If he comes, it is good. If he does not come, we irrevocably give away his properties. He answered him, we also act in this way, we have the herald announce for thirty days. If he comes, it is good. If he does not come, we irrevocably give away his properties. He said to him, think of it, if he was in distant corners. He said to him, we send three letters, one after thirty days, one after the next thirty days, and one after the next thirty days. If he comes, it is good. If he does not come, we irrevocably give away his properties. {NAME} said, that is, if he was present at the trial and then fled. But if he was not present at the trial, we cannot irrevocably give away, but only announce.
[Ketubot 9:8.5] You find that one may say that Ḥanan and {NAME} said the same thing. Just as Ḥanan said, she shall swear only at the end, so {NAME} says, she shall swear only at the end. Just as you say, practice follows Ḥanan, so here practice follows {NAME}.
[Ketubot 9:9.1] MISHNAH: If she produced her bill of divorce without a ketubah, she collects her ketubah . [Ketubot 9:9.2] HALAKHAH: “From encumbered property, how is that?” {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If somebody disputes a court document, he is not trustworthy. {NAME} said to him: Is that not the Mishnah? “If she produced her bill of divorce without a ketubah, she collects her ketubah ”! {NAME} said to him: Babylonian, after I removed the clay from the pearl, you say to me: Is that not the Mishnah? There is a registrar of agreements; as you say, if a document is lost, one writes a replacement. [Ketubot 9:9.3] {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of Rav: At a place where one writes ketubah documents, if he says I wrote, but she says you did not write, the burden of proof is on her to prove that he did not write. But at a place where one does not write ketubah documents, if he says I wrote, but she says you did not write, the burden of proof is on him to prove that he wrote.
[Ketubot 9:9.4] {NAME} found {NAME} prozbol and ran to give it to him. I tore it without discarding? Here, I discarded and tore it.
[Ketubot 9:10.1] MISHNAH: Two bills of divorce and two ketubot , she collects two ketubot . Two ketubot and one bill of divorce, or one ketubah and two bills of divorce, or one ketubah, and a bill of divorce, and death; she collects only one ketubah since a person who divorces his wife and takes her back, takes her back on the basis of her prior ketubah . If a minor was married off by his father, [his wife’s] ketubah is valid since he kept her by that understanding. If a proselyte converted together with his wife, her ketubah is valid since he kept her by that understanding.
[Ketubot 9:10.2] HALAKHAH: “If she produced her bill of divorce without a ketubah, she collects her ketubah ,” etc. “Two bills of divorce and two ketubot ” etc. But only if the bill of divorce is dated between the two ketubot . So far if they are equal. If one was for a mina, the other for 200 [ zuz ]? {NAME} and {NAME} and {NAME}. One said, she collects the first one. The other said, she collects the second one and the excess she collects from the date of the second.
[Ketubot 9:10.3] {NAME} said before {NAME}: Does this not mean that if a person borrows from another, and then he borrows again, he has to declare “in addition to the first paper you have on me”? It is frequent that a woman says, my ketubah is lost, write me another. Is it frequent that a man say, my paper is lost, write me another? But it is possible that he should declare for him.
[Ketubot 9:10.4] {NAME} brought this case before {NAME}: Did not {NAME} say in the name of {NAME}: Nobody should use a paper on which he borrowed and paid the loan back to take out another loan on the same day? He said to him, here if he had paid back, there if he did not pay back. {NAME} stated before {NAME}: Two Amoraïm, one said for ketubah but not for individual stipulations, the other said, both for ketubah and for individual stipulations.
[Ketubot 9:10.5] One understands a proselyte. A minor? Can a minor divorce? {NAME} said, I explained it following what {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: Only if he slept with her when he regained sight or became sane mentally. And here, if he slept with her after he reached adulthood.
[Ketubot 10:1.1] MISHNAH: If somebody was married to two women when he died, the first one precedes the second, and the heirs of the first precede the heirs of the second. If the first one he had married died, then he married the second one and he himself died, the second and her heirs precede the heirs of the first.
[Ketubot 10:1.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody was married to two women,” etc. The Mishnah refers to ketubah, but for sustenance both are equal. Between ketubah and burial, what has precedence? Between ketubah and a loan attested to by witnesses, what has precedence? Between ketubah and daughters’ dowry, what has precedence? For him who says, one collects for dowry from mortgaged property, daughters’ dowry has precedence. But for him who says, one does not collect for dowry from mortgaged property, daughters’ dowry does not have precedence.
[Ketubot 10:1.3] It says only, “she died”. Therefore, if she was divorced, her status is that of a creditor. As it was stated: “He married a woman and wrote her a ketubah. He divorced her but did not pay the ketubah. He married another woman and wrote her a ketubah. He took back the first one and wrote her a ketubah in addition to the first ketubah . The [second ketubah ] of the first [wife] has precedence over that of the second [wife] and her heirs, and the second [wife] and her heirs have precedence over the heirs of the first.”
[Ketubot 10:1.4] {NAME} says, the heirs of the first say to the heirs of the second: If you are creditors, take what is yours and leave; otherwise let us split evenly between yourselves and us. {NAME} said to him: Biblical inheritance “jumped” on the sons of the second; they take their mother’s ketubah and come back to split. {NAME} said, they disagree if there is an excess denar. But if there is no excess denar, even {NAME} will agree with {NAME} that both parties split evenly. {NAME} said to him, a situation which was stated without disagreement you turn into a disagreement. They must disagree if there is no excess denar. But if there is an excess denar even {NAME} agrees with {NAME} that biblical inheritance “jumped” on the sons of the second; they take their mother’s ketubah and come back to split.
[Ketubot 10:1.5] Debts diminish and, equally, debts add. How is this? If there was a field which in the future would return in the jubilee year, you consider it virtual [property].
[Ketubot 10:1.6] How is that? If he preliminarily married Rachel, definitively married Leah, and only then definitively married Rachel. In the opinion of the rabbis, Rachel has precedence; in the opinion of {NAME} she does not have precedence. They say, even {NAME} will agree that since in the end he definitively married Rachel, Rachel has precedence. To what can this be compared? To one who took out a loan from another person and said to him, if I have not paid it back by twelve months, all my properties shall be mortgaged to you. If the twelfth month arrived and he has not paid back, his properties become mortgaged from that moment on. But if he said, all my properties shall be mortgaged to you only after twelve months, they become mortgaged only after twelve months. The status of the days in between is in dispute between {NAME} and the rabbis. In {NAME} opinion, the properties became pledged by the document. In the rabbis’ opinion, the properties became pledged by the money.
[Ketubot 10:2.1] MISHNAH: If somebody was married to two women who both died, and then he died, and the orphans demand their mothers’ ketubot , if [the estate] is sufficient only for both ketubot they split evenly. If there was an excess denar, these take their mother’s ketubah and those take their mother’s ketubah . If the orphans say, we accept the properties of our father for the value of an extra denar in order to take their mother’s ketubah ; one does not listen to them but one appraises the properties in court.
[Ketubot 10:2.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody was married to two women,” etc. That refers to what {NAME} said, that a man should be induced to give generously to his daughter. If that is so, then even if there is no excess denar? {NAME} said, in case you can uphold their words with the words of the Torah, you uphold their words with the words of the Torah. But in case you cannot uphold their words with the words of the Torah, you disregard their words and uphold the words of the Torah.
[Ketubot 10:2.3] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If one of the brothers died, they all split evenly. {NAME} said, that is necessary if they did not yet divide the estate. You should not say that he should be considered nonexistent and his house should inherit from him. If there was a (male) firstborn, you say the firstborn takes a double portion. What does he take? A double portion among his house or among all brothers? {NAME} stated: If there were two groups of daughters, they all split evenly. If there was a firstborn, you say the firstborn takes a double portion. What does he take? A double portion among his house or among all ketubot ?
[Ketubot 10:2.4] At which point in time does one appraise? The students of {NAME} say, at the end. {NAME} said to them, are you not those who speak in the name of your teacher, “that is necessary if they did not yet divide the estate”? But one assesses from the first moment!
[Ketubot 10:3.1] MISHNAH: If the estate contained expected property, it does not have the status of property in actual possession. {NAME} says, even if there was no mortgageable property, it does not count unless there is mortgageable property in the value of at least a denar more than the two ketubot.
[Ketubot 10:3.2] HALAKHAH: “If the estate contained expected property,” etc. {NAME} said, they disagree about the basic claim of the two ketubot . {NAME} says, real estate, but the rabbis say, movables. But for the excess denar everybody agrees that it is movable. {NAME} said, everybody agrees about the basic claim of the two ketubot that it must be real estate. Where do they disagree? About the excess denar, where {NAME} says, real estate, but the rabbis say, movables. {NAME} in the name of Rav: But in Syria they routinely collect from bronze and bedspreads. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Only from bedspreads of that night. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: The people in Arabia routinely collect from camels and spices. Similarly, only from spices of that night? {NAME} widow collected from movables following her place’s custom.
[Ketubot 10:4.1] MISHNAH: If somebody was married to three women when he died, the ketubah of one was a mina, of the other one 200, and of the other one 300. If the estate is only 100, they divide equally. If it was 200, the one who claims a mina takes 50, and those who claim 200 and 300 each take three gold denars. If it was 300, the one who claims a mina takes 50, the one who claims 200 takes a mina, and the one who claims 300 takes six gold denars. Similarly, if three who invested together lost or gained they would split in this manner.
[Ketubot 10:4.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody was married to three women,” etc. {NAME} said, sharpness of the judges. As in the case of two mortgages written on one field, to whom the court wants to hand it over in possession they hand it over. The Mishnah disagrees with {NAME}: “If the estate is only 100, they divide equally.” Was this said for the sharpness of the judges? And did we not state: If the heirs inherited an instrument of indebtedness, the male firstborn takes a double portion; and if an instrument of indebtedness was presented to them, the male firstborn pays a double portion. Was this said for the sharpness of the judges? {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: There is no difference, whether two mortgages were written on one field or one mortgage was written on two fields, on whom the court decide they hand it over in possession.
[Ketubot 10:4.3] {NAME} said, if they empower one another. If the third empowered the second to deal with the first. She said to her, is not a mina due to you? Take 50 and leave!
[Ketubot 10:4.4] “Similarly, if three who invested together lost or gained they would split in this manner.” {NAME} said: You say that in case the tetradrachma lost or added value. But for earnings or losses they split evenly. That is difficult! One gave 100 denars and the other gave ten, and you say so? The colleagues say, he may say to him, by my contribution the merchandise rose. So far, if they ran after little merchandise. If there was much merchandise? {NAME} said, he may say to him, by the time you sold one piece, I am selling ten. That is, at a nearby place. If it was far away? {NAME} said, he may say to him, by the time you go and return once, I am going and returning ten times. There, we have stated: “If [the ox] gored an ox worth 200, the last one takes 100, the one before him 50, and the two first ones a gold denar.” {NAME} in the name of Rebbi [Ze‘ira]: The same holds for earnings. {NAME} said, the statement of {NAME} disagrees with {NAME}. {NAME} said before {NAME}: Does {NAME} not agree if they contracted between themselves that each can take according to his contribution? Oxen are as if contracted. He turned around and said, they disagree explicitly: {NAME} said, if nothing was said, they split evenly; {NAME} said, if nothing was said, each takes according to his contribution.
[Ketubot 10:5.1] MISHNAH: If somebody was married to four women when he died, the first one precedes the second, the second the third, and the third the fourth. The first one swears to the second, the second to the third, and the third to the fourth; the fourth is paid out without an oath. {NAME} said, should she be preferred because she is the last one? She also should be paid only after an oath. If all [ ketubot ] were executed on the same day, one who precedes another one even if only by an hour has acquired [precedence]; therefore in Jerusalem one used to note hours. If [the documents] were all executed at the same hour and there is only one mina, they split evenly.
[Ketubot 10:5.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody was married to four women when he died,” etc. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: {NAME}, if one document was produced against (the wife) buyers, they all divide evenly. {NAME} said before {NAME}: Does this not disagree with {NAME}, since {NAME} said, sharpness of the judges? As in the case of two mortgages written on one field, to whom they want to hand it over in possession they hand it over. And here, he says so? Not with two mortgages, what about one? He did not hear what {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: There is no difference, whether two mortgages were written on two fields or two mortgages were written on one field, to whom the court decide they hand it over in possession. Rebbi instituted that one follows {NAME} in matters of annona , head taxes, and real estate taxes.
[Ketubot 10:5.3] As the following. Relatives of {NAME} bought fields from the family of {NAME}. Those from the family of {NAME} went and married women, and gave them šeqi‘in .
