Therefore, not if he had it signed and afterwards shaved it off. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Only if he wrote on the male horn. But if he wrote on the sheath it is as if separated and is valid. {NAME} asked: Is that the same for preparation of produce? If he desired that it should rain on an animal and [the rain] dropped from the animal on food. There, {NAME} said “a scroll”, since a scroll is special in not being a living being, so no living being; and here, does he say so? There is a difference since it is written, “any drinkable drink in any vessel shall be impure”. Then also if it rained into cisterns, ditches and caves? There is a difference here, for it is written: “a vessel”.
[Gittin 2:4.1] MISHNAH: One does not write on anything connected to the ground. If he wrote on anything connected, detached it, signed, and delivered it, it is valid, but {NAME} declares it invalid unless both writing and signing took place when it was detached. {NAME} says, one writes neither on erased papyrus nor on διφθέρα because these can be falsified but the Sages declare valid.

[Gittin 2:5.1] MISHNAH: Everybody is acceptable to write the bill of divorce, even an insane, a deaf-and-dumb, or a minor. Everybody is acceptable to bring the bill of divorce except an insane, a deaf-and-dumb, a minor, a blind person, or a Gentile.
[Gittin 2:5.2] HALAKHAH: “Everybody is acceptable to write the bill of divorce,” etc. {NAME} said, only if a sane person watches over them. {NAME} asked: But is it not written: “He shall write for her,” in her name? {NAME} said, it is necessary that one reserve the essential text for him. [Gittin 2:6.1] MISHNAH: If the minor received it and became an adult, the deaf-and-dumb and started talking, the blind and became seeing, the insane and became sane, the Gentile and converted, it remains invalid. But if a hearing person became deaf-and-dumb, then regained his hearing, a seeing person became blind, then regained his vision, a sane person became insane, then regained his sanity, it is valid. This is the principle: Whenever the beginning and the end was in full competence, it is valid.

[Gittin 2:7.1] MISHNAH: Even women who cannot be believed if they say that [a woman’s] husband died are trustworthy to bring her bill of divorce: Her mother-in-law, her mother-in-law’s daughter, her co-wife, her sister-in-law, and her husband’s daughter. What is the difference between divorce and death? The writing is the proof. A woman may herself bring her own bill of divorce, but she still is required to say that it was written and signed before her.
[Gittin 2:7.2] HALAKHAH: “Also those women who cannot be believed if they say that [a woman’s] husband died,” etc. Would you believe her if it was written but not signed [in her presence]? [Gittin 3:1.1] MISHNAH: Every bill of divorce which was not written for a particular wife is invalid. How? If one was walking in the market and heard the scribes dictating “Mr. X divorces his wife Y from place Z” and said, these are mine and my wife’s names, it is invalid and cannot be used to divorce by. In addition, if he wrote [a bill] to divorce his wife but had second thoughts, and a fellow townsman came and said to him, my name is identical with yours and my wife’s name is identical with your wife’s, it is invalid and cannot be used to divorce by. In addition, if he had two wives with identical names and wrote a document to divorce the older one by, he cannot use it to divorce the younger. In addition, if he said to the scribe: write that I may divorce either one I wish, it is invalid and cannot be used to divorce either one.
[Gittin 3:1.2] HALAKHAH: “Every bill of divorce which was not written for a particular wife,” etc. Who is dictating? School teachers. What means “in addition”? There it was not written as a bill of divorce but here it was written as a bill of divorce. What means “in addition”? There it was written neither in his name nor in her name but here it was written in his name but not in her name. What means “in addition”? There it was written in his name but not in her name but here it was written in his name and in her name but it was not written for divorce from the start.
[Gittin 3:1.3] Rav said, none of these are invalid except for the last which is invalid. Issi said, all are invalid except for the first which is not invalid. {NAME} said, all are invalid. The word of {NAME} implied that none are invalid since {NAME} said, if he wrote the essential text with the formula, it is valid. Does the word of {NAME} imply that none are invalid? Since {NAME} asked: if one wrote a bill of preliminary marriage not for a specific name, does preliminary marriage take hold? If he had a problem with divorce, would he ask about preliminary marriage? Since in the case of divorce, where the document is required to be for a specific name and he did not write for a specific name, divorce will not touch her, is it not logical that in the case of preliminary marriage, where a specific name is not required and he did not write for a specific name, preliminary marriage take hold with her? That should be obvious to him. Really, the following is obvious to him: Since one inferred the bill of preliminary marriage only from divorce, and in the case of divorce she is not divorced, in the case of preliminary marriage she is not preliminarily married.

[Gittin 4:1.1] MISHNAH: If somebody sent a bill of divorce to his wife and caught up with the agent, or he sent another agent after him and said: the bill of divorce I gave you is annulled, it is annulled. [Gittin 4:2.3] “Because of the public good.” They say in the name of {NAME}: That she should not risk bastardy. Some say in the name of {NAME}: That she should not remain anchored. He who said, that she should not remain anchored, [is afraid that] she turns out to be anchored if she thought that he annulled when he did not annul. He who said, that she should not risk bastardy, [is afraid that] her children will be bastards if she thought that he did not annul when he annulled, she goes and marries without a bill of divorce. If she thought that he annulled when he did not annul, another man comes and marries her preliminarily; the preliminary marriage is valid but she thinks it is invalid. She waits until her first husband dies, then she goes and marries [another man]; the result is that her children will be bastards. {NAME} said, I went with a caravan and heard {NAME} and {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: That she should not risk bastardy. {NAME} said, even the one who said that she should not remain anchored also agrees that she should not risk bastardy.
[Gittin 4:2.4] If he transgressed and annulled? Let us hear from the following: “If he annulled it is annulled, the words of Rebbi. {NAME} says, he can neither annul it nor add to his condition.” {NAME} says it correctly. What is the reason of Rebbi? It is the word of the Torah that he has the power to annul but they said, he shall not annul. Can their word uproot the words of the Torah? But is it not from the Torah that one may [give as heave] olives for oil and grapes for wine, but because of robbing the tribe they said not only that one may not give heave [in this way] but if he transgressed and gave, his heave is not heave. {NAME} said to {NAME}: Who could tell exactly what your ancestor meant?
[Gittin 4:2.5] “Mr. X and all his names.” Think of it, if his name was Reuben and he went away under the name of Simeon. But: “I am X and every other name which I have.” “In addition, they said if he had two wives, one in Judea and one in Galilee, and he is known by two names, one in Judea and one in Galilee. He used [his name] in Judea to divorce the one in Galilee and [his name] in Galilee to divorce the one in Judea. Neither one is divorced.” This baraita if he was in Judea and wrote to divorce in Galilee or in Galilee and wrote to divorce in Judea. But if he was in Judea and wrote to divorce in Judea, or in Galilee and wrote to divorce in Galilee, she is divorced. {NAME} said, according to the rules he has to say: “I am X with every other name which I have in Galilee.” If he was at another place, he can divorce either one he wishes. {NAME} said, one says that if he did it. But to start out he has to follow {NAME}. {NAME} said, if he is known by (another) name at another place, he has to mention all three.
[Gittin 4:2.6] There, we have stated: “One writes a bill of divorce for a man even if his wife is not with him, and a receipt for a woman even if her husband is not with her, and the husband pays the fee.” {NAME} said, he has to know both of them. {NAME} said, he has to know the husband for the bill of divorce and the wife for her receipt. {NAME} asked before Rebbi [ ]: Think of it, if he brought another woman and divorced by means of her. He said to him, let the witnesses come and testify. But did not {NAME} say that they considered witnesses who signed a document as if their testimony had been cross-examined in court? There, if they said, we did not sign at all. But here if they say, we signed this but not that. The Mishnah disagrees with {NAME}: “In earlier times, his name and her name and the names of his and her towns could change.” If he knows them, why would he change their names? There are people who know others by sight but do not know their names. The Mishnah disagrees with {NAME}: “{NAME} instituted that one should write Mr. X and all his names, Mrs. Y and all her names, because of the public good.” The Mishnah about one who is forced to divorce, {NAME} speaks about one who divorces on his initiative; some want to say if he divorces at another place.
[Gittin 4:2.7] For example Doso, Dodo’s brother, divorced his wife. The case came before the rabbis who said that she should pay the fee. But did we not state: “the husband pays the fee”? {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If she forgives him her ketubah .
[Gittin 4:3.1] MISHNAH: A widow can be paid from the orphans’ property only by an oath. When they avoided letting her swear, {NAME} instituted that she should make a vow on the instruction of the orphans for anything they would decide on and collect her ketubah , and that witnesses sign the bill of divorce because of the public good. Hillel instituted prozbol for the public good.
[Gittin 4:3.2] HALAKHAH: “A widow can be paid from the orphans’ property only,” etc. Earlier they swore falsely and buried their children, since it is written: “For vain [vows] I smote your children.” In addition, they fear vows more than oaths. If she transgressed and swore? {NAME} said, if she swore, she swore. Rav said to his daughter-in-law: If I were not a person readily making concessions, even the cover on your head would be my property. {NAME} said, she acquires the garments which she is wearing. A Mishnah supports {NAME}: “Neither his wife’s garments nor his children’s are his property.”
[Gittin 4:3.3] {NAME} said, why did they require a date on the bill of divorce? Because of an actual case. It so happened that a man was married to his sister’s daughter who committed adultery when she was still married. He predated the bill of divorce and said, it is better she should be judged as single rather than as a married woman.
[Gittin 4:3.4] {NAME} said, I asked before {NAME}: Following him who says tithes are from their words. But following him who says tithes are from the Torah, does Hillel institute anything against the words of the Torah? {NAME} said, from the moment that Israel was exiled to Babylonia, did they not become free from all commandments connected with the Land, but the remission of debts applies both in the Land and outside the Land from the words of the Torah? {NAME} turned and said, ( Deut . 15:2 ) “this is the word of the abandonment, remit” as long as abandonment is followed in the Land as a word of the Torah, remission of debts applies both in the Land and outside the Land from the words of the Torah, but when abandonment is followed in the Land as their word, remission of debts applies both in the Land and outside the Land from their word. There, they say that even one who holds that tithes are from the Torah will hold that the Sabbatical is from their word. ( Deut . 15:2 ): “This is the word of the remission, remit!” Rebbi says, two remissions are the Sabbatical and the Jubilee. As long as the Jubilee is operative, the Sabbatical is from words of the Torah. If the Jubilees are abolished, the Sabbatical is operative from their words. When were the Jubilees abolished? ( Lev . 25:10 ) “For all its inhabitants.” In the time when they lived on it, not when they went from it into exile. If they lived on it but did (not) intermingle, the tribe of Judah in Benjamin, and the tribe of Benjamin in Judah, I could think that the Jubilee was operative. The verse mentions its inhabitants, “All its inhabitants;” you find that when the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh went into exile, the Jubilees were disestablished.
[Gittin 4:4.1] MISHNAH: If a slave was kidnapped and ransomed, if it was as a slave he shall serve, if as a free person he shall not serve; {NAME} says, in any case he shall serve. A slave whom his master gave as mortgage to others and then freed in strict law does not owe anything, but for the public good one forces the master to formally manumit him and he writes a bond for his own value. {NAME} says, only the one who manumits writes.
[Gittin 4:4.2] HALAKHAH: “If a slave was kidnapped and ransomed,” etc. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: It would be logical that even as a slave he should not have to serve. And why did they say, he has to serve? That a slave should not run away to the kidnappers. {NAME} said, a baraita implies this: “His master pays his ransom and frees him.” They said that only about his master, not anybody else. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: It would be logical that even as a free person he should have to serve. Why did they say that he does not have to serve? Not to damage the reputations of free persons. {NAME} said, but it is so: “{NAME} says, in any case he shall serve; just as Israel are obligated to ransom free persons so they are obligated to ransom slaves.” The first Tanna is of the opinion that they are obligated to ransom free persons but they are not obligated to ransom slaves. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Practice follows {NAME}.
[Gittin 4:4.3] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: {NAME} said in the name of Rebbi: A person who had given up hope to recover his slave is not entitled to enslave him but has to write him a bill of manumission. {NAME} heard this and said, {NAME} taught us that correctly. Did they not infer the rules of a bill of manumission from women? Just as a woman is not freed if [the husband] has given up hope, but she needs a bill of divorce from him, so a slave is not freed if [the master] has given up hope, but he needs a bill of manumission.
[Gittin 4:4.4] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If a slave fled from the kidnappers to his master, the master may not enslave him but has to write him a bill of manumission. {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: If somebody declares his slave as ownerless he can neither enslave him nor write him a bill of manumission. {NAME} said to him, everybody says that he needs one; do you say that he does not need? Would he hinder him from eating the Passah [sacrifice]? As it was stated: “The slave of any man, acquisition of his money, if you circumcise him.” Anytime he serves his master, he prevents his master from eating the Passah; if he does not serve his master, he does not prevent his master from eating the Passah.
[Gittin 4:4.5] If [the master] blinded [the slave’s] two eyes simultaneously, or broke two of his teeth simultaneously, the slave thereby obtains his freedom. One after the other, he obtains his freedom from the first [injury] and [the master] has to pay for the second. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Following the opinion that [the master] does not have to write a bill of manumission for him. But following the opinion that [the master] has to write a bill of manumission for him, can you say that he has to pay him? Not only does this apply to one who gains his freedom for a tooth or an eye, from where also that he may gain his freedom by a cap, or הרנירק טיאונוס, or the king’s freedom? The verse says, “he shall send him to freedom”, in any way. What is the status of his children? The children of him who leaves for a tooth or an eye are slaves, the children of him who leaves by the loss of hope are free. {NAME} said, that is unreasonable; it is the other way around. The children of one who leaves for a tooth or an eye are free because the Torah freed him. The children of one who leaves by the loss of hope are slaves because the Torah did not free him.
[Gittin 4:4.6] If a convert died and Jews plundered his property, if there were slaves, either adult or underage, they gain their freedom. {NAME} said, the adults gain their freedom, the minors do not become free. Why? They are no longer property after their owner’s death. Then even adults? {NAME} said, since adults are competent to acquire themselves, they gain their freedom. Minors, who are not competent to acquire for themselves, do not gain their freedom. {NAME} said, practice follows {NAME}. The opinions of {NAME} are contradictory. There, {NAME} in the name of {NAME} and {NAME} in the name of Rebbi said: A person who has given up hope to recover his slave is not entitled to enslave him. They said, what {NAME} said about enslaving, if he did not give, he did not give; perhaps practice would be to enslave him, therefore he has to write him a bill of manumission. And here, he says so! We heard that {NAME} said, {NAME} taught us that correctly, perhaps practice follows {NAME}. The slave girl of {NAME} ran away and he gave up hope to recover her. He went to ask {NAME} and {NAME}. They said, he is not entitled to enslave her. How is it to write her a bill of manumission? They said to him, if you wrote, you did the right thing. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: A slave who married as a free person in the presence of his master gained his freedom. {NAME} said, yesterday I was sitting and formulating: If somebody writes a document of preliminary marriage for his slave or a document of definitive marriage for his girl slave, Rebbi says, they acquired, but the Sages say, they did not acquire. The first Tanna follows Rebbi: he acquired.
[Gittin 4:4.7] Who frees? Rav says, either his first or his second master. {NAME} says, only his first master alone is able to free. {NAME} objected before {NAME}: Does not a baraita disagree with Rav? [Gittin 4:5.1] MISHNAH: A person who is half slave and half free works for his master one day and for himself one day, the words of the House of Hillel. The House of Shammai say, you provided for his master but you did not provide for him. He can marry neither a slave woman nor a free woman: shall he be alone? But the world was created only for procreation and increase, as it is said: “He did not create it to be empty, He formed it to be settled.” For the public good one forces his master to manumit him and he writes a bond for half his value. The House of Hillel changed and instructed following the House of Shammai.
[Gittin 4:5.2] HALAKHAH: “A person who is half slave and half free,” etc. How is it possible that anyone be half slave and half free? Explain it either following Rebbi, since Rebbi said that a person can free half of his slave, or following everybody in the case of a slave belonging to two partners, when one of them manumitted his part. If he found anything of value, on his master’s day it belongs to his master, on his own day it belongs to him. But would he not on the next day turn it over to his master? If he entered a preliminary marriage. On his master’s day, one would not consider his marriage, on his own day one would consider his marriage. But did not {NAME} say in {NAME} name: If a person who is half slave and half free entered a preliminary marriage, one does not consider his marriage. In parallel, if he divorced one does not consider his divorce.

[Gittin 4:6.1] MISHNAH: If somebody sells his slave to Gentiles or outside the Land, the slave gains his freedom. One does not smuggle kidnap victims out because of the public good; {NAME} says, because of the welfare of the kidnap victims. One does not buy Torah scrolls, phylacteries, and mezuzot from Gentiles for more than their worth because of the public good.
[Gittin 4:6.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody sells his slave to Gentiles,” etc. To a Gentile even in the Land. Who frees him? His original owner pays for him and the second frees him. “Or outside the Land,” even to a Jew. Let us say that if the second owner knew, both of them split the price; otherwise the first pays for him and the second frees him. “I X ben Y sold my slave Z to Antiochia”, he gains his freedom. But if he is in Lydda, he did not gain his freedom. It was stated: A slave goes outside the Land with his master. Therefore, if he sold him there, he is sold. If he came from outside the Land to the Land with the intention to return, one forces him to return. With the intention not to return, one does not force him to return. If he fled from outside the Land to the Land, he may return him. If he fled from the Land to outside the Land, {NAME} in the name of the Elder {NAME} said, it is permigtted. The great {NAME} said, it is permitted. {NAME}, the son of the great {NAME} said, it is forbidden. {NAME} said, they do not disagree. He who says, it is permitted, if he is used to flee there. But he who says, it is forbidden, if he is not used to flee there. {NAME} said, they do not disagree. He who says, it is permitted, if he can return him from there; but he who says, it is forbidden, if he cannot return him from there.
[Gittin 4:6.3] There could be terms. If he entered into terms with him, it is permitted. That means, with adults. With minors, the terms can be with their masters. That is, if the master was a Jew. If he was Gentile? {NAME} sold his slave and entered into terms with his master. {NAME} the goldsmith had slaves who fled to Bnoton. [Gittin 4:6.5] It was stated: “It is prohibited to buy from a Gentile who sells Torah scrolls, phylacteries, and mezuzot .” But was it not stated: “It happened that a Gentile in Sidon sold phylacteries and mezuzot . The case came before the Sages who said that it was permitted to buy from him.” That one was a Gentile who reverted to his error.
[Gittin 4:7.1] MISHNAH: If somebody divorces his wife because of bad reputation, he cannot take her back; because of a vow, he cannot take her back. {NAME} says, for any vow known in public, he cannot take her back; not known in public, he can take her back. {NAME} says, for any vow which needs investigation by a Sage, he cannot take her back; if it does not need investigation by a Sage, he can take her back. {NAME} said, they forbade one because of the other. {NAME} said, it happened in Sidon that one said to his wife, a qonam if I do not divorce you, and he divorced her, and the Sages permitted him to take her back, for the public good.
[Gittin 4:7.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody divorces his wife because of bad reputation,” etc. And it was stated: “Why did the Sages say that he who divorces his wife because of bad reputation cannot take her back? For if he divorced his wife because of bad reputation, when she went, married another, and bore him children, after some time it turned out that the accusations were baseless and he said, if I had known that the accusations were baseless, even if somebody had offered me a hundred minas for my wife I would not have divorced her, then the bill of divorce would be invalidated and her children bastards. But since he knows that if he divorces her, she will be forbidden to return to him, from the start he gives her a perfect bill of divorce.”
[Gittin 4:7.3] It was stated: “Why did they say that he who divorces his wife because of a vow cannot take her back? For if he divorced his wife because of a vow, when she went, married another, and bore him children, after some time it turned out that the vow was void and he said, if I had known that the vow was void, even if somebody had offered me a hundred minas for my wife I would not have divorced her, then the bill of divorce would be invalidated and her child a bastard. But since he knows that if he divorces her, she will be forbidden to return to him, from the start he gives her a perfect bill of divorce.” {NAME} said, you can see that he was looking for a pretext to divorce her since it must have been a vow which does not need investigation by a Sage! {NAME} said, you can see that he was looking for a pretext to divorce her since it must have been a vow which was not public knowledge! “{NAME} said, they forbade one because of the other.” The law should be that he can take her back even if it was a vow which needs investigation by a Sage, for the Elder uproots the vow. Why did they forbid a vow which needs investigation by a Sage? Because of a vow which does not need investigation by a Sage.
[Gittin 4:8.1] MISHNAH: If somebody divorces his wife because she is a she-ram, {NAME} says, he cannot take her back, but the Sages say, he may take her back. [Gittin 5:1.1] MISHNAH: For tort victims one estimates with best quality land, for a creditor with average quality, and for a woman’s ketubah with lowest quality. {NAME} says, also for a woman’s ketubah with average quality.
[Gittin 5:1.2] HALAKHAH: “For tort victims one estimates with best quality land,” etc. “By an inference de minore ad maius , for Temple property.” {NAME} said before {NAME}, where do we hold? If to qualify as damages, is that not what we stated “his neighbor’s ox” but not the ox of Temple property? If for bodily damages, is that not what {NAME} stated: A private person can claim damages but not the Temple? But we must deal with one who said, I obligate myself to give 100 minas to the Temple, when his ox went and did damage. You should not say, [the Temple] is a creditor and should collect from average quality land. Therefore, it was necessary to say that “for tort victims one estimates with best quality land, by an inference de minore ad maius , for Temple property.”
[Gittin 5:1.3] {NAME} stated: “Full and partial damages are collected from encumbered property.” One understands full damages. Are partial damages not collected from the animal’s body? {NAME} said, explain it when it was a docile ox which did damage and then his owner went and sold it. Its body already was encumbered to the injured party. {NAME} said, explain it if he converted it into a loan. Then it should be foreclosed only by average quality land! Since the debt originated in a damage claim, he may collect from best quality.
[Gittin 5:1.4] “His field”, except if it was mortgaged. “His vineyard”, except Temple property. Where do we hold? If somebody caused damage and then dedicated to the Temple, that is what we have stated: “If he dedicated 90 minas but his debt was 100 minas.” If somebody dedicated to the Temple and then caused damage, that is what we have stated: “ ‘His neighbor’s ox’ but not the ox of Temple property.” {NAME} said, explain it if an ox of Temple property grazed on a private field. {NAME} told him, we require Temple real estate and you say “on a private field”? But we must hold about one who said: I am obligating myself for 100 minas to the Temple; then went and caused damage. You should not say that between damages and a loan given before witnesses damages are privileged, and here damages are privileged against the Temple; therefore it was necessary to say “his vineyard”, except Temple property.
[Gittin 5:1.5] “His field,” except movables. “His vineyard,” except potential property which is not similar in status to that in possession. “ ‘His field,’ except movables.” About those who did not claim movables from the start. Is this different from what we stated: There is not only real estate; from where if he wanted to pay money? The verse says: “Money he shall return to its owner.” What did you mean to say that real estate is primary? Or should we say that money is primary? Then it should be irrevocably given to [the claimant] from the start! Do we not see rabbis who irrevocably give him real estate! “ ‘His vineyard,’ except potential property which is not similar in status to that in possession.” {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If his father dug a cistern which caused injury during his father’s lifetime. Property fell to him after his father’s death. I might say that this property should be encumbered for that damage; therefore, it was necessary to say “his vineyard” to except potential property which is not similar in status to that in possession.
[Gittin 5:1.6] “The best of his field and the best of his vineyard he shall pay,” i. e., the party responsible for the damage, the words of {NAME}. {NAME} says, “the best of his field and the best of his vineyard”, of the person suffering the damage. It is difficult for {NAME}, he suffered damage, and you say so? But the court see what the field was worth before it was damaged and estimates accordingly. As it was stated, it is possible if the grazing was on best quality land, one estimates from best quality, from lowest quality one estimates from lowest quality. How is this? The best of the lowest quality is quite good. If you say so you provide a windfall for the person suffering the damage. One looks at the field as if it was full of first quality [produce] and estimates for him from the best quality land; least quality one estimates from least quality land. It turns out that he pays with best quality for best quality and from least quality for least quality. From where has {NAME} that “for tort victims one estimates with best quality land”? It is not from the Torah, it is a decree. “Why did they say, ‘for tort victims one estimates with best quality land’? Because of the robbers. That a man should say, why should I have robbed [land] in my hand, or land subject to a suit for damages on my hand? Tomorrow, the court will see my good field, take it from me, and support it by the verse, ‘the best of his field and the best of his vineyard he shall pay.’ ” So far his real estate. His pledge was inferred from his real estate. Since his real estate [is taken] from the best quality, also his pledge [is taken] from the best.
[Gittin 5:1.7] ” ‘For creditors, average quality,’ because of tricksters. That a man should not see a desirable field in his neighbor’s hand, lend him money, and contrives to take it from him. Then one should estimate only from the least quality! {NAME} said, that is correct; but not to lock the door before people needing to borrow. For tomorrow he may need to borrow and does not find [a lender.]”
[Gittin 5:1.8] {NAME} preached: “And the man,” that is the agent of the court. For if the creditor enters, he removes the best. If the borrower enters, he removes the worst. How is this? The agent of the court enters and removes from average quality. {NAME} says, it is a word from the Torah that the creditor should enter, for it is written: “The man whose creditor you are should bring the pledge out for you.” That is, his pledge. His real estate was inferred from his pledge. Since his pledge [is taken] from average quality, also his real estate [is taken] from average quality.
[Gittin 5:1.9] This is obvious: A loan that is disputed is not remitted. A loan that was disputed but is now a [confirmed] loan, is remitted. {NAME} asked: Is this also true for judgments? A loan that was disputed can be collected. A disputed loan turned into a [confirmed] loan is collected from property of average quality.
[Gittin 5:1.10] If there is only best quality, one collects from the best quality, [only] average quality one collects from average quality, [only] worst quality one collects from worst quality. Best and average, torts are assessed from best quality, creditors and a woman’s ketubah from average. Average and worst, torts and creditors are assessed from average, a woman’s ketubah from worst. If his best quality was like everybody’s best quality, it is best quality. If his average quality was like everybody’s average quality, it is average quality. If his worst quality was like everybody’s worst quality, it is worst quality. If his best quality was like everybody’s average? {NAME} and {NAME} asked: Let us hear from the following: Average and worst, torts and creditors are assessed from average, a woman’s ketubah from worst. But just as you need in the case that you have best and average quality, torts push creditors to the average, so in this case, of average and worst quality, should not torts push creditors to the worst quality? {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Explain it that he had best quality which he sold, and the creditors were already pushed to average quality.
[Gittin 5:1.11] “For a woman’s ketubah with lowest quality.” {NAME} said, they taught only for a ketubah of a mina or 200 [ zuz ], but a ketubah of a thousand denar she collects from average quality. {NAME} said, even a ketubah of a thousand denar she collects only from lowest quality. It turns out that this disagreement parallels the following disagreement: “While she lives in her father’s house, she always can collect her ketubah ; if she lives in her husband’s house, she can collect her ketubah for 25 years.” {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: One stated this only for the ketubah of a mina or 200 [ zuz ]. But a ketubah of 1’000 denar she collects forever. {NAME} quoted in the name of {NAME}: Even a ketubah of 1’000 denar she can collect only up to 25 years. It turns out that {NAME} follows {NAME} and {NAME} {NAME}. As we have stated there: “If somebody signs over his property to his sons and signs over some real estate to his wife, she loses her claim to ketubah .” Rav said, if he sells through her. {NAME} says, if he distributes in her presence. {NAME} said, they stated here a relaxation of the laws of ketubah . {NAME} said, the reason of {NAME} is that it applies not only to a ketubah of a mina or two hundred, but even regarding a ketubah of one thousand denar they proclaimed a relaxation of the laws of ketubah .
[Gittin 5:2.1] MISHNAH: One does not collect from encumbered property as long as there is free property, even if the latter is of lowest quality. One may collect from orphans’ property only from the lowest quality.
[Gittin 5:2.2] HALAKHAH: “One cannot collect for usufruct,” etc. {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: One pays from an orphan’s property only a document on which interest is due, and some say, also a woman’s ketubah . {NAME} said, because of her sustenance. {NAME} said, who is worried about sustenance? {NAME}! Since {NAME} said, it depends on the collection. What about it? For attraction, that everybody should be eager to marry her. Some say, also for robbery and torts. {NAME} said, we stated both of these. Robbery from the following: “If it was mortgageable, he has to pay.” For torts from the following: “One pays from an orphan’s property only from the least valuable.” So is the Mishnah: One pays for torts from an orphan’s property only from the least valuable. But was it not stated: If the son took his father’s place, one estimates torts from the most valuable land, creditors from average quality, and a woman’s ketubah from the least valuable. {NAME} said, there about an adult orphan, here about an underage orphan.
[Gittin 5:3.1] MISHNAH: One cannot collect for usufruct, for improvement of the land, or for sustenance of the wife and the daughters from incumbered property, for the public good.
[Gittin 5:3.2] HALAKHAH: “One does not collect from encumbered property,” etc. {NAME} said, because they have no fixed amount.
[Gittin 5:3.3] If [Reuben] robbed a field from Simeon and sold it to Levi, then Simeon came and foreclosed it from Levi; then Levi collects from Reuben’s encumbered property and Simeon collects the usufruct from Levi’s free property. If Levi in the meantime improved [the property], Levi collects the capital from Reuben’s encumbered property and the improvement from Simeon’s free property. {NAME} in the name of {NAME} said, only if a third party’s buying preceded the improvement by this one. But if the improvement by this one preceded a third party’s buying, Levi can collect the capital even from Simeon’s encumbered property. {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of {NAME} said: With usufruct one proceeds in the same way. If he spent four denars and the improvement is worth six, Levi collects four denars from Reuben’s encumbered property and another two from Simeon’s free property. {NAME} in the name of the rabbis there: Since he did not enter with permission, his hand is weak against Simeon. {NAME} in the name of the rabbis there: Since he entered with permission, his hand is strong against Reuben.
[Gittin 5:3.4] Reuben robbed a field from Simeon and sold it to Levi; Levi went and gave it to Jehudah as a gift. Then Simeon foreclosed it from Jehudah. Jehudah has no regress on Levi since it was a gift. Levi has regress on Reuben since it was a sale. Did he not give it away as a gift? He can say to him, it was my intention to give it to him so he would return me favors. Reuben robbed a field from Simeon and gave it to Levi as a gift; Levi sold it to Jehudah. Jehudah has regress on Levi since he sold it; Levi has no regress on Reuben since it was a gift; as {NAME} said in the name of the rabbis: No easement is created by a gift.
[Gittin 5:3.5] Reuben robbed a field from Simeon and sold it to Levi, and he did not have time to write the foreclosure document before he died: whose is it? {NAME} and {NAME}: One said, if he wrote the foreclosure document, it is Reuben’s, if not, it is Levi’s. The other one said, whether he wrote or did not write, it belongs to Levi. {NAME} said, it is reasonable that it does not belong to Reuben since he can say to him, I sold you something which was not mine. {NAME} said, it is not reasonable that it should not be Levi’s, since Reuben can tell him, is this not before you? You are good to confirm the sale.
[Gittin 5:3.6] Can one collect dowry from encumbered property? {NAME} said that {NAME} does not collect. Who collects? {NAME} and {NAME} collect. {NAME} was appointed custodian of orphans’ property. There were orphan [girls] who asked for dowry. They stood up and complained.

For the sister of {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Even if they died, the widow is sustained by them.
[Gittin 5:3.9] What is the situation of grandchildren? {NAME} said, grandchildren are like children. {NAME} said, grandchildren are not like children. {NAME} and {NAME} were sitting together. They wanted to say, the same situation applies to grandchildren here as there. {NAME} said to them, inheritance by biblical law jumped on grandchildren.
[Gittin 5:3.10] There, we have stated: “You have in your hand a mina of my father’s; you have to get from me only 50 denars. He does not have to swear since he is like a person who returns a find.” {NAME} said, in this case they instituted a regulation as they instituted for a find, as we have stated: “The finder of a lost object shall not swear because of the public good.” {NAME} said, this Mishnah [applies] when he said to him, you found my two oxen. But if he said, I found your two oxen and returned both of them, but the other said, you returned only one, in that case they did not institute the rule. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: In this case they did institute. But in the first case, it is a word of the Torah, as it was stated: I could think that if he said to him, you found my two oxen, but the other said, I found only one, should he be obligated [to swear]? The verse says, “or if he found a find and disowned it;” that excludes this one who did not disown. But if he said to him, I was standing on my roof when I saw you dragging away two tied oxen, two tied oxen you dragged away from me, and he says, only one I dragged away; in that case they made no regulation. Similarly: “I was standing with my father when he was dying and he claimed from you a mina and you agreed to it,” and the other says, “I agreed only for 50;” in that case they made no regulation.
[Gittin 5:4.1] MISHNAH: If orphans rely on a property owner or if their father appointed a guardian for them; these are obligated to tithe their produce. A guardian appointed by the orphans’ father shall be made to swear; if he was appointed by the court he shall not be made to swear. {NAME} says, it is the other way around.
[Gittin 5:4.2] HALAKHAH: “If orphans rely on a property owner, etc.” ( Num . 18:28 ) “you” excludes partners, “you” excludes guardians, “you” excludes one who gives heave from what is not his. Did we not state ( Terumot 3:3): “Partners who gave heave one after the other?” But one must be for Great Heave, the other for heave of the tithe. Did we not infer the laws of the Great Heave from heave of the tithe? But one is for practice, the other for action. “You” excludes guardians; but did we not state: “Orphans dependent on a home owner, or for whom the father had appointed a guardian, must tithe their produce.” The colleagues say, here for a permanent guardian, there for a temporary guardian. {NAME} asked, does that apply to: “he may sell slaves but not real estate?” But here one deals with an adult orphan, there with an underage orphan.
[Gittin 5:4.3] {NAME} said, as a matter of principle one does not appoint guardians for orphans to their detriment, only to their profit; but if they are detrimental, they are detrimental. {NAME} said, neither as a matter of principle nor as a reaction, neither for profit not for detriment. A Mishnah disagrees with {NAME}: “One appoints a guardian for them” There is a difference about an ox, lest it continue to cause damage. If it did do damage, from whom does one take payment? {NAME} said, from the orphans. {NAME} said, from the guardian. And even if {NAME} never taught this, does not his word imply it since he said if in the end they are detrimental, they are detrimental?
[Gittin 5:4.4] A guardian appointed by the orphans’ father shall be made to swear, for usually he is not checked out. If he was appointed by the court he shall not be made to swear for usually he was checked out. {NAME} says, it is the other way around; a guardian appointed by the orphans’ father shall be made to swear, for he is like one who is paid; if he was appointed by the court he shall not be made to swear for for he can say to him, I am doing this as a favor to you. It turns out that {NAME} follows the rabbis and {NAME} {NAME}. Does {NAME} follow the rabbis? Even if he holds with {NAME}, a person acts as a trustee in order to be declared trustworthy. Does {NAME} [follow] {NAME}? Even if he holds with the rabbis, a person is apt to slip away from an oath but not from payments.
[Gittin 5:5.1] MISHNAH: If someone causes impurity, or dema‘ , or libation wine, if it was unintentional he is free, intentional he is obligated. If Cohanim in the Temple intentionally made [a sacrifice] piggul , they have to pay.
[Gittin 5:5.2] HALAKHAH: {NAME} did not go to the assembly. He was standing with {NAME} and asked him, what new was said? He said: So says {NAME}, a person causing impurity does not have the status of a perpetrator, fromthe following: “Heave which became impure.” He answered: Explain it, if it became impure by itself; then you cannot infer anything, because of a Mishnah: “If somebody judged, absolved the guilty and obligated the innocent, declared the pure impure and the impure pure.” For {NAME} said in the name of Rav: If he touched it with his hand. {NAME} said: If he touched it with his hand. {NAME} says, it should have been logical that even intentionally he should have been free. Why did they say that he is obligated? That he should tell. And {NAME} said, it should have been logical that even unintentionally he should have been obligated. Why did they say that he is free? Because of a fine. The strength of {NAME} comes from this: “If someone causes anything to become impure, or dema‘ , or libation wine, if it was unintentional he is free, intentional he is obligated,” and {NAME} said, he pays a fine. A baraita supports {NAME}: “A person who puts a yoke on another’s cow is free in human law but guilty in Heaven’s law.”
[Gittin 5:5.3] So far if he thought that it was profane. If he knew that it was heave but he thought that it was permitted to make it impure? Let ushear from the following: “If Cohanim in the Temple intentionally made [a sacrifice] piggul , they have to pay.” Could the Cohen think that it was profane? Is there piggul of profane things? But we must hold that he knew that it was holy but thought that it was permitted to make piggul of sacrifices. And here, if he knew that it was heave but thought that it was permitted to make it impure.
[Gittin 5:5.4] {NAME} in the name of Rav: If he mixed. If he made a libation and then mixed it, at the start he committed a capital crime and at the end he has to pay? {NAME} objected: Think of it, if he killed somebody and broke the flask, at the start he committed a capital crime and in the end he has to pay? {NAME} objected: Think of it, if he set fire to somebody’s grain stack on the Day of Atonement, at the start he committed a capital crime and in the end he has to pay? “If someone causes anything to become impure, or turn into dema‘ , or libation wine, if it was unintentional he is free, intentional he is obligated,” and {NAME} said, he pays a fine.
[Gittin 5:6.1] MISHNAH: {NAME} testified about a deaf-mute girl who was married off by her father, that she must be divorced by a bill of divorce, and about an underage girl who was married to a Cohen, that she may eat heave and her husband inherits from her if she dies, and about a stolen log which was used to build a house, that [the owner] has to take the value, and about a purification sacrifice of a stolen animal which was not known in public, that it atones because of the order of the altar.
[Gittin 5:6.2] HALAKHAH: “{NAME} testified,” etc. {NAME} asked before {NAME}. His testimony seems reasonable for a hearing woman of sound mind, that she is divorced with or without her acquiescence. But a deaf-mute woman who has no will should not be divorced except with her acquiescence. But is it not testimony “that is an example”; does one add to a testimony? {NAME} is of the opinion that this refers to a hearing girl who was married off by her father (and mother) and became deaf-and-dumb. {NAME} is of the opinion that this refers to an underage girl who was married off by her father (and mother) and became divorced.
[Gittin 5:6.3] {NAME} said, why did they say “an Israel underage girl eats heave,” that all should be eager to marry her for her attractiveness. {NAME} said, only if she knows how to keep her [valuables given for] preliminary marriage. {NAME} said, a Mishnah said so, “married to a Cohen she eats heave.” {NAME} said, since {NAME} said, for her attractiveness, that means, even if she does not know how to keep her [valuables given for] preliminary marriage.
[Gittin 5:6.4] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: An underage girl has no definitive marriage to let her eat heave. {NAME} said, a Mishnah said so, “married to a Cohen she eats heave.” {NAME} asked: If she was definitively married but had no intercourse, [the husband] sent her to her father’s house and she grew up, may she eat heave? Let us hear from the following: “Based on her earlier definitive marriage.”
[Gittin 5:6.5] “If somebody stole a log and used it in building. The House of Shammai say, he has to tear down the entire building and return it. If he stole it planed, but if he stole and planed it himself, he owes him money. If he stole and planed it on the spot, what is the rule? Since {NAME} said, because of civilisation, this implies that there is no difference between the Land and outside the Land. If he wants to take [the value of] his logs and stones, what is the rule? One tells him, wait until he dwells in it. {NAME} said, one pays him immediately.
[Gittin 5:6.6] {NAME}: By law, it should not atone even if it was [not] known in public. Why did they say that it atones? Not to let the altar be deserted. {NAME} said, by law, it should atone even if it was known in public. Why did they say that it does not atone? Not to let the altar accept robberies. How many are “public”? {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Three people. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: “You brought robbed goods with the lame and the sick.” Since lame and sick are obvious, so everything must be obvious.
[Gittin 5:7.1] MISHNAH: There was no law of siqarii in Judea for those killed in the war. After those killed in the war there was a law of siqarii . How is this? If one bought from a siqarius and afterwards from the original owner, his acquisition is void; from the original owner and afterwards from the siqarius , his acquisition is valid. If one bought from a husband and afterwards from the wife, his acquisition is void; from the wife and afterwards from the husband, his acquisition is valid. This is the earlier Mishnah; a later court said that he who buys from a siqarius gives a quarter to the original owner. When is this? If they have no means to buy, but if they have the means to buy, they precede everybody else. Rebbi (Joshua) assembled a court who voted that if it was in the siqarius ’s hand for twelve months, any who wants to buy shall buy and give a quarter to the original owner.
[Gittin 5:7.2] HALAKHAH: “There was no law of siqariqon in Judea” etc. In earlier times they decided on a persecution in Judea because they had a tradition from their forefathers that Jehudah had killed Esaw, as it is written: “Your hand is on your enemies’ neck.” They went and enslaved them, took their fields and sold them to third parties. The original owners could come and repossess; therefore the land was left absolutely in the hand of the siqariqon since they refrained from buying. “They decreed that the law of siqariqon should not apply in Jehudah. When was this said? About war killings before the war. But about anybody killed in and after the war, the notion of siqariqon does not apply.” But are those killed before the war not like those killed after the war? Explain it that a siqariqon came and robbed and suppressed; there was no time left to write the sales contract before murder engulfed the entire world, that practice should not be partial.
[Gittin 5:7.3] “The law of siqariqon always applies in Galilee.” The law of siqariqon does not apply to movables. It was stated: “The law of siqariqon does not apply to foreclosures for a debt and for tenant fees. [A foreclosure for nonpayment of] tenant fees waits twelve months for the owners.” {NAME} said, after twelve months one announces on four consecutive Sabbaths. He explained it in two ways. If he took it from a tenant and gave it to a tenant and the first wants to foreclose, he says to him, are you not a tenant? Leave it for me and what you cut, you cut. If he took it from the owner and gave it to a tenant, the [owner] wants to foreclose, he tells him, what use do you have if you take it from me and he will take it from you, but what I can afford I shall give to you.
[Gittin 5:7.4] So far, if there were two contracts. If there was one contract? {NAME} and {NAME} both say, certainly the sale is invalid; i. e., if he bought from the wife and then bought from the husband. {NAME} and {NAME} both said, certainly the sale is valid; i. e., if he bought from the husband and then bought from the wife. But is not all the wife’s property administered by the husband? For the yield.
[Gittin 5:7.5] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: So it is: If he sold to a first person and she signed, to a second and a third and she signed, she can collect from the last. If it is insufficient, she collects from the one before the last. If this is insufficient, she collects from the one before the penultimate. On this, Rav said: For property which she brought him in her ketubah . But property which she brought to him as paraphernalia, she collects from any she wants.

The artless, small children. {NAME} said, because of their livelihood. {NAME} said, even though {NAME} raises difficulties in collecting forfeits, he agrees that those who give their children to artisans that they collect forfeits because of the livelihood of people.
[Gittin 5:9.1] MISHNAH: The following was said for communal peace: A Cohen reads first, after him a Levite, after him an Israel, for communal peace. Traps for wild animals, birds, or fish fall under the category of robbery, for communal peace; {NAME} says, complete robbery. [Gittin 5:9.2] HALAKHAH: “The following was said for communal peace,” etc. The saying of {NAME} implies that it is of the words of the Torah, for {NAME} stated: “Moses wrote this Torah and gave it to the Cohanim, the Levites (etc.)” and afterwards “to all the Elders of Israel.” The saying of {NAME} implies that it is of their words, as {NAME} said, never did I recite the benediction before a Cohen and I did not allow an Israel to do it before him. The saying of {NAME} implies that it is of their words, as {NAME} said, in a city of only Cohanim, an Israel reads first because of communal peace.
[Gittin 5:9.3] {NAME} and {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: In a city of only Cohanim, all of them lift their hands. For whom do they recite the blessing? For their brothers to the North and South. [Gittin 5:9.4] “One puts an eruv in an old house.” {NAME} said, the Mishnah speaks of a prior dweller.
[Gittin 5:9.5] “A cistern which is close to a water canal is filled first.” Only if it passes through it. {NAME} said, even if it is close by. There, they say what is farther away but easy to drink from precedes one which is close by but difficult to drink from.
[Gittin 5:9.6] Following the opinion of the rabbis there it is acceptable since there, they say in the name of {NAME}: One to whom one gives a nut and he throws it away, a pebble and he keeps it, what is found in his hand is as if found on a garbage heap; a nut and he keeps it, a pebble and he throws it away, what is robbed from him is robbed because of communal peace; a nut or a pebble he takes, hides them, and produces them later, what is robbed from him is total robbery. He can acquire for himself but not for others. {NAME} said, just as he can acquire for himself so he can acquire for others. Everybody agrees that his gift is not a gift since it is written ( Ex . 22:6 ): “If a man give.” The gift of a man is a gift, but the gift of a minor is no gift, the words of the Sages. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of {NAME}, robbing from him is not clear unless he grew two pubic hairs. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}, that is, to recover from him by a law suit, but to have to bring a sacrifice for [a false] oath only if he grew two pubic hairs. But following the rabbis here, {NAME} asked that even for himself he should not be able to acquire since it is written ( Ex . 22:6 ): “A man to his neighbor”, until he be like his neighbor. {NAME} in the name of {NAME} explained it by the method of the artless. As we have stated there: “For underage children, their buying is buying and their selling selling, for movables.” But did we not state there: “He cannot make them acquire through his minor son or daughter or his Canaanite male or female slave, because their hand is like his hand.” {NAME} say, here a minor with knowledge, there a minor without knowledge.
[Gittin 5:9.7] “Traps for wild animals, birds,” etc. That is, about large ones. But small ones are as if inside his house.
[Gittin 5:9.8] “If a poor person knocks off [olives] from high up in the olive tree, what is under him falls under the category of robbery, for communal peace; {NAME} says, complete robbery.” That means, on the earth. But if he plucks with his hand, his hand acquires for him.
[Gittin 5:9.9] “One does not hinder poor Gentiles [from taking] gleanings, forgotten sheaves, or peah , for communal peace.” It was stated: “In a town where Gentiles and Jews live together, one appoints overseers of charity from Gentiles and Jews; one provides for the Gentile and Jewish poor, visits Gentile and Jewish sick, buries Gentile and Jewish dead, and consoles Gentile and Jewish mourners. Also, one washes Gentile and Jewish clothes for the sake of peaceful coexistence.”
[Gittin 5:9.10] A weaver asked {NAME}, what about a Gentile wedding feast? He wanted to permit it to them from this: “Because of peaceful coexistence.” {NAME} told them, did not {NAME} state that the holiday of a Gentile wedding feast is forbidden? {NAME} said, if it had not been for {NAME}, we would have come to permit their strange worship; praised be He Who separated us from them.
[Gittin 5:10.1] MISHNAH: A woman may lend to her neighbor, whom she suspects in matters of the Sabbatical, a coarse sieve, a fine sieve, grindstones, or an oven, but she should neither cull nor grind with her. The wife of a Fellow may lend to the wife of a vulgar a coarse sieve and a fine sieve, she may cull, grind, and sift with her, but she may not touch hers once water has been put in because one does not support transgressors. All this has only been said for communal peace. One encourages Gentiles in the Sabbatical year but not Jews. One greets them for communal peace.
[Gittin 5:10.2] HALAKHAH: “A woman may lend to her neighbor,” etc. {NAME} asked before {NAME}: Does our Mishnah deal with the implicit case, rather than the explicit? He said to him, is the implicit case not explicit? He said to him, I can say a coarse sieve to count coins, a sieve to sift sand, grindstones to grind spices, a stove to put in flax bundles.
[Gittin 5:10.3] {NAME} asked: For what did they impose a fine? At a place where they sow and eat or at a place where they sow but do not eat? What is the difference? If one saw him buying from Saracens. It is forbidden; if you say at a place where they sow and eat, if one saw him buying from Saracens it is permitted.
[Gittin 5:10.4] {NAME} asked: Has this been said for all of this chapter or only for this Mishnah? {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: From the fact that we state this Mishnah in Giṭṭin it follows that it was said only for this Mishnah.
[Gittin 5:10.5] There, we have stated: One does not knead or form bread with a baker working in impurity. And it was stated additionally: One should neither cull nor grind with him. And here, it says so? {NAME} said, here for profane [bread], there for heave. Can you say heave at a baker’s? The colleagues say, one if he washes, there if he does not wash. The Mishnah supports the colleagues: “But she may not touch hers once water has been put in.”
[Gittin 5:10.6] {NAME}, {NAME}. One said: “Plough it well then, I will rent it from you after the Sabbatical.” The other one said: “May you succeed” For him who says, plough it well, then I will rent it from you after the Sabbatical, what means “one greets them” in a Jewish way? “May you succeed.” For him who says to the Gentile “may you succeed”? Explanation: {NAME} and {NAME} passed by one of the ploughmen in the Sabbatical. {NAME} said to him, are you not Jewish? {NAME} said to him, did not Rebbi teach us ( Ps . 129:8 ): “The passers-by did not say, the blessing of the Eternal be on you,” these are the nations of the world who pass out of the world, they did not say to Israel “the blessing of the Eternal is on you.” What does Israel say to them, “we bless you in the Name of the Eternal.” All blessings that come into the world because of us are not enough for you; not only do you not say, come and take from these blessings for yourselves, but you roll over us pro-rated contributions and fines, head taxes and annonae .
[Gittin 6:1.1] MISHNAH: Somebody who says, accept this bill of divorce for my wife, or bring this bill of divorce to my wife, may retract if he wants to retract. If a woman said, accept the bill of divorce for me, he cannot retract even if he wants to retract. Therefore, if the husband said, it is not possible for me that you accept for her but bring and deliver it to her, he may retract if he wants to retract. {NAME} says, even if she says, take my the bill of divorce for me, he cannot retract even if he wants to retract.
[Gittin 6:1.2] HALAKHAH: “Somebody who says, accept this bill of divorce for my wife,” etc. Everywhere you say that “accept” is the equivalent of “obtain,” but here you say that “accept” is the equivalent of “bring”? There is a difference, for one can obtain something for a person without him being present. {NAME} objected: Think of it, if she was shouting to obtain a divorce? I say, maybe she changed her mind. But did we not state: “A woman herself may bring her bill of divorce”? Could you say that she may have changed her mind? There, she is damaging herself; here it is to her detriment.
[Gittin 6:1.3] {NAME} said: If she said, bring me my bill of divorce, but he went and said to him, your wife said, accept the bill of divorce for me, even after the bill came into her hand it is not a valid bill of divorce, since he thinks that she will be divorced by the acceptance of the agent but she can be divorced only by her own acceptance. {NAME} objected: But did we not state that if a woman said, accept the bill of divorce for me, it is not a valid bill of divorce until it reaches her hand? Then even if the bill came into her hand it should not be a valid bill! For she thinks that she will be divorced by the acceptance of the agent but she can be divorced only by her own acceptance. If he knows that practice is that “accept” and “obtain” mean “bring”. But did we not state: “If an underage girl said, accept the bill of divorce for me, it is not a valid bill until the bill of divorce reaches her hand.” Then it should not be a valid bill even if the bill of divorce reaches her hand. For she thinks that maybe she is divorced by the acceptance of the agent, but she can be divorced only by her own acceptance. If he knows that a minor cannot appoint an agent.
[Gittin 6:1.4] {NAME} said in the name of Rav: A woman cannot appoint an agent to accept her bill of divorce from her husband’s agent. {NAME} heard this from him and repeated after him forty times.
[Gittin 6:1.5] {NAME} asked: So far if she said, bring me, but [the agent] said [to the husband] “receive for me”. If she said, receive for me but [the agent] said [to the husband] “bring me”? If was found stated in both cases, this is a bill of divorce and if he wants to retract he cannot retract. But did we not state: “He shall deliver into her hand,” that includes not only her hand, from where through his agent’s hand, into her agent’s hand, from his agent to her agent, and from her agent to his agent; the verse says, “he shall deliver, he shall deliver.” Who said, “it is impossible for me”? Rebbi! As it was stated: “If she said, bring me my bill of divorce, but he said to him, your wife said, accept my bill of divorce for me: If he brought it to her, gave it to her, he acquired it for her, it was received for her; if he wants to retract, he may not retract, the words of Rebbi. {NAME} says, ‘bring it to her, give it to her,’ [if he wants to retract, he may retract; ‘acquire it for her, receive it for her’, if he wants to retract, he may not retract. Rebbi says, in any of these cases] he may not retract except if he says, ‘It is impossible for me that you accept it for her, but give it to her.’” It is difficult for Rebbi, “here you have it from my word”, if he wants to retract, he may retract. It is difficult for {NAME}, “here you have it from her word”, if he wants to retract, he may retract! {NAME} said, he becomes his and her agent. {NAME} said, everywhere we have stated “his and her agent”, she is both divorced and not divorced.
[Gittin 6:1.6] {NAME} said before {NAME}: Is not this disagreement the same as that disagreement, as we have stated there: “If a man was talking with a woman about her bill of divorce or her preliminary marriage and gave her the bill of divorce or [some valuable for] preliminary marriage and did not spell it out, {NAME} says it is sufficient; {NAME} says he has to be explicit.” Then Rebbi follows {NAME} and {NAME} {NAME}. He said to him, what do you have in your hand, did not {NAME}, {NAME}, {NAME}, say in the name of {NAME}, when do they differ? [If they thought about] other things but if he still was on the same subject, it is a bill of divorce. But here, even if they are still on the same subject there is disagreement.
[Gittin 6:1.7] {NAME} asked before {NAME}: Is it the same for a gift? Can a person appoint an agent for anything that is not his? He said to him, there the Torah gave her the right to a bill of divorce and she appoints an agent to receive what is rightfully hers. Can you say in regard to a gift that a person can appoint an agent for anything that is not his? In addition, from what {NAME} and {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of {NAME} said, if somebody said to give a gift to another and he wants to retract, he may retract. {NAME} stood near {NAME} and said to him, is that a just “yes”? He said to him, at the moment he said it, it was a just “yes”.
[Gittin 6:1.8] If [the husband] said to [another person]: Bring my wife’s bill of divorce, or her daughter’s, or her sister’s, then he went and delivered it to her, it is no divorce. But if [the other] said: Give a bill of divorce to his wife, and [the husband] said, here is my wife’s bill of divorce, or her daughter’s, or her sister’s, and he went and gave it to her, it is a divorce. {NAME} and {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: These are Rebbi’s words. But the Sages say, only if she says, it should be mine in your hand.
[Gittin 6:1.9] {NAME} said, practice follows {NAME}: if she said “take for me, it should be mine in your hand.” A man sent a bill of divorce to his wife. She told [the agent]: “It should be mine in your hand.” The casecame before Rav, who said, if he wants to retract he cannot retract. Does he disagree? There is a difference between “it should be in your hand” and “it should be mine in your hand.” {NAME} said, I know the beginning and the end. A woman appointed an agent to accept her bill of divorce from the husband’s agents. The case came before Rav, who said, if he wants to retract he cannot retract. Rav’s opinion has switched! There, {NAME} said in the name of Rav: A woman cannot appoint an agent to accept her bill of divorce from her husband’s agent, and here, he says so? [Gittin 6:2.1] MISHNAH: A woman who said, accept my bill of divorce for me, needs two groups of witnesses; two who say that she appointed in their presence and two who say that in their presence he received it and tore it up, even if the first ones are the latter ones, or one of the first together with one of the latter and a third person is associated with them. A preliminarily married adolescent girl, or her father, can accept her bill of divorce. {NAME} says, no two hands can acquire together; only her father alone can accept her bill of divorce. Any female who cannot take care of her bill of divorce cannot be divorced. If an underage girl said, accept the bill of divorce for me, it is no valid bill until the bill of divorce reaches her hand. Therefore, if the husband wants to retract he can retract since an underage person cannot appoint an agent. But if her father said to [an agent]: Go and receive my daughter’s bill of divorce, if [the husband] wants to retract he cannot retract.
[Gittin 6:2.2] HALAKHAH: “A woman who said, accept my bill of divorce for me,” etc. Two say that she appointed in their presence and two say that in their presence he received and tore it. But if he agrees, the agent should be able to be added. Explain it, it he was a relative. This implies that a relative can act as agent.
[Gittin 6:2.3] “A preliminarily married adolescent girl, or her father, can accept her bill of divorce.” {NAME} said, like the disagreement about divorce is the disagreement about preliminary marriage. {NAME} said, everybody agrees about preliminary marriage that [her father] contracts but not she herself. {NAME} agrees about a definitive marriage that she is not empowered to marry herself off and let her father lose her earnings. In the opinion of {NAME} she has no legal standing relative to her father and cannot appoint an agent. In the opinion of {NAME} she has legal standing relative to her father and can appoint an agent. A Mishnah disagrees with {NAME}: “A man contracts a preliminary marriage by himself and through his agent and a woman contracts a preliminary marriage by herself and through her agent.” He explains it about an adult woman. But did we not state: “If an underage girl said, accept the bill of divorce for me, it is no valid bill until the bill of divorce reaches her hand.” He explains it about an orphan. But did we not state: “If her father said to [an agent]: Go and receive my daughter’s bill of divorce, if [the husband] wants to retract he cannot retract.” He explains that the Mishnah deals with cases; the first part about an orphan and the second part if she has a father. A Mishnah disagrees with {NAME}. “A man may contract a preliminary marriage for his adolescent daughter either by himself or by his agent.” He explains that following {NAME}, since {NAME} said, “no two hands can acquire together; only her father alone can accept her bill of divorce.” {NAME} said, a rabbi came out from the assembly and said, a case was decided following {NAME}. Can one rely on that? It was no question of relying on him since it was as from the sea to the frying pan.
[Gittin 6:2.4] The colleagues said, they disagree about courtyard and four cubits. {NAME} said, she has both courtyard and four cubits. {NAME} said, she has neither courtyard nor four cubits. {NAME} said, they disagree about the courtyard but she has no four cubits. What did {NAME} say about outstretched hands? {NAME} asked, does an agent’s courtyard act as his hand?
[Gittin 6:2.5] If she is definitively married, she but not her father. An underage girl, her father but not she; if she is definitively married, both she and her father. If she has understanding, she but not her father. Who is an underage girl who needs to be divorced [by herself]? {NAME} said, any female who is given her bill of divorce together with something else and she produces it after some time.
[Gittin 6:3.1] MISHNAH: If somebody says, deliver this bill of divorce to my wife at place X and he delivered it at another place, it is invalid. But if he said, she is at place X, and he delivered it at another place, it is valid. If a woman says, accept my bill of divorce at place X, and he accepted it at another place, it is invalid, but {NAME} declares it valid. Bring my bill of divorce from place X and he brought it from another place, it is valid.
[Gittin 6:3.2] HALAKHAH: “If an underage girl said, accept the bill of divorce for me,” etc. The Mishnah does not follow {NAME}. But following {NAME} she is (not) divorced unless [the husband] tells [the agent]: Do not divorce her except at place X. “If he said, she is at place X and he delivered it at another place,” {NAME} agrees that he only indicates a place; the rabbis agree that he only indicates a place.
[Gittin 6:4.1] MISHNAH: “Bring my bill of divorce”, she may eat heave until the bill is delivered to her. “Receive my bill of divorce,” she is immediately forbidden to eat heave. “Receive my bill of divorce at place X,” she may eat heave until the bill arrives at that place; {NAME} forbids immediately.
[Gittin 6:4.2] HALAKHAH: : “If a woman says, accept my bill of divorce,” etc. What is the reason of {NAME}? I say that he found it behind the door. [Gittin 6:5.1] MISHNAH: If somebody says: “Write a bill of divorce and deliver to my wife, divorce her, write a letter and deliver to her”, they should write and deliver. “Discharge her, provide for her, treat her according to the law, do what is necessary;” he did not say anything. Earlier, they said that if somebody was led away in a neck-iron when he said, write a bill of divorce for my wife, they should write and deliver. They reconsidered and said, also one who leaves on a ship or in a caravan. {NAME} said, also the dangerously sick.
[Gittin 6:5.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody says: “Write a bill of divorce and deliver to my wife,” etc. If somebody says in Aramaic “divorce her,” it is as if he said in Hebrew “divorce her.”
[Gittin 6:5.3] “ ‘Discharge her, provide for her, treat her according to the law, do what is necessary;’ he did not say anything.” I say, he meant sustenance.
[Gittin 6:5.4] {NAME} said, not only a neck-iron of mortal danger but also a neck-iron of money. [Gittin 6:5.5] As the following: Ganiba was lead out to be executed. He said, One should give money to {NAME} from the wine of Kefar Panaya. They did not give him; they were considering what Rav said, “an heir is like the buyer of encumbered property.” Just as a loan before witnesses cannot be collected from encumbered property, so it cannot be collected from heirs. If they did not give it as payment of a debt, they should have given as a gift! They were considering what {NAME} said, for {NAME} asked: Does his gift follow the rules of the gift of a sick person? {NAME} brought {NAME} who stated for him: A gift is like a bill of divorce. {NAME} said to him, perhaps like bills of divorce which one cannot deliver if not delivered during his lifetime, so a gift is not called a gift if not delivered during his lifetime? He said to him, here comes the rabbi with sophistication to let {NAME} lose money! You cannot, for we have stated there: “Give a mina to X; then he died. One shall give after death.” Following {NAME}. For {NAME} disagrees, they should give him, as {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: A loan before witnesses can be collected from the heirs on condition that they inherited real estate. {NAME} said, that is, if somebody was with him until the moment of his death. But if he goes in and out, I am saying that already he gave him. [Gittin 6:5.6] It was stated: Also the sick person. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Practice follows {NAME} about the dangerously ill. What is the difference between a dangerously ill and a sick person? A sick person is a normal case; any who gets sick suddenly is dangerously ill. In a normal case, the relatives visit him immediately; unrelated persons visit him after three days. If he falls ill suddenly, everybody visits him immediately. An example: {NAME}, {NAME}, and {NAME} went to visit {NAME} after three days. He said to them: Do you want to sustain the baraita in my case?
[Gittin 6:6.1] MISHNAH: If somebody was thrown into a cistern and said, anybody hearing my voice should write a bill of divorce for my wife, they should write and deliver. If a healthy person said, write a bill of divorce for my wife, he wants to make fun of her. It happened to a healthy person who had said, write a bill of divorce for my wife, that he went on the roof, fell down, and died. {NAME} said, the Sages said that if he jumped, it is a bill of divorce; if the wind pushed him, it is no bill of divorce.
[Gittin 6:6.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody was thrown into a cistern,” etc. {NAME} said, {NAME} taught us, only if they saw a man’s shadow. There we have stated: “One testifies by the light of a candle or by the light of the moon and one permits to remarry on the basis of a disembodied voice”, and {NAME} said, only if they saw a man’s shadow. {NAME}, in the name of {NAME}: That means, in the fields, but in town even without a man’s shadow. But did we not state: “If somebody had been thrown into a cistern,” and {NAME} said, only if they saw a man’s shadow? {NAME} said, damaging spirits were as frequent in cisterns as they are frequent on the fields.
[Gittin 6:6.3] If it was doubtful whether he jumped or the wind pushed him? Let us hear from the following: {NAME} says, if he fell down immediately, it is a bill of divorce; if he fell after some time it is no bill of divorce. But is “immediately” not a case of doubt whether he jumped or the wind pushed him? This implies that in case of doubt whether he jumped or the wind pushed him, it is a bill of divorce.
[Gittin 6:6.4] If somebody slaughtered with the intention of sprinkling [the victim’s] blood in idolatry or to burn its fat for idolatry, {NAME} said, the intention invalidates, {NAME} said, the intention does not invalidate. {NAME} objected before {NAME}: Did we not state: “{NAME} said, that is a matter of a conclusion de minore ad majus . Since in a case where thought makes sanctified food unusable, etc.,” and thought invalidates for piggul and leftover. He said to him, truly thought invalidates for piggul and leftover; but if somebody slaughtered with the intention of sprinkling [the victim’s] blood in idolatry or to burn its fat for idolatry, the intention does not invalidate. If he slaughtered and then the blood was sprinkled in an idolatrous rite and the fat was burned in an idolatrous rite, there was such a case in Caesarea and they pronounced neither prohibition nor permission. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: This means that they were not apprehensive. If you say that they were apprehensive, they should have taught a prohibition. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: This means that they were apprehensive. If you say that they were not apprehensive, they should not have dealt with the case.
[Gittin 6:7.1] MISHNAH: If one said to two persons, give a bill of divorce to my wife, or to three persons, write a bill of divorce and deliver to my wife, they should write and deliver. If he said to three persons, deliver a bill of divorce to my wife, they shall ask others to write since he appointed them as a court, the words of {NAME}. This instructions for practice did Ḥananiah from Ono send from jail: I know from tradition that if someone said to three persons, deliver a bill of divorce to my wife, they shall ask others to write since he appointed them as a court. {NAME} said, we told the messenger that we also know from tradition that even if he said to the Supreme Court in Jerusalem, deliver a bill of divorce to my wife, they shall learn, write, and deliver. If he said to ten persons, write a bill of divorce for my wife, one writes and two sign. All of you shall write, one writes and all sign. Therefore, if one of them died, the bill of divorce would be void.
[Gittin 6:7.2] HALAKHAH: “If one said to two persons, give a bill of divorce to my wife,” etc. The Mishnah follows {NAME}, from the next sentence: “If he said to three persons;” and {NAME} said, the reason of {NAME} is that we find everywhere that others write and the court signs, also here others write and the court affixes their signatures.
[Gittin 6:7.3] {NAME} asked before Rebbi: What reason did they have to say that practice follows {NAME}? He said to him, because I never met him.
