It is obvious that she can leave by a bill of divorce at least since ({NAME} said in {NAME} name: If a person who is half slave and half free entered a preliminary marriage, one does not consider his marriage. In parallel, if he divorced one does not consider his divorce. It is obvious that she can leave by a bill of divorce at least). {NAME} said in {NAME} name: Aquila the proselyte translated before {NAME} “and she is a slave girl נֶחֱרֶפֶת to a man”, by “one who was pounded before a man”, as you say, “she spread morsels on it.” {NAME} said in {NAME} name: So {NAME} explained it before the Sages. “And she is a slave girl נֶחֱרֶפֶת to a man”, by “one who was pounded before a man”, as you say, “in morsels by a pestle.”
[Kiddushin 1:1.33] Can she regain her autonomy through her master’s death or by the end of six [years]? What is the problem? Following {NAME}? But {NAME} said that the verse speaks about a woman half slave and half free engaged to be married by a free man. Therefore, his problem is following {NAME}, since {NAME} said that the verse speaks about a Canaanite slave girl married to a Hebrew slave, since this is marriage sanctioned by the Torah: “If his master give him a wife.” But his problem is whether she regains her autonomy through her master’s death or by the end of six [years] for him who says that the Hebrew slave does not serve the heir.
[Kiddushin 1:2.1] MISHNAH: A Hebrew slave is acquired by money or a document; he regains his autonomy by years, or the Jubilee, or reduction of the amount. The Hebrew slave girl in addition regains her autonomy by indicators of puberty. The pierced slave is acquired by piercing; he regains his autonomy in the Jubilee or by the master’s death.
[Kiddushin 1:2.2] HALAKHAH: “A Hebrew slave is acquired by money,” etc. It is written: “If your Hebrew brother or sister be sold to you,” he bracketed the male Hebrew with the female. Since the female Hebrew can be acquired by money or contract, also the male Hebrew can be acquired by money or contract. One understands money since it is written: “She leaves gratis, without money [due].” From where by contract? The female Hebrew is inferred from the free woman, and the male Hebrew from the female. This is a combination of inferences. That follows {NAME} who accepts combination of inferences. Following {NAME} who rejects combination of inferences? It was found that {NAME} stated: In the case of the word חֻפְשָׁה, “free” is inferred from חֻפְשָׁה. Everywhere {NAME} rejects combination of inferences and here, he accepts combination of inferences? {NAME} stated it in the name of the Sages. From where is it derived for {NAME}? “Sending away, sending away.” Since “sending away” mentioned there means by a contract, also “sending away” here means by a contract. But it does not compare. There it is to gain autonomy, here it is to be acquired by others! {NAME} said, “sale, sale”. Since “sale” mentioned there means by a contract, “sale” here also means by a contract. But since there it is possible by possession, then here it should be possible by possession. {NAME} said, the male Hebrew is like the female Hebrew.
[Kiddushin 1:2.3] “By money”. “The money of his sale price shall be;” he can be redeemed by money, not by produce nor by vessels. Everywhere you treat money’s worth like money, but here you do not treat money’s worth like money. {NAME} said, there is a difference, because the verse repeated “money, of money”. {NAME} said, but if he wants to reduce, he can leave for the reduced amount even for produce, even for vessels. {NAME}, {NAME} father, said that this is only if he did not give them their money’s worth. But if he gave them their money’s worth, it is like money.
[Kiddushin 1:2.4] “By a document.” {NAME} said, by a money document; therefore not by a gift document, since maybe he would renege. But then, could he not renege even with a money document? He said to him, maybe there comes a year of famine and his master reneges.
[Kiddushin 1:2.5] The order of sale is the following: I X sold my daughter to Y. The order of preliminary marriage is the following: I X gave my daughter to Y in preliminary marriage. {NAME} asked before {NAME}: If he switched and said, I Y acquired X’s daughter, I Y took X’s daughter in preliminary marriage? He said to him, what is the difference? But if he changed the language of sale to that of preliminary marriage or vice-versa, he did not do anything.
[Kiddushin 1:2.6] It is written: “Six years he shall work.” How much does he work? I could think that he leaves at the end of six [years]. The verse says, “and in the seventh he shall leave.” I could think that he leave at the end of seven [years]. The verse says, “six years he shall work.” How is that? He works the entire six and leaves at the start of the seventh. “And in the seventh he shall leave.” The seventh from the sale and not the Seventh of the world. Do you say, the seventh from the sale and not the Seventh of the world? Since it says, “six years he shall work,” this spells out six years. How can I confirm “and in the seventh he shall leave?” The seventh from the sale and not the Seventh of the world. Say it is the opposite. {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: It is written: “and in the seventh,” “and in the seventh”. {NAME} said, if you say, in the Seventh of the world, what would the Jubilee free? {NAME} said, this follows him who said that the Jubilee does not become part of a Sabbatical period. But following him who said that the Jubilee becomes part of a Sabbatical period, sometimes it falls in the middle of a Sabbatical period. {NAME} say, even following him who said that the Jubilee becomes part of a Sabbatical period, we could deduce from here that the Sabbatical year frees the slaves and the Jubilee the pierced ones.
[Kiddushin 1:2.7] From where even if he fell ill? The verse says, “in the seventh year he shall leave into freedom gratis.” I could think, even if he fled; the verse says, “six years he shall work.” What did you see to include this and to exclude that? After the verse included, it excluded. I am including the one who remains in his power and am exluding the one who is not in his power. {NAME} said that {NAME} asked: I understand that if he fell ill and fled afterwards, he has to make up [the time lost]. If he fled and then fell ill? {NAME} said, let us hear from the following: “If a woman rebels against her husband, one writes him a bill of rebellion on her ketubah .” And {NAME} stated: One writes a bill of rebellion on the ketubah of a menstruating woman or a sick one, a preliminarily married one and one waiting for her levir. Where do we hold? If she rebelled against him while she was menstruating, the Torah instructed her to rebel. But we must hold that she rebelled when she was not menstruating and then started menstruating. Here she is unable to rebel, nevertheless you say, one writes. Here also, if he rebelled and then fell ill he has to make up. For he can say to him, if you had stayed with me, you would not have become sick. {NAME} said, that argument even works in the first case. If he fell ill and fled afterwards, he has to make up, since he can say to him, if you had stayed with me, you would have recuperated sooner.
[Kiddushin 1:2.8] “He regains his autonomy by years.” Some Tannaїm state: He may be sold for less than six [years], but he cannot be sold for more than six. But some Tannaïm state: He may not be sold for less than six [years] or more than to [year] seven. {NAME} said, the reason of that Tanna: Sometimes he is sold two or three years before the Jubilee; then the Jubilee arrives and frees him automatically.
[Kiddushin 1:2.9] “Or the Jubilee,” as it is written, “in the Jubilee he shall leave.” “Or reduction of the amount,” as it is written: “If there still are many years.” Do we not know that if there are many there are not few, and if there are few there are not many? {NAME} said, sometimes the years are worth more than the wages, sometimes the wages are worth more than the years. How do you explain the following? If he was sold for a mina each and improved so that now he is worth 200 each, from where that one computes for him only by a mina each? The verse says, “according to the years he shall compute his redemption.” We learned that one sold to a Gentile is advantaged when he comes to be redeemed. From where that one sold to an Israel is advantaged when he comes to be redeemed? “Hireling, hireling” for an equal cut. Since the hireling is advantaged in redemption when he is sold to a Gentile, so too the hireling is advantaged in redemption when he is sold to an Israel. Rebbi says, why does the verse say “he shall be redeemed, he shall be redeemed,” three times? To add all redemptions that they have to follow this order.
[Kiddushin 1:2.10] “If he be not redeemed by these.” {NAME} says, by these to freedom, by all others to servitude. {NAME} says, by these to servitude, by all others to freedom. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Both interpret the same verse: “Unless he be redeemed by these.” {NAME} interprets: “Unless he be redeemed by these” but by others he is made to serve before he leaves. {NAME} interprets: “Unless he be redeemed by these”, by these he completes before he leaves. The words of the Sages? {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: In both cases to freedom. It was stated thus: “If his hand achieves,” his own hand. “Or he found for his redemption.” Since his own hand achieves for himself, what others achieve also is for himself.
[Kiddushin 1:2.11] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Following him, who said “for servitude”, he makes up before he leaves. But was it not stated: After he redeemed him it is as if he were sold to him, he enslaves him before he leaves. {NAME} said, there is no “enslaves him before he leaves”, only “he makes up before he leaves.” If his relatives want to redeem him from the first [master’s], they redeem. If his relatives want to redeem him from the second [master’s], they cannot redeem. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: That follows him who said: “by these to freedom, by all others to servitude.”
[Kiddushin 1:2.12] {NAME} asked before {NAME}: There it is written “he computes” and here it is written “he computes”. Here you compute months and years so he may leave, there you do not compute months and years so he may leave. He said to him, the difference is that the Torah compared him to the hireling. Since the latter computes months and years and leaves, so this one computes months and years and leaves.
[Kiddushin 1:2.13] “She leaves gratis,” these are the days of adulthood; “without money,” these are the indicators [of adolescence.] Could He not have mentioned only one of them? If only one of them were mentioned, would I not have said that if she leaves with indicators [of adolescence], then certainly in the days of adulthood? But in that case I would have said that they are identical with the days of adulthood. Would this not be logical? She is emancipated from the power of the father and she is emancipated from the power of the master; since she is emancipated from the power of the father by some indicators [of adulthood], she is emancipated from the power of the master by the same indicators. Therefore, it was necessary to say, “she leaves gratis,” these are the days of adulthood, “without money,” these are the indicators [of adolescence.] Or maybe the other way around? {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: “Without money.” At a place where there is money for the father, there is no money for the master.
[Kiddushin 1:2.14] “If he did not allot her, he must let her be redeemed.” This teaches that he cannot allot her for himself unless there is time for her handywork to be worth a peruṭah and that a peruṭah be left to be deducted, the words of {NAME}. But the Sages say, he allots any time until sundown. {NAME} said, everybody agrees that for a Hebrew slave only if a peruṭah ’s worth is left. {NAME} says it correctly, what is the rabbis’ reason? There is no money left, there is no handiwork left? {NAME} said, he allots her by speech.
[Kiddushin 1:2.15] {NAME} stated: How does he allot her? He tells her in front of two [witnesses]: “You are allotted to me.” In {NAME} opinion, he gives her money for the allotment at the end. In the rabbis’ opinion, the money for allotment was given at the first hour. What is the difference between them? Her earning power. For him who says, he gives her money for the allotment at the end, her earning power belongs to her husband. For him who says, the money for allotment was given at the first hour, her earning power belongs to her father. Even for him who says, the money for allotment was given at the first hour, her earning power belongs to her husband. It is as if he said: “You are preliminarily married to me on condition that your earning power belong to me.”
[Kiddushin 1:2.16] If he was married to her sister who died. For him who says, he gives money for the allotment at the end, she needs additional money. For him who says, the money for allotment was given at the first hour, she does not need additional money. Even for him who says, the money for allotment was given at the first hour, she needs additional money. Why? Everybody agrees that preliminary marriage is impossible in an incestuous relationship.
[Kiddushin 1:2.17] Is {NAME} of the opinion that the “allotment” discussed here is preliminary marriage by biblical standards? {NAME} said, it turns out that {NAME} Jehudah agrees with {NAME}. As it was stated: By the deposit you hold for me; if she went and found that it was stolen or lost, if there was a peruṭah ’s worth left, she is preliminarily married; otherwise, she is not preliminarily married. By the loan you are holding from me, if she went and found that it was stolen or lost, even if there was no peruṭah ’s worth left, she is preliminarily married. {NAME} says in the name of {NAME}, a loan is like a deposit: If there was a peruṭah ’s worth left, she is preliminarily married; otherwise, she is not preliminarily married. Just as {NAME} equates loan and deposit, so {NAME} equates “allotment” and loan.
[Kiddushin 1:2.18] “If he allots her to his son.” He allots her to his son but may not allot her to his brother. He should be able to allot her to his brother by an argument de minore ad majus ! If he may allot her to his son who may not take his place for ḥalîṣah and levirate, should it not be logical that he may allot her to his brother who may take his place for ḥalîṣah and levirate? No. If you would accept the son since he will take [the father’s] place in a field of inheritance, what can you say about his brother who will not take his place in a field of inheritance? Would it be reasonable that he may allot her to him? The verse says, “if he allots her to his son.” He allots her to his son but may not allot her to his brother.
[Kiddushin 1:2.19] “If he allots her to his son;” but he may not allot her to his grandson. {NAME} asked before {NAME}: In matters of inheritance you recognize the grandson like a son but here you do not recognize the grandson like a son? {NAME} said, if anybody explains this matter, I shall pour him spiced wine. {NAME} answered: In matters of inheritance where the brother can take the place of a son and all others can take the place of the son, the grandson takes the place of a son. But here, where neither the brother nor any other relative can take the place of a son, the grandson cannot take the place of a son. {NAME} answered: In matters of impurity you consider a brother like a son and all [near] relatives like a son but not a grandson like a son. They said, there went the spiced wine.
[Kiddushin 1:2.20] “If he allots her to his son;” with [the girl’s] agreement. {NAME} said, there is no agreement here. {NAME} said so, the statement follows {NAME}. {NAME} said, even if you say the statement follows {NAME}, is he not a minor? “If he allots her to his son;” with [the latter’s] agreement. {NAME} said, he allots her to his minor or adult son, with or without the latter’s agreement. {NAME} said, he allots her only to his adult son with the latter’s agreement.
[Kiddushin 1:2.21] “A male nine years and one day old makes a widow for the High Priest or a divorcee or one who performed ḥalîṣah for a common priest.” In the opinion of {NAME} who must explain this for a marriage, she should also be free from levirate or ḥalîṣah , as we have stated: “If he married a woman, that one is free from levirate or ḥalîṣah .” {NAME} said, following {NAME} it comes following {NAME}, as it was stated so: If a male nine years and one day old up to twelve years and one day old grew two pubic hairs, they are warts. {NAME} said, they are indicators [of puberty]. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Only if they were still there at the time of indicators.
[Kiddushin 1:2.22] {NAME} asked: When they remained until the time of indicators, does he retroactively become a man or from that time onward? For {NAME} it is obvious that he becomes a man retroactively, so certainly also for the future, for he explains the position of {NAME} by {NAME}. Why does {NAME} not explain the position of {NAME} by {NAME} since he asked, when they remained until the time of indicators, does he retroactively become a man or from that time onward? {NAME} said, because he had difficulty. {NAME} asked before me: When they remained until the time of indicators, does he retroactively become a man or from that time onward? One understands the case of a widow. But a divorcee? Explain it if he copulated with her after he became an adult and divorced her. Ḥalîṣah ? Explain it if he copulated with her, died, and the [adult] brothers performed ḥalîṣah ; she had ḥalîṣah because of him. In that case, even if he was younger than nine [years]! {NAME} said, that is correct. But because in all cases one stated “nine”, one stated this with them.
[Kiddushin 1:2.23] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: {NAME} learned from Aḥaz, as it was stated: Aḥaz produced a child at age nine, Haran at age six, and Caleb at age ten following him who identifies {NAME} with {NAME}.
[Kiddushin 1:2.24] If he sold her to one and gave her in preliminary marriage to another, the father played with the master, the words of {NAME}; but the Sages say that the father did not play with the master. It is as if somebody said to a woman, “you are preliminarily married to me after 30 days,” since if somebody said to a woman, “you are preliminarily married to me after 30 days,” and another came and married her preliminarily (after) 30 days, is she not preliminarily married to the second man? “From now after 30 days.” Since if somebody said to a woman, “you are preliminarily married to me from now after 30 days,” and another came and married her preliminarily within the 30 days, is she not preliminarily married to both of them? From then when he wants. Everybody agrees that if he definitively married her off, the father played with the master.
[Kiddushin 1:2.25] “As a slave girl.” Only as a slave girl: this teaches that he may sell her on condition that he not have the right of allotment over her, the words of {NAME}. But the Sages say, he did not do anything, for he stipulated against what is written in the Torah, “and the stipulation of anybody who stipulates against what is written in the Torah is invalid.” But does {NAME} not agree that “the stipulation of anybody who stipulates against what is written in the Torah is invalid”? He accepts it if it is impossible to keep the stipulation in the end, but here it is possible to keep the stipulation in the end. Do the rabbis not agree about a stipulation which it is possible to keep in the end? They agree to it in money matters, but this is a personal matter. But did we not state: A person may marry a woman and stipulate with her that she have no claim on him for food, clothing, or marital relations? One understands food and clothing. But are marital relations not a personal matter? {NAME} said, explain it for an underage girl. How can that Tanna explain “as a slave girl”? He may sell her as a widow to the High Priest, as a divorcee or one who received ḥălîṣah to a common priest. How can that Tanna explain “as a servant”? {NAME} said, explain it by a widow from preliminary marriage. But was it not stated: A person may sell his daugher into marriage and repeat, into servitude and repeat, into marriage after servitude, but not into servitude after marriage? {NAME} said, these are different Tannaïm. He who states “a widow to the High Priest” agrees to servitude after marriage; he who does not state “a widow to the High Priest” does not agree to servitude after marriage. How does the latter Tanna explain “as a servant”? {NAME} said, explain it if [the master] was married to her sister.
[Kiddushin 1:2.26] {NAME} stated: Just as he cannot sell her into servitude after marriage, so not into servitude after servitude. What is {NAME} reason? “By his being unfaithful to her.” Once he can be unfaithful to her, he cannot be unfaithful to her a second time. How do the rabbis explain {NAME} reason? “She being in his garment;” from the moment that [her master] spread his garment on her, her father no longer has any power over her.
[Kiddushin 1:2.27] {NAME} asked before {NAME}: Should not the Hebrew slave girl leave by definitive marriage, by an argument de minore ad majus ? Since indications [of puberty] which do not emancipate her from her father’s power, free her from her master’s power, is it not logical that definitive marriage, which emancipates her from her father’s power, shall free her from her master’s power? He said to him, I have only the Mishnah: “The Hebrew slave girl in addition regains her autonomy by indicators of puberty.” {NAME} said, the Hebrew slave girl leaves at the death of her master. What is the reason? “Also your slave girl you shall treat in the same way;” and it is written: “He shall be for you a permanent slave.” He bracketed the Hebrew slave girl with the “pierced slave”. Since the “pierced slave” leaves at his master’s death, the Hebrew slave girl also leaves at her master’s death. It turns out that {NAME} parallels the following Tanna, as it was stated: The Hebrew slave serves the son but not the daughter; the Hebrew slave girl serves the daughter but not the son. Some Tannaїm state: The Hebrew slave girl as well as the Hebrew slave serve neither the son nor the daughter. How does the Tanna confirm “your slave girl you also shall treat in the same way”? He explains it about the allowance, as it was stated: The following are given allowances: The one who leaves after six years or in the Jubilee, and the Hebrew slave girl who becomes autonomous by indicators of puberty. But one does not give allowances to one who leaves by the reduction of the amount or following the master’s death.
[Kiddushin 1:2.28] It is written: “His master shall bring him to the judges, or he shall bring him to the door.” How is that? The one who was sold by the court, “his master shall bring him to the judges.” The one who sold himself, “or he shall bring him to the door.” {NAME} asked: It is obvious that the court writes the contract for him who was sold by the court. Who is writing the contract for him who sells himself? It is written: “It shall not be hard in your eyes to send him away free from you; for twice the hire of a hireling he served you for six years.” The hired hand works during the day; he does not work in the night. The Hebrew slave works both day and night. It is written: “He shall not treat him harshly before your eyes,” and you say so? {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: His master marries him to a Canaanite slave; it turns out that he serves him day and night. {NAME} asked before {NAME}: Think of it, if he was buying a Cohen! He answered him: Would the case of an Israel not also be permission of something prohibited following {NAME}? {NAME} here changed his mind.
[Kiddushin 1:2.29] {NAME} preached: The earlobe was pierced, lest a Cohen become disqualified. {NAME} says, he was pierced at his cartilage. Therefore, {NAME} says that a Cohen cannot be pierced lest he become blemished and be disqualified for service. Could not the cartilage be pierced less than the size of a vetch seed? Maybe it would result in the size of a vetch seed. Let it be the size of a vetch! The Torah said, “he shall return to his inheritance,” as he was. He cannot be pierced unless he had a wife and children. “By an awl”. Not only an awl, from where even a buck-thorn, even a thorn, even glass? The verse says, “he pierces”. This follows {NAME}.
[Kiddushin 1:2.30] Following {NAME}? {NAME} stated: At three places teaching circumvents Scripture and at another place the interpretation.The Torah said, “in a scroll”, but practice said on anything separated from the ground. The Torah said, “in dust”, but practice said in anything on which plants grow. The Torah said, “with an awl”, but practice said, even a buck-thorn, even a thorn, even glass. And at one place the interpretation: {NAME} stated: “It shall be on the seventh day that he shave all his hair,” inclusion. “His head, his beard, and his eyebrows,” detail. Since it continues “and all his hair he shall shave,” it repeats inclusion. Inclusion, detail, and inclusion is judged only by what is similar to the detail. Since the detail is explained as place of bunching and exposed, it should refer only [hair growing] in bunches at exposed places. But practice is that he shaves to be like a gourd. “With an awl”, since an awl is made of metal, so anything made of metal. {NAME} said, this is a large drill. {NAME} says, that is the engraving-knife. “He shall bring him to the door.” I could think, even if it was lying flat. The verse says, “or to the door-post”. Since the door-post is upright, so also the door has to be upright: a shame to him and to his family.
[Kiddushin 1:2.31] It was stated: {NAME} says, why at the door? Because by the door they went from servitude to freedom. The students asked {NAME}: Why should the slave be pierced in his ear rather than in any of his other body parts? He said to them, the ear which heard at Mount Sinai: “You shall have no other powers besides Me,” and removed from himself the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven but accepted the yoke of flesh and blood; the ear which heard before Mount Sinai: “For the Children of Israel are My servants,” and went and acquired another master; therefore the ear should come and be pierced for he did not follow what his ear heard.
[Kiddushin 1:2.32] “His ear.” Since “his ear” mentioned there means the right ear, also here the right ear. “If the slave says saying”, two sayings, one at the end of the sixth year and one at the start of the seventh year. One at the end of the sixth year, while he still is in his servitude and one at the start of the seventh year, “I will not go free.” “I love my master, my wife, and my children.” This teaches that he cannot be pierced unless he have a wife and children, unless he love his master and his master love him; unless the property be blessed because of him as it is said: “For he feels well with you.”
[Kiddushin 1:2.33] “He regains his autonomy in the Jubilee,” as it is written: “He leaves in the Jubilee together with his children.” “Or at the master’s death,” as it is written: “He shall be for you a perpetual slave,” all the days of his master’s lifetime.
[Kiddushin 1:3.1] MISHNAH: A Canaanite slave is acquired by money, or contract, or possession. He gains his autonomy by money through a third party or a document by himself, the words of {NAME}. But the Sages say, by money also by himself or a document through a third party, if only the money comes from a third party.
[Kiddushin 1:3.2] HALAKHAH: “A Canaanite slave is acquired by money,” etc. It is written: “They shall be inherited by your children after you, to be possessed as inheritance” This brackets slaves with landed property. Since real estate can be acquired by money, or contract, or possession, so a Canaanite slave can be acquired by money, or contract, or possession.
[Kiddushin 1:3.3] From where that landed property is bought by money, or contract, or possession? “Fields will be bought by money, writing on a scroll and signing, and testifying of witnesses.” “And signing”, these are the witnesses on the contract. “And testifying of witnesses,” these are the witnesses to possession. Or maybe these are only the witnesses on the contract? These are already written: “Writing on a scroll and signing.”
[Kiddushin 1:3.4] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}; {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Real estate cannot be bought for less than a peruṭah . What is the reason? “Fields will be bought by money.” This disagrees with what {NAME} said: Any šeqalim mentioned in the Torah are tetradrachmas, in the Prophets pounds 340 , and in the Hagiographs centenarii . {NAME} said, except for the šeqalim paid to Ephron, which were centenarii . What is the reason? “For full money he shall give it to me.” There is no comparison since here it is written “money” but there “ šeqalim ”. They objected, is there not the rapist, for whom “money” is written and you say “ šeqalim ”?
[Kiddushin 1:3.5] This does not follow {NAME}, for {NAME} said that walking acquires, as it was stated: If one walked across a field in length and breadth, he acquired up to the place he walked to, the words of {NAME}. But the Sages say that he did not acquire up to the moment he acted in possession. Everybody agrees that if somebody sells a path to another, when the latter went, he acquired. What is the reason? “Arise, walk in the Land in length and breadth, for I shall give it to you.”
[Kiddushin 1:3.6] A Mishnah says that slaves follow the rules of real estate. A baraita states, the rules of movables. A baraita states, neither the rules of realestate nor the rules of movables. A Mishnah says that slaves follow the rules of real estate, as we have stated there: “Possession of houses, cisterns, ditches, and caves, bath houses, and dovecots, olive presses, and irrigated fields, and slaves.” A baraita states, slaves do not follow the rules of movables. As it is stated: What is possession of a slave? He tied his shoe for him, or untied his shoe, carried his things to the bath. {NAME} says, if he lifted him, that is possession. If he lifted his master, there is no stronger possession than this. A statement of the rabbis says that slaves follow the rules of movables. For {NAME} said in the name of rabbis, there is no lien for a gift; one does not collect from slaves as from real estate. {NAME} asked {NAME}, who are those rabbis? He told him, {NAME} and {NAME}. A widow took a slave girl. The case came before {NAME} who said, what she took, she took. {NAME} took her away, for she thought that she was hers but she was not hers. Not of real estate, as it was stated: Real estate and slaves; he took possession of the real estate. If you say that slaves follow the rules of real estate, when he took possession of the real estate he would have taken possession of the slaves, since {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: If he had two fields, one in Judea and one in Galilee. If he took possession of the one in Judea with intention to take possession also of that in Galilee, or of the one in Galilee with intention to take possession also of that in Judea, he acquired. Not of movables. If you say that slaves follow the rules of movables, when he took possession of the movables he would have taken possessionof the slaves, since we did state there: “For property that is not guaranteed will cause guaranteed properties to be objects of swearing about them.”
[Kiddushin 1:3.7] “By money.” {NAME} said, from another person to his master, therefore not from his master to another person. {NAME} said, even from his master to another person. What brings this? From his master to himself. {NAME} asked before {NAME}: “Here you have money that your field shall be unencumbered.” He answered, it is unencumbered. “That it be ownerless”? He answered, it is not ownerless. What is the difference between the cases? Here he advantaged a thinking person, there he did not advantage any thinking person. Think of it, if he was deaf-mute? He said to him, “a man.” Think of it, if he was underage? [Kiddushin 1:3.8] {NAME} said, it follows Rebbi, since Rebbi said that a person can free half of his slave. But do the rabbis not hold that a person can free half of his slave? They admit it for a slave held in partnership. But there is a difference for a slave who entirely belongs to him, for it is as if he gave something from his right into his left hand. Does Rebbi hold that it is not as if he gave something from his right into his left hand? He admits it if he gave to him through a third party. Do the rabbis not hold that he may give to him through a third party? The rabbis hold that one who can acquire by himself can acquire through a third party; one who cannot acquire by himself cannot acquire through a third party. Rebbi says, even though he cannot acquire by himself, he can acquire through third parties.
[Kiddushin 1:3.9] If he picked up a find and said, for the purpose that I own it rather than my master. Does he and his master own it automatically or does he own it but not his master? Let us hear from the following: “If a person is by a vow prevented from benefitting his son-in-law but wants to give money to his daughter, he says to her: These coins are given to you as a gift on condition that your husband have no claim to them, except what you put into your mouth.” It was stated: “Neither do you”. {NAME} said, who stated “neither do you”? {NAME} since {NAME} makes the hand of a slave the hand of his master. For a gift [we follow] {NAME} that the wife’s hand is her husband’s hand; for a find [do we follow] the rabbis? {NAME} said before {NAME}, is there not a difference, for he is as if he acquired by somebody else’s opinion? He said to him, is it not a case a fortiori ? Since in her case, when she would acquire by somebody else’s opinion, you say that what a wife acquired, her husband acquired: here where he acquires by his own opinion, a fortiori what the slave acquired his master must acquire.

[Kiddushin 1:5.3] Then they changed it to clipping. What is clipping? If a man sold his inherited field, his relatives brought amphoras, filled them with roasted kernels and nuts and broke them before children. The children were collecting them and saying, X was clipped from his inheritance. When he brought it back, they were doing the same and saying, X returned to his inheritance. {NAME} said, also if a man married an unsuitable woman, his relatives brought amphoras, filled them with roasted kernels and nuts and broke them before children. Or maybe these are only the witnesses to the contract? These are already written: “Writing on a scroll and signing.”

[Kiddushin 1:6.1] MISHNAH: If anything is given instead of money, if one entered in possession, the other is obligated for its exchange. How is this? Brothers having common property who are obligated for agio are free from animal tithe.” When they split and then joined again. “But if they are obligated for animal tithe they are free from agio.” If they never split.

[Kiddushin 1:6.4] {NAME}, {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of Rav: If he sold a cow for money, then grabbed him and said, give me that money. He answered, for what do you need it? [Kiddushin 1:6.5] The Mishnah: “Possession of Heaven is by money, possession of any individual by taking hold.” How? If the treasurer paid with Temple money for movables, they are in the Temple’s possession anywhere they are, for it is written: “The Eternal’s are the earth and what fills it, dry land and its inhabitants.”
[Kiddushin 1:6.6] “A promise to Heaven is like delivery to an individual.” How? If he bought a cow from the Temple for 200. If he did not have occasion to pay the 200 until the going rate was a mina , he has to pay 200. That means, a promise to Heaven is like delivery to an individual. A cow from the Temple for a mina . If he did not have occasion to pay the mina until the going rate was 200, he has to pay 200. That is what is written: “He has to add a fifth of its estimated value, then it is delivered to him.” Therefore, if he adds, it is delivered to him; if he does not add, it is not delivered to him. “ ‘This steer as elevation offering, or this house as a qorbān ,’ they are in the Temple’s possession wherever they are, for it is written: “The Eternal’s are the earth and what fills it,” etc. But among private persons one obtains possession only be taking hold.”
[Kiddushin 1:7.1] MISHNAH: For any commandment a father has to fulfill towards his son, men are obligated but women are free. For any commandment the son has to fulfill towards his father, men and women are equally obligated. For any positive commandment activated by time, men are obligated but women are free. For any positive commandment not activated by time, men and women are equally obligated. For any prohibition, whether or not activated by time, men and women are equally obligated except for “do not destroy”, “do not shear,” and “do not become impure for the dead.” Leanings and weavings, presentations, taking of fistfuls, burnings and neck breakings, sprinklings and receptions apply to men but not to women except for the flour offerings of the suspected wife and the nezirah ; those do weave.

[Kiddushin 1:9.3] {NAME} preached: “A dead fly will permanently spoil perfumer’s oil.” Does not one dead fly spoil perfumer’s oil? And this person by one sin spoiled all merits he had. {NAME} preached: “ So the abyss opened wide and its mouth swallowed the one without law.” It does not say “without laws”, but “without law”, him who has not a single merit that should help him on the scale of merit. That is, for the Future World. But in this world, even if 999 angels plead for his conviction and one angel pleads for his acquittal, the Holy One, praise to Him, lends His weight to the scale of merit. What is the reason? “If there is for him one angel out of a thousand, to tell a man his straightness. He will act with him in grace and say, let him be redeemed, not go down to destruction; I found weregilt.” {NAME} said, if you find a saying of {NAME}, bend your ear like this funnel and listen, since {NAME} reported that {NAME}, said: Even if 999 angles plead for his conviction and one angel pleads for his acquittal, the Holy One, praise to Him, lends His weight to the scale of merit. Not only this entire angel, but if 999 aspects of that angel plead for conviction and one aspect for acquittal, the Holy One, praise to Him, lends His weight to the scale of merit. What is the reason? It does not say, “if there is for him one angel of a thousand,” but “one out of a thousand”, one aspect out of a thousand aspects of that angel. What is written afterwards? “He will act with him in grace and say, let him be hurt, not go down to destruction; I found weregilt.” “Let him be hurt,” by suffering. “I found weregilt,” he found means to redeem himself. That is, in this world. But in the Future World, if he has a majority of merits, he inherits paradise; a majority of sins, he inherits hell. If he was 50–50. {NAME} said, “he carries his iniquity.” {NAME} said, it is written: “He carries.” What does the Holy One, praise to Him, do? He grabs one of his demerits, and the merits decide. {NAME} said: “You, Eternal, are acting in grace, for You will complete for everybody according to his deeds.” And if he has none, You will give him from Yours. That is {NAME} opinion, for {NAME} said, “You, Eternal, are acting in grace,” this teaches that He turns to the aspect of grace.
[Kiddushin 1:9.4] {NAME} said that {NAME} asked about: “Justice watches over the one ambling in simplicity but evil falsifies sin.” “Evil pursues the sinners but He well rewards the just.” “He watches over the feet of His pious, but the wicked will be silenced in darkness, etc.” “If He scoffs with the scoffers, but to the meek He gives kindness.” “Sages inherit honor, but shame lifts the silly.” Fencing makes a fence, and doors entry. And so it is, fencing makes a fence and a door entry. But {NAME} asked in the name of {NAME}: If somebody guards himself once, twice, and three times from a sin, from then on the Holy One, praise to Him, will guard him. What is the reason? “Lo, all this God will work, twice or three times with a man.”
[Kiddushin 1:9.5] {NAME} said, but only if the person does not revert. What is the reason? It does not say “The triple thread will never snap” but rather “The triple thread will not quickly snap.” If you work on it, it will split. {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: There is no forgetting before the Holy One, praise to Him, but for Israel He becomes forgetful. What is the reason? It is written “He forgets sin.” And so David says: “You forgot Your people’s sin, You covered up all their misdeeds, Selah.”
[Kiddushin 2:1.1] MISHNAH: A man may contract a premininary marriage either in person or through an agent, and a woman may be taken in preliminary marriage either in person or through an agent. A man may give away his adolescent daughter in preliminary marriage himself or through his agent. If a man say to a woman: Be married to me preliminarily by this date fruit, be preliminarily married by that one, she is preliminarily married if one of them was worth a peruṭah , otherwise she is not preliminarily married. By this and by that one, she is preliminarily married if together they are worth a peruṭah , but if she was eating immediately what she received, she is not preliminarily married unless one of them was worth a peruṭah .
[Kiddushin 2:1.2] HALAKHAH: “A man may contract a premininary marriage either in person or through an agent,” etc. From where that a person’s agent may act in his stead? {NAME} said: “The entirety of the assembly of the congregation of Israel shall slaughter it in the evening.” But do all of them slaughter? Does not one slaughter for the many? From here [it follows that] a person’s agent may act in his stead. And that would be the same as: “Everybody should take for himself a sheep for the family, a sheep to a house.” Did everyone take? Did not one take for the many? From here [it follows that] a person’s agent may act in his stead. {NAME} said, there is a difference, for a person may slaughter the Passover sacrifice of another without the latter’s knowledge. If you wanted to say that a person may separate the Passover sacrifice for another without the latter’s knowledge, you cannot say so, for {NAME} said in the name of {NAME} that a person may slaughter the Passover sacrifice of another without the latter’s knowledge, but nobody may separate the Passover sacrifice for another without the latter’s knowledge.
[Kiddushin 2:1.3] The House of Shammai say, an agent may not testify as witness. But the House of Hillel say, an agent may testify as witness. How is that? If he sent two, in the opinion of the House of Shammai there is an agent and two witnesses. In the opinion of the House of Hillel, all three can be agents and all three can be witnesses. {NAME} said, the matter is reasonable if the preliminary marriage was executed by document. But if he executed the preliminary marriage by money, he became an interested party in his testimony. {NAME} said, since the Torah made him trustworthy, even if he executed the preliminary marriage by money, he did not become an interested party in his testimony. {NAME} said, there came a case before Rav who admitted the agent as witness. A person deposited his amphoras in another’s corral; [the latter] reneged. The case came before {NAME} who admitted the agent as witness and made him swear [by the testimony of] the porter.
[Kiddushin 2:1.4] Some baraita implies that the agent of a person acts in his stead, and some baraita implies that the agent of a person does not act in his stead. “If he definitively will substitute, if he himself will dissolve.” We may hold that a person’s agent cannot act in his stead because Scripture excluded him. “He shall lean his hand,” not the hand of his son nor the hand of his slave nor the hand of his agent. We may hold that a person’s agent can act in his stead but [in this case] Scripture excluded him. “His master shall pierce his ear with an awl;” “his master” but not the latter’s son, “his master” but not the latter’s agent. We may hold that a person’s agent can act in his stead but Scripture excluded him. Some Tannaïm state: “He shall pierce”, to include the agent. This follows {NAME}. Following {NAME}? “His master”, anybody acting on his master’s authority.
[Kiddushin 2:1.5] We have stated: “A preliminarily married adolescent girl, or her father, can accept her bill of divorce.” {NAME} said, like the disagreement about divorce is the disagreement about preliminary marriage. {NAME} said, everybody agrees about preliminary marriage that her father contracts but not she herself. {NAME} agrees about a definitive marriage that she is not empowered to marry herself off and to let her father lose her earnings. In the opinion of {NAME} she has no legal standing relative to her father and cannot appoint an agent. In the opinion of {NAME} she does have legal standing relative to her father and can appoint an agent. A Mishnah disagrees with {NAME}: “A man contracts a preliminary marriage either in person or through his agent and a woman contracts a preliminary marriage either in person or through her agent.” He explains it about an adult woman. But did we not state: “If an underage girl said, accept the bill of divorce for me, it is no valid bill of divorce until it reaches her hand.” He explains it about an orphan. But did we not state: “If her father said to [an agent]: Go and receive my daughter’s bill of divorce, if [the husband] wants to retract he cannot retract.” He explains that the Mishnah deals with cases; the first part about an orphan and the second part if she has a father. A Mishnah disagrees with {NAME}. “A man may contract a preliminary marriage for his adolescent daughter either by himself or by his agent.” He explains that following {NAME}, since {NAME} said, “no two hands can acquire together.” {NAME} said, a rabbi came out from the assembly and said, a case was decided following {NAME}. Can one rely on that? It was no question of relying on him since it was as from the sea to the frying pan.
[Kiddushin 2:1.6] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If an underage girl married herself off preliminarily with two pubic hairs, her father repudiates the marriage but not she herself. This follows neither {NAME} nor {NAME}. If following {NAME}, there is no place for repudiation. If following {NAME}, the marriage is valid by biblical standards. It follows only {NAME}. Even though {NAME} says that everybody agrees about preliminary marriage that her father contracts but not she herself, he agrees in this case that the father repudiates on her behalf.
[Kiddushin 2:1.7] {NAME} and {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If she was preliminarily married with agreement but definitively married without agreement: there was such a case and the father came and removed her from the bridal chamber. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: He had an indication that {NAME} disagreed with {NAME}. But this does not disagree. Just as {NAME} said there, she is not empowered to marry herself off and let her father lose her earnings, so {NAME} said here, she is not empowered to marry herself off and let her father lose her earnings. {NAME} and {NAME} came in the name of {NAME}: If she was preliminarily married without agreement and was being definitively married without agreement: there was such a case and the father came and annulled her preliminary marriage.
[Kiddushin 2:1.8] If she was preliminarily married with agreement but definitively married without agreement, may she eat heave? Rav said, she does eat; but {NAME} said, she may not eat. {NAME} said, Rav’s reason is that if she was preliminarily married with agreement, the permanence of the status quo implies the assumption that he definitively married her with agreement. {NAME} said, Rav’s reason is that by the earlier Mishnah, a preliminarily married daughter of an Israel may eat heave. What is the difference between them? Her earnings. According to {NAME}, for Rav her earnings belong to her husband; according to {NAME}, for Rav her earnings belong to her father. If she should die, who inherits from her? According to {NAME}, for Rav her husband inherits; according to {NAME}, for Rav her father inherits if she dies. {NAME} stated, for Rav her husband inherits if she dies. If she was preliminarily married without agreement and definitively married without agreement, may she eat heave? {NAME} said, she does eat. Come and see: If she was preliminarily married with agreement and definitively married without agreement, {NAME} says that she may not eat; here he says she may eat? {NAME} treats her as an orphan.
[Kiddushin 2:1.9] Mishnah: “Be married to me preliminarily by this date fruit,” etc. The Mishnah [presents the case] that she said, I cannot accept this one, try that one; I cannot accept this one, try that one. “By this and by that one and by that one.” Who is the Tanna of Wawim ? {NAME}. [Kiddushin 2:1.10] {NAME} in the name of Rav: “ ‘Be preliminarily married to me by this tetradrachma after thirty [days].’ Even if she spent it within the thirty [days], she is preliminarily married; also {NAME} will agree to this.” What is the difference between this and a loan? A loan was not given for preliminary marriage, while this was given from the start for preliminary marriage. Just as {NAME} said that anybody who deviates from the orders of the owner is called a robber, so {NAME} says here, anybody who deviates from the orders of the owner is called a robber. The one who said that one cannot preliminarily marry with a robbed item refers to an item which he has no chance to remove from her hand. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: the one who said that one may preliminarily marry with a robbed item refers to an item which the owner gave up hope to recover. The one who said that one cannot preliminarily marry with a robbed item refers to an item which the owner did not give up hope to recover.

[Kiddushin 2:1.18] “ ‘Hold this tetradrachma for me’ and at the moment of delivery he said, ‘lo, you are preliminarily married to me,’ she is preliminarily married. [Kiddushin 2:1.19] A person gave a pledge to another; the other reneged on it. {NAME}, {NAME}, and {NAME} all three say it was a deal about flax seed and he had given partial payment. Is a woman usually acquired split? {NAME} and {NAME} both said, a sale usually may be split, the acquisition of a wife cannot be split.
[Kiddushin 2:2.1] MISHNAH: “Be preliminarily married to me by this cup of wine,” but it turned out to be honey; “of honey” but it turned out to be wine; “by this silver denar,” but it turned out to be of gold, “gold denar” but it turned out to be of silver; “on condition that I be poor”, but he turned out to be rich; “rich” but he turned out to be poor; she is not preliminarily married. {NAME} said, if he tricked her by understatement she is preliminarily married. “On condition that I be a Cohen,” and he turned out to be a Levite; “a Levite” and he turned out to be a Cohen; “a Gibeonite” and he turned out to be a bastard, “a bastard” and he turned out to be a Gibeonite; “a villager” and he turned out to be from a walled city; “from a walled city” and he turned out to be from a village; “on condition that my house be close to the public baths” and it turned out to be far, “far” and it turned out to be close; “on condition that I have a grown-up daughter or slave-girl” and it turned out that he had none, “on condition that I have not” and it turned out that he did have; “on condition that I have children” and it turned out that he had none, “on condition that I not have children” and it turned out that he did have. Il all these cases she is not preliminarily married even if she says, I had the intention to be preliminarily married to him regardless. The same holds if she misinformed him.
[Kiddushin 2:2.2] HALAKHAH: “Be preliminarily married to me by this cup of wine,” etc. If this cup and its contents together have the value of a peruṭah , she is preliminarily married; otherwise she is not preliminarily married. “Acquire it and its contents,” if its contents are worth a peruṭah , she is preliminarily married; otherwise she is not preliminarily married; she acquired only its contents.
[Kiddushin 2:2.3] “{NAME} said, if he tricked her by understatement she is preliminarily married.” {NAME} said, {NAME} agrees that she is not preliminarily married if he tricked her by misstating his personal status. {NAME} said, the Mishnah says this: “ ‘On condition that I be a Cohen,’ and he turned out to be a Levite.”
[Kiddushin 2:2.4] One understands “Cohen and he turns out to be a Levite.” “Levite and he turns out to be a Cohen”? She may say, I do not want one who is haughty towards me. One understands “from a walled city” and he turned out to be a villager; “from a village” and he turned out to be from a walled city? She may say, I want to be in a quiet place. “On condition that my house be close to the public baths” and it turned out to be far. One understands “close and it turned out to be far.” “Far and it turned out to be close”? She can say, I want to take a walk going and returning. “On condition that I have a daughter or slave-girl hairdresser” and it turned out that he had none, that one understands. “On condition that I have” and it turned out that he did not have?
