It is better that “the bull shall be stoned” shall be interpreted following “the bull shall be stoned” rather than that “the bull shall be stoned” should be interpreted following “the bull by stoning shall be stoned”.
[Bava Kamma 4:5.3] {NAME} said, I heard something from {NAME} in this matter, but I do not remember what it was. {NAME} told him, maybe it was the following: At the start the discussion refers to the tame animal. It added weregilt for the notorious. Then it added damages for both of them. I could think that as it added damages, it added the payment for the slave; the verse says “but the owner of the bull is free;” free from paying for a slave. {NAME} said, everywhere you are more restrictive for a slave than anything else since even if he is scabbed one pays thirty tetradrachmas; I would have said also (for his father and his mother) the same; the verse says “but the owner of the bull is free;” free from paying for fetuses. Everywhere you are more restrictive for a notorious than for a tame one, would you be more restrictive here for a tame one than for a notorious? But it must be so: Men who act unintentionally are liable; bulls who act unintentionally are not liable. Does this mean that if they acted intentionally, they were liable? The verse says, “but the owner of the bull is free;” free from paying for a slave. Another Tanna stated: “But the owner of the bull is free;” free from paying for a slave. But is it not written: “If people quarrel”, people but not bulls. {NAME} said, so is the baraita : Men who act unintentionally are liable; bulls who act unintentionally are not liable. Does this mean that if they acted intentionally, they were liable? The verse says, “but the owner of the bull is free;” free from paying for a slave. But is it not written: “When they quarrel,” “when they brawl”. Is not quarrel the same as brawl? Since there the act was intentional, so here the act was intentional; or since here the act was unintentional, so here the act was unintentional. What about this? As {NAME} said, at the start it treats the tame animal, etc.
[Bava Kamma 4:5.4] From where damages for a slave? The verse says, “or it gores a son, or it gores a daughter, …, and if a slave, etc.” {NAME} and {NAME}. One said, the addition may not be more than the main thing. But the other said, he has to pay the entire damages.
[Bava Kamma 4:6.1] MISHNAH: A bull which was rubbing itself against a wall which then fell on a human, [or which] intended to kill an animal but killed a human, a Gentile but killed a Jew, stillbirth but killed a viable child, is free from prosecution.
[Bava Kamma 4:6.2] HALAKHAH: “A bull which was rubbing itself against a wall,” etc. “A man who kills any human soul,” to include a hit which is potentially deadly. Some Tannaïm state, even if it is not deadly. {NAME} said, even if it is deadly but a third person came and killed, the killer is guilty. “And it killed a man or a woman,” just as a man lets his sons inherit his injury claims, so a woman lets her sons inherit her injury claims. But does not a man inherit from his wife? {NAME} said, so did {NAME}, the father of the Mishnah, explain: One teaches here about weregilt which is due after death.
[Bava Kamma 4:6.3] If somebody sells a bull to another person and it turns out to be goring. Rav said, it is an acquisition in error, but {NAME} says, he can tell him: I sold it to you to be slaughtered. “He shall give weregilt for his person.” Some Tannaїm state: The attacker’s person. Some Tannaїm state: The person suffering the damage. Following him who said, the person suffering the damage, [assume] the first one injured him fatally and then the second came and kept him in confusion. If you say that damages are fully required, the first one pays damages and the second pays the weregilt. If you say that damages are not fully required, the first one pays weregilt but the second is not liable. Following him who said, the attacker’s person, if you say that damages are fully required, the first one pays weregilt and the second is not liable. If you say that damages are not fully required, neither one is liable.
[Bava Kamma 4:7.1] MISHNAH: A bull belonging to a woman, a bull belonging to orphans, a bull under a guardian, a wild bull, a bull of Temple property, a bull belonging to a proselyte who died without heirs, these are subject to the death penalty. {NAME} says that a wild bull, a bull of Temple property, a bull belonging to a proselyte who died without heirs, are not subject to the death penalty since they have no owners.
[Bava Kamma 4:7.2] HALAKHAH: “A bull belonging to a woman, a bull belonging to orphans,” etc. What is {NAME} reason? “It was testified to before its owners and they did not watch it;” those have no owners who could be responsible for damages. {NAME} stated: In matters of damages, {NAME} declares liable but {NAME} declares not liable. What about weregilt? {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Everybody agrees that he is liable for weregilt. But some say, {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Just as they disagree for damages so they disagree for weregilt. {NAME} asked before {NAME}: How does one actually act? He said to him, following {NAME} that in matters of damages, {NAME} declares liable but {NAME} declares not liable; therefore, in matters of weregilt everybody agrees that he is liable.
[Bava Kamma 4:8.1] MISHNAH: If one dedicates a bull which is led out to be stoned, it is not dedicated, and if it was slaughtered, its meat is forbidden. If its owner dedicated it before sentence was pronounced, it is dedicated, and if it was slaughtered, its meat is permitted.
[Bava Kamma 4:8.2] HALAKHAH: “A bull which is led out to be stoned,” etc. It was stated: If a bull was led out to be stoned when its witnesses were found to be false, {NAME} said, the first to come acquires it; {NAME} said, it was false despair. Similarly, if a slave was led out to be killed when his witnesses were found to be false, {NAME} said, he acquired himself; {NAME} said, it was false despair.
[Bava Kamma 4:9.1] MISHNAH: If it was handed over to an unpaid trustee, or a borrower, or a paid trustee, or a lessee, they entered instead of the owner; a notorious animal pays full damages, a tame one half damages. If he tied it down with a rope and locked it in as he should, if then it broke out and caused damage he is liable whether tame or notorious. {NAME} says, for the tame he is liable, for the notorious he is not liable since it was said: “if its owner would not guard it,” but it was guarded. {NAME} says, this one can be guarded only by the knife.
[Bava Kamma 4:9.2] HALAKHAH: “If it was handed over to an unpaid trustee,” etc. {NAME} said, the words of {NAME} that watching for damages is on the level of an unpaid trustee; {NAME} said that watching for damages is on the level of a paid trustee. {NAME} said, the words of {NAME}: If one handed over a bull to an unpaid trustee, if it went off and did damage, he is not liable; if it went out and became torn, he is not liable. To a paid trustee, if it went off and did damage, he is liable; if it went out and became torn, he is not liable. {NAME} said, the words of {NAME}: If one handed over a notorious bull to an unpaid trustee, if it went off and did damage, he is liable; if it went out and became torn, he is not liable. To a paid trustee, if it went off and did damage, he is liable; if it went out and became torn, he is liable. {NAME} said, was it not watched? But the Torah declared him liable. {NAME} said, for every guarding required by the Torah, even if it was done by enclosing in an iron wall, one only qualifies by personal presence. Therefore one determines whether he is qualified for watching; then he is not liable, otherwise he is liable.
[Bava Kamma 5:1.1] MISHNAH: A bull gored a cow and her fetus was found beside her. If it is not known whether she gave birth before she was gored or gave birth after she was gored, he pays half the damages for the cow and a quarter for the fetus. And similarly, if a cow gored an ox and her calf is found next to her, but it is not known whether she gave birth before or after she gored, he pays half the damage from the cow and a quarter from the calf.
[Bava Kamma 5:1.2] HALAKHAH: “A bull gored a cow”, etc. Do all cows have miscarriages? Should we follow the majority of cases? This implies that in criminal cases and in money matters one does not apply a majority argument. {NAME} said, in another case they applied a majority argument in criminal cases and in money matters, as {NAME} stated: “If a camel was in heat among camels and one finds one of them dead, I am saying that certainly the one in heat killed it.”
[Bava Kamma 5:1.3] And {NAME} said, so is the Mishnah: He pays half of the damage from the cow and the owner of the calves returns a quarter to the owner of the cow. {NAME} said, each of them gives half. What is the difference between them? If the calves died. According to him who said, he pays half of the damage from the cow and a quarter of the damage from the calf, each one pays his part of the damage. According to him who said, he pays half of the damage from the cow and the owner of the calves returns a quarter to the owner of the cow, one pays the damage, but the other one says, I did not want these, here they are before you.
[Bava Kamma 5:1.4] “And similarly, if a cow gored an ox,” etc. {NAME} asked before {NAME}: Because it is in doubt; therefore if it were certain, each one would give half? Would I say that a foot of a person is the entire person? Each one would give half? He said to him, the Mishnah deals with a notorious animal. “Its foot is sold to you,” he sold half. “Its second foot is sold to you,” he sold half of the [remaining] half. {NAME} said, all these traditions are Levi’s.
[Bava Kamma 5:2.1] MISHNAH: If a potter put his pots in a private courtyard without permission and an animal of the owner broke them, [the owner] is not liable; if [the animal] was hurt, the owner of the pots is liable. But if he puts them there with permission, the owner of the courtyard is liable.
[Bava Kamma 5:2.2] HALAKHAH: “If a potter put his pots,” etc. If he put his pots in a private courtyard without permission and a bull came from another place and broke them, he is not liable. If it was hurt by them, he is not liable. This implies that ‘horn’ is not liable in a courtyard which belongs to neither party.
[Bava Kamma 5:3.1] MISHNAH: If somebody put his produce in a private courtyard without permission and an animal of the owner ate them, [the owner] is not liable; if [the animal] was hurt, the owner of the produce is liable. But if he puts them there with permission, the owner of the courtyard is liable.
[Bava Kamma 5:3.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody put his produce in a private courtyard,” etc. If he put his produce in a private courtyard without permission and a bull came from another place and ate them, he is not liable. If it was hurt by them, he is not liable. This implies that the ‘tooth’ is not liable in a courtyard which belongs to neither party.
[Bava Kamma 5:4.1] MISHNAH: If somebody put his bull in a private courtyard without permission and the owner’s bull gored it or his dog bit it, [the owner] is not liable; if it gored the owner’s bull, he is liable. If it fell into his cistern and caused it to stink, he is liable. If his father or son were inside, he pays weregilt. But if he put it in by permission, the owner of the courtyard is liable; Rebbi says, in all these cases, only if he agreed to watch.
[Bava Kamma 5:4.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody put a bull in a private courtyard,” etc. “If somebody put a bull in a private courtyard without permission, and a bull came from another place. If it gored, hit, bit, walloped, or kicked, he pays full damages, the words of {NAME}. But the Sages say, for ‘tooth’ and ‘foot’ he is liable; for goring, or hitting, or biting, or walloping, or kicking, or pushing, a tame [bull] pays half the damages, a notorious full damages from storage.”
[Bava Kamma 5:4.3] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Practice follows Rebbi. {NAME} said, practice follows Rebbi. {NAME} said, everybody agrees that in a house, if he tells him, “put it in,” [he implies] “and I shall watch it.” Everybody agrees that on a field, if he tells him, “put it in,” [he implies] “and you watch it.” Where do they disagree? In a courtyard. Rebbi says, a courtyard is like a field, but the Sages say, a courtyard is like a house. There, we have stated: If somebody assembles sheaves in another person’s field without permission.” [{NAME} said,] sheaves on a field are like vessels in a house? {NAME} said, explain it by one which has a lock.
[Bava Kamma 5:5.1] MISHNAH: If a bull intended [to hurt] another bull but hit a woman who then had a miscarriage, he is not liable. But if a man intended [to hurt] a neighbor but hit a woman who then had a miscarriage, he pays for the children. How does he pay for the children? One estimates the worth of the woman before and after she gave birth. {NAME} said, but the value of a woman increses after giving birth! But one estimates how much the children would have been worth and gives [the value] to the husband; if she does not have a husband, to the latter’s heirs. If she was a freedwoman or a proselyte, he is not liable.
[Bava Kamma 5:5.2] HALAKHAH: “If a bull intended,” etc. A bull which intended [to attack] another; therefore, if it intended to hit the woman is he liable? Does it make a difference whether it intended to hit the woman or intended to hit another [bull]? Then why was it stated here? {NAME} said, because he had to state the next clause: “But if a human intended [to hurt] another human but hit a woman who then had a miscarriage, he pays for the children.”
[Bava Kamma 5:5.3] It was stated: “I am selling you a fertile slave girl, her children increase her value. {NAME} says, this is buttocks.” It is written: “If quarrelling men hit a pregnant woman and she loses her children.” {NAME} said, from the meaning of “and she loses her children” would I not know that she was pregnant? Then why does the verse say “pregnant”? It tells you that he is not liable unless he hits her at the place of her pregnancy. Therefore, if he hit her on the palm of her hand or the sole of her foot, he is not liable. “As the woman’s husband will put on him”. Do I understand, even if the pregnancy is not his? The verse says, “pregnant”. It tells that he pays only to the master of the pregnancy. {NAME} asked, if somebody sleeps with his mother or his sister, is that one not also the master of the pregnancy? The verse says “husband”, somebody who may be called “husband”. This excludes those who cannot be called “husband”.
[Bava Kamma 5:5.4] {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: Fetuses do not gain freedom by ‘tooth and eye.’ One understands “eye”. Tooth? {NAME} said, so is the baraita : Fetuses do not gain freedom by their mother’s ‘tooth and eye.’
[Bava Kamma 5:6.1] MISHNAH: One who digs a pit in the public domain is liable if an ox or a donkey fell in and died. Anyone who digs a pit, a ditch, a cave, rectangular excavations, or bases for poles, is liable. Then why is it said “a pit”? Just as a pit to be life-threatening must be ten handbreadths deep, so everything to be life-threatening must be ten handbreadths deep. If it was less than ten handbreadths deep when an ox or a donkey fell in and died, he is not liable, but if they were damaged, he is liable. One who digs a pit in a private domain and opens it to the public domain, in the public domain and opens it to a private domain, in a private domain and opens it to another private domain, is liable.
[Bava Kamma 5:6.2] HALAKHAH: “One who digs a pit in the public domain,” etc. It is written: “If a man open a pit” and “if a man dig a pit.” One pit for damages, the other pit for death. {NAME} said, both the pit of death and the pit of damages were added from the same verse, but when it comes to the pit of death you say he is not liable for vessels, but when it comes to the pit of damages you say he is liable for vessels! This is not only if he dug, from where if he bought, inherited, or it was given to him as a gift? The verse says, “if a man acquire a pit.” Has one the right to abandon his damages in the public domain? {NAME} said, explain it following {NAME} who said, three [handbreadths] close to a domain are like that domain.
[Bava Kamma 5:6.3] {NAME} asked: Can the depth be considered like the height? How is that? If about him who comes from up high, he sees it. But for him who comes from below.
[Bava Kamma 5:7.1] MISHNAH: A pit dug by two partners; if the first went by and did not cover it, the second and did not cover it, the second is liable. If the first covered it, the second came and uncovered it, the second is liable. If the first covered it, the second came, found it uncovered but did not cover it, the second is liable. If he covered it appropriately but an ox or a donkey fell in and died, he is not liable. If he did not cover it appropriately and an ox or a donkey fell in and died, he is liable. If it fell forward because of the noise of the excavation, he is liable, backward because of the noise of the excavation, he is not liable. If an ox and its equipment fell in and broke, a donkey and its equipment was torn, he is liable for the animal but not liable for the equipment. If the ox falling in was deaf-mute, insane, or young, he is liable; a son or daughter, a slave or slave-girl, he is not liable.
[Bava Kamma 5:7.2] HALAKHAH: “A pit dug by two partners,” etc. How is a pit of two partners possible? {NAME} said, explain it if they both together put in the last stone. And why did they not explain that each of them dug ten handbreadths? Because he wants to explain it for a pit ten handbreadths deep of two partners.
[Bava Kamma 5:7.3] “If the first went by and did not cover it, the second and did not cover it, the second is liable.” {NAME}, {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: One gives him time to cut cedars from Lebanon. That can be a stringency and it can be a leniency. Sometimes he is close to the Lebanon, sometimes he is far from the Lebanon.
[Bava Kamma 5:7.4] “If he covered it appropriately.” How much does it have to be covered? It shall be as we have stated there: “That [it can withstand] a truck full of stones driving over it.”
[Bava Kamma 5:7.5] {NAME} said, in front of him, whether forward ot behind he is (not) liable. Outside, forward he is (not) liable, behind he is [not] liable.
[Bava Kamma 5:7.6] “If an ox and its equipment fell in and broke, a donkey and its equipment and was torn, he is liable for the animal but not liable for the equipment.” {NAME} said, when it became disoriented because of the air, but if it hit the ground he is liable. {NAME} and {NAME} both say, even if it hit the ground, he is not liable: The Torah absolved from liability when it fell down. “An ox or a donkey fell in there;” “an ox” and not an ox and its equipment; “a donkey” and not a donkey and its equipment. Since it looked logical: If a pit of damages, where one is not liable for death, one is liable for vessels; would it not be logical that for a pit ten handbreadths deep, for which one is liable for death, should one not be liable for vessels? The verse says, “an ox or a donkey fell in there;” “an ox” and not an ox and its equipment; “a donkey” and not a donkey and its equipment.
[Bava Kamma 5:7.7] “If the ox falling in was deaf-mute, insane, or young, he is liable”. {NAME} said, so is the Mishnah: an ox which is deaf-mute, an insane ox, [an underage ox]; “a son or daughter, a slave or slave-girl, he is not liable”.
[Bava Kamma 5:8.1] MISHNAH: The ox and any domestic animal equally are under the rules of falling into a pit, separating from Mount Sinai, paying double restitution, returning lost property, unloading, muzzling, interbreeding, and the Sabbath. Wild animals and birds follow the same rules. Then why was it said “ox or donkey”? But the verse speaks of the actuality.
[Bava Kamma 5:8.2] HALAKHAH: “The ox and any domestic animal equally are under the rules of falling into a pit,” etc. Falling into a pit, “and an ox or a donkey fell in there.” Separating from Mount Sinai, “neither animal nor man shall live.” Paying double restitution, “from ox to donkey”. To return lost property, “you shall certainly return them.” Unloading, “do remove.” Muzzling, “do not muzzle an ox while threshing.” Interbreeding, “your animal you shall not breed kilaim .” The Sabbath, “that your ox and your donkey may rest.”
[Bava Kamma 5:8.3] “Wild animals and birds follow the same rules.” {NAME} said, the sea goose is kilaim with domesticated goose. {NAME} said, the Mishnah does not say so, but an ox and a bison are kilaim with one another; a donkey and a wild donkey are kilaim with one another. {NAME} said, Rebbi stated a complete Mishnah: “Wild animals and birds follow the same rules.” {NAME} said, and I brought this from the House of Levi: A rooster with a pheasant, a rooster with a peacock-hen are kilaim even though they are similar one to the other.
[Bava Kamma 6:1.1] MISHNAH: He who brings a flock into a corral and locks them in as he should, but they managed to get out and caused damage, is liable. If they broke out in the night or robbers broke in and they managed to get out and caused damage, he is not liable. If robbers let them out, the robbers are liable.
[Bava Kamma 6:1.2] HALAKHAH: “He who brings a flock into a corral,” etc. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: In disagreement. {NAME} said, it is everybody’s opinion. {NAME} said, {NAME} statement is convincing since watching the animal itself is written only for “horn”. What about it? {NAME} said, in disagreement. {NAME} said, it is everybody’s opinion. Some say, it follows {NAME} who said, in no case is he liable.
[Bava Kamma 6:1.3] So far if [the corral] was fenced in on four sides. If it was fenced in on three sides and breached on one side, and [an animal] left through the breach, what is the rule? Let us hear from the following: “If his wall fell in from the noise of earthquakes or thunder and he rebuilt it as required, he is not liable, otherwise he is liable.” The only problem is if three better built walls fell together with it.
[Bava Kamma 6:1.4] It was stated: {NAME} said, four persons are not required to pay but Heaven will not forgive them until they pay up: A person who knows testimony beneficial to another but does not testify is not required to pay but Heaven will not forgive him until he pays up. A person who hires false witnesses against another and collects is not required to pay but Heaven will not forgive him until he pays up. A person who bends standing grain towards a fire or who makes a breach in a fence for animals is not required to pay but Heaven will not forgive him until he pays up.
[Bava Kamma 6:1.5] “If robbers let it out, the robbers are liable.” {NAME} said, if they let it out as part of their robbery. But if they let it out to get lost, the robbers are not liable.
[Bava Kamma 6:2.1] MISHNAH: If he left it in the sun or handed it over to a deaf-and-dumb, an insane, or an underage person, he is liable. If he handed it over to a shepherd, the shepherd takes his place. If it fell into a garden and caused damage, it pays for what it profited. If it entered in due course, it pays for what it damaged. How does it pay for what it damaged? One estimates a bet se’ah of the field; how much was it worth and how much is it worth. {NAME} says, if it ate ripe produce it pays for ripe produce, whether one or two se’ah .
[Bava Kamma 6:2.2] HALAKHAH: It was stated: “If a shepherd handed his flock over to another shepherd, the first is liable, the second is not liable.” Rav and {NAME} both said, since he handed it over to a responsible person, he is not liable.
[Bava Kamma 6:2.3] “If he handed it over to a shepherd, the shepherd takes his place. If it fell into a garden and caused damage, he pays for what it profited.” {NAME} said, if it fell on vegetables. But if it stood up and grazed, he pays for what it damaged.
[Bava Kamma 6:2.4] “If it entered in due course, he pays for what it damaged.” {NAME} said, on that field itself he is not liable, but for another field he is liable. {NAME} and {NAME} both said, even if it grazed on that entire field he is not liable; he only is liable if it left the field for the public domain and from the public domain entered another field. But what is the rule if it fell into a garden and then entered another garden? In the opinion of {NAME} who said, on that field itself he is not liable, here he will be liable. In the opinion of {NAME} and {NAME} who both said, even if it grazed on that entire field he is not liable; he only is liable if it left the field for the public domain and from the public domain entered another field. But if it fell into a place which it could have entered, or it entered a place into which it could have fallen? {NAME} said, that is the Mishnah; it fell into a place into which it only could have fallen. But if it fell into a place which it could have entered? Each case is problematic for one of them. One needs the first case, that he pays what it profited; the other needs the other case, that he pays what it damaged.
[Bava Kamma 6:2.5] It was stated: “One does not estimate a bet kor because it would diminish, nor a bet qab because it would inflate. But one estimates a bet se’ah of the field in question, how much it was worth and how much is it worth now. {NAME} said, when? If it ate shoots of the fig tree or plucked shoots of vines. But if it ate unripe grapes or unripe figs, one estimates them as fully grown fruits. {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: If it ate fully grown produce, he pays for fully grown produce, [fruits of] trees, one estimates trees for him. Trees one estimates by the bet se’ah . {NAME} said in the name of {NAME}: Produce not yet one-third ripe is estimated under the rules of trees.” In the House of {NAME} they said, one estimates a three- qab in sixty three- qabs . {NAME} said, one estimates a stalk in sixty stalks.
[Bava Kamma 6:2.6] A person stole a hard date. The case came before {NAME} who said to him, go and estimate for him at the top of the date palm. {NAME} said, it was a preserve of unripe dates.
[Bava Kamma 6:3.1] MISHNAH: If somebody stacks his sheaves on another person’s field without permission and the field’s owner’s animals ate them, he is not liable. If it was damaged by it, the owner of the stack is liable. But if he stacked his sheaves with permission, the field’s owner is liable.
[Bava Kamma 6:3.2] HALAKHAH: If somebody stacks his sheaves on another person’s field without permission.” {NAME} said, are sheaves on a field like vessels in a house? {NAME} said, explain it by one which has a lock.
[Bava Kamma 6:4.1] MISHNAH: He who causes a fire through the hand of a deaf-mute, an insane, or an underage person is not liable in human law but liable in Heaven’s law. If he causes it through a hearing person, the hearing person is liable. If one person brings the fire and another one the wood, the one bringing the wood is liable. If one brings the wood and another one the fire, the one bringing the fire is liable. If another person came and fanned the flames, the one who fanned is liable. If the wind fanned it, none of them is liable.
[Bava Kamma 6:4.2] HALAKHAH: “He who sets a fire,” etc. {NAME} said, if he handed him a glowing coal. But if he handed him an open flame he is liable. {NAME} said, coal and flame are the same. It is difficult according to {NAME}, for if somebody saw another person’s glowing coal rolling by and did not extinguish it, is he not free from liability? They said, explain it if he handed him an ownerless glowing coal, or also an ownerless flame, and one cannot infer anything.
[Bava Kamma 6:4.3] Some Tannaĩm state: וְלִיבָּה. Some Tannaïm state: וְנִיבָּה. He who says וְלִיבָּה. As it is written, “in the flaming fire”. He who says וְנִיבָּה, “it was in my heart like burning fire.”
[Bava Kamma 6:4.4] There, they say, the Mishnah speaks of a catastrophic wind, but in case of normal wind he is liable. {NAME} and {NAME} both say, even in case of normal wind he is not liable; for sometimes it blows, sometimes it does not blow.
[Bava Kamma 6:5.1] MISHNAH: He who sets a fire which consumes wood, or stones, or dust, is liable since it is said: “If fire gets out of control and finds thorns, etc.” If it crossed a wall four cubits high, or a public road, or a brook, he is not liable.
[Bava Kamma 6:5.2] HALAKHAH: “He who sets a fire which consumes wood,” etc. Since thorns are flammable, do I only include flammable material? The verse says, “a stack”. Since a stack of sheaves is particular in that it was harvested, do I only include harvested material? The verse says, “standing grain.” Since all of these are particular in that they are flammable, do I only include flammable material? If it swept his furrow or damaged his stone, from where? The verse says, “or the field.” Should it only have mentioned thorns, standing grain, and stack, but not mentioned field? In the opinion of {NAME} this is acceptable since he says, he pays for everything inside. But according to the rabbis, who say that he only pays for a stack of wheat or barley sheaves, why did it mention “field”, why did it mention “stack”?
[Bava Kamma 6:5.3] “If it crossed a wall four cubits high, or a public road, or a brook, he is not liable.” {NAME} said, the Mishnah speaks of burning fire. But if it is wind-whipped everybody agrees that he is liable. {NAME} said, the Mishnah speaks of wind-whipped fire, but if it is burning he is not liable.
[Bava Kamma 6:6.1] MISHNAH: If somebody starts a fire inside his property, how far does it have to spread? {NAME} says, one looks at it as if he started it at the center of a bet kor {NAME} says, sixteen cubits like a public road; and {NAME} says, 50 cubits; and {NAME} says “the person setting the fire shall certainly pay,” everything depends on the setting of the fire.
[Bava Kamma 6:6.2] HALAKHAH: “If somebody starts a fire inside his property,” etc. “It happened that a fire crossed the Jordan, because it was a firestorm. How far may a fire spread? {NAME} says sixteen cubits like a public road, if there is wind thirty cubits. {NAME} says thirty cubits, if there is wind fifty cubits. {NAME} says 50 cubits, if there is wind a hundred cubits. It happened in Arabia that a fire jumped more than three hundred cubits. When is this? If it jumps. But if there is wood or it burns continuously, he is liable even up to a mil . If it crossed a river or a pond eight cubits wide, he is not liable.”
[Bava Kamma 6:7.1] MISHNAH: He who sets fire to a stack of sheaves which contains implements, {NAME} says, he has to pay everything contained in it but the Sages say, he pays only for a stack of wheat sheaves or a stack of barley sheaves. If a goat was tied to it, and a slave was nearby, and they were burned, he is liable. If a slave was tied to it, and a goat was nearby, and they were burned, he is not liable. But the Sages agree with {NAME} that one who sets fire to a building has to pay everything contained in it since people regularly store things in houses.
[Bava Kamma 6:7.2] HALAKHAH: “He who sets fire to a stack of sheaves,” etc. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: The Sages agree with {NAME} about threshing tools which usually are hidden there. The argument of {NAME} seems inverted. There he says except what is hidden, but here he says including what is hidden? But does not {NAME} simply explain “stack”? Why was “stack” written? That he has to pay for all that is in it. The argument of the rabbis seems inverted. There they say, including what is hidden; but here they say, except what is hidden? But did not {NAME} say in the name of {NAME}: The Sages agree with {NAME} about threshing tools which usually are hidden there? {NAME} said, if there are no witnesses. But if there are witnesses, everybody agrees with Rebbi (Yose) as it was stated: “If it was a stack of wheat sheaves covered with barley or a stack of barley sheaves covered with wheat, he pays for a stack of barley.” As the following: A person deposited a tied sack with another person, when something happened. This one said, it was full of dross, but the other said, it was full of raw silk. [ ] He swears and collects.
[Bava Kamma 6:7.3] {NAME} asked: Can one argue for him an argument which does not apply to him? Let us hear from the following: {NAME} sharecropper deposited a pound of gold with somebody. {NAME} and {NAME} sharecropper died; the case came before {NAME}. He said, does not everybody know that all {NAME} sharecrooper had was {NAME} property? It should be given to {NAME} sons. {NAME} had adult and underage sons. He said, the adult one should take half and when the underage ones grow up, they should receive half. {NAME} died; the case came before {NAME} who said, that argument means nothing [since there are people who do not flout their wealth]; it should be given to the sharecropper’s sons. The trustee told him, I already disbursed half of it. He told him, what you gave, you gave by court order and what you will give, you will give by court order. May the sharecropper’s sons say to {NAME} sons, give us what you took? They can tell them, what was done was done by court order. May the underage ones say to the adult, let us share with you? May they tell them, we found a find? {NAME} said, the case between the adult and underaged ones is compared to one who gave a gift.
[Bava Kamma 6:8.1] MISHNAH: If a spark came from under a hammer and caused damage, he is liable. If a camel was loaded with flax and while it walked in the public domain the flax entered a store, was lit by the storekeeper’s light, and set the building on fire, the camel’s owner is liable. If the store owner put his light outside, the store owner is liable. {NAME} says, in case of a Ḥanukkah light he is not liable.
[Bava Kamma 6:8.2] HALAKHAH: “If a spark is coming from under a hammer,” etc. “{NAME} stated: In case of a Ḥanukkah light he is not liable because he acted with permission. But the Sages say, in any case he is liable, as, e. g., those who build huts in front of their stores on Tabernacles because it is permitted; but if somebody else is hurt by them, he is liable.”
[Bava Kamma 7:1.1] MISHNAH: The obligation to make double restitution is more frequent than that of paying quadruple or quintuple restitution since the obligation to make double restitution applies both to living things and to inanimate objects; but the obligation of paying quadruple or quintuple restitution only applies to oxen and sheep, as it is said: “If a man steal an ox or a sheep,” etc. He who steals from a thief does not pay double restitution, nor does the one who slaughters or sells after a thief pay quadruple or quintuple restitution.
[Bava Kamma 7:1.2] HALAKHAH: “The obligation to make double restitution is more frequent,” etc. From where does he get this? From “if being found it is found”. This includes not only ox, or donkey, or sheep: Since He says “alive”, it includes all living beings. “The stolen goods”, to include movables. Why “ox, or donkey, or sheep”? If it were restricted to anything useful for the altar, one should have stated “ox and sheep”. [If it were restricted to anything useful for the priests, one should have stated “ox and donkey.] {NAME} stated: It excludes real estate which is not movable; it excludes slaves from whom you only have service; it excludes documents which only are for proof.
[Bava Kamma 7:1.3] {NAME} asked: Why did we not state that double restitution is due if a claim of theft is made in a partnership, where quadruple or quintuple restitution does not apply?
[Bava Kamma 7:1.4] It was stated: “It was stolen from the man’s house”, but not from the woman’s house? Is not “his neighbor” only written in respect of the borrower? But one has to say that “he who steals from a thief does not pay [double restitution, nor does the one who slaughters or sells after a thief pay] quadruple or quintuple restitution. If something was stolen which then was stolen from him; [when in the end the stolen object was found, to whom does he pay? To the first owner, to the second, to both of them? If something was stolen which then was stolen from him]; the owners apprehended the second thief who swore to them. If you say that one takes it away from the second, he has to bring a sacrifice for the oath. If you say that one does not take it away from the second, he does not have to bring a sacrifice for his oath. If something was stolen which then was stolen from him and the second thief decides to return it, if you say that he has to return it to the owners, they might not inform the first thief. If you say that he has to return it to the first thief, that one might not inform the owners. What does he have to do? He returns it to the owners in the presence of the thief.
[Bava Kamma 7:2.1] MISHNAH: He who stole according to the testimony of two people and slaughtered or sold according to their testimony or the testimony of two others, has to pay quadruple or quintuple restitution. He who stole and sold on the Sabbath, stole and sold to pagan worship, stole and slaughtered on the Day of Atonement, stole from his father, slaughtered, or sold, and then his father died, stole, slaughtered, and then dedicated it to the Temple, has to pay quadruple or quintuple restitution. He who stole and slaughtered for medical purposes or for the dogs, he who slaughtered and it turned out torn, he who slaughtered a profane animal in the Temple courtyard, has to pay quadruple or quintuple restitution. {NAME} frees from liability in these two cases.
[Bava Kamma 7:2.2] HALAKHAH: Did not {NAME} say in the name of {NAME}: If he is intentional about fat but in error about a sacrifice, he can be warned, is whipped, and brings a sacrifice. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: ( Deut . 25:2 ) “Because of his guilt.” If two alternatives are presented to the court, one chooses one of them. This excludes matters in the power of Heaven.
[Bava Kamma 7:3.1] MISHNAH: One was convicted of theft on the testimony of two witnesses and of slaughtering or selling on their testimony; if they are found perjured they pay everything to him. If he was convicted of theft on the testimony of two witnesses and of slaughtering or selling on the testimony of two others who all were found perjured, the first group pays double restitution and the second group triple. If the second group were found perjured, he pays double restitution while they pay triple. If one of the second group was found perjured, the second testimony is invalidated. If one of the first group is found perjured, the entire testimony is invalidated since if there is no theft there is no slaughter or sale.
[Bava Kamma 7:3.2] HALAKHAH: “A person convicted of theft on the testimony of two witnesses,” etc. {NAME} said, this implies that a perjured witness is not disqualified by the court but is disqualified by himself. Explain it by warning, as it was stated: “{NAME} said, when has this been said? For two testimonies with two warnings. But for one testimony and one warning any testimony which is partially disqualified is totally disqualified.” What does it mean that if it is partially disqualified it is totally disqualified? If they were standing and testifying against him on then tenth of Nisan that he had stolen an ox on the first of Nisan. He slaughtered or sold on the tenth of Nisan. They were shown to be perjured on the fifteenth of Nisan. Any testimony which they delivered between the tenth and the fifteenth of Nisan is retroactively disqualified. {NAME} said, explain it if they deliver their testimony in one group and you cannot infer anything, as we have stated: “They were the first and they were the later [witnesses]. If they were shown to be perjured at first, there is nothing. At the second time, there is one testimony. At the third time, there are two testimonies.” And how is that if they give testimony in one group, you cannot infer anything? It comes only based on multiple testimony.
[Bava Kamma 7:3.3] “One was convicted of theft on the testimony of two witnesses,” etc. So far if the witnesses for theft and those for slaughter came together. If witnesses for theft appeared but were not accepted and after that came witnesses for slaughter. One tells them “witnesses for theft already had appeared but were not accepted, but on the strength of your testimony we shall accept them.” If the witnesses for slaughter turn out to be perjured, they pay because of the witnesses for theft. {NAME} does not say so but: So far if the witnesses for theft and those for slaughter came together. If witnesses for slaughter appeared but were not accepted and after that came witnesses for theft. One tells them “witnesses for slaughter already had appeared but were not accepted, but on the strength of your testimony we shall accept them.” If the witnesses for theft turn out to be perjured, they pay because of the witnesses for slaughter.
[Bava Kamma 7:4.1] MISHNAH: A person convicted of theft on the testimony of two witnesses, who slaughtered or sold by the testimony of a single witness or his own confession, pays double restitution but does not have to pay quadruple or quintuple. One who stole and slaughtered on the Sabbath, or stole and slaughtered for idolatry, or stole from his father and after his father’s death slaughtered or sold, or stole, dedicated it, and afterwards slaughtered or sold, pays double restistution but not quadruple or quintuple. {NAME} says, for sancta for which he is liable by a warranty he has to pay quadruple or quintuple, but if there is no warranty, he is not liable.
[Bava Kamma 7:4.2] HALAKHAH: “One who stole and slaughtered on the Sabbath,” etc. Did not {NAME} say in the name of {NAME}: If he is intentional error about fat but in error about a sacrifice, he can be warned, is whipped, and brings a sacrifice. Who stated it? [{NAME}, as we have stated]: “{NAME} says, for sancta for which he is liable by a warranty he has to pay quadruple or quintuple, but if there is no warranty, he is not liable.”
[Bava Kamma 7:4.3] {NAME} asked: If somebody redeems a string of dry figs from the Temple treasurer, does it become ṭevel for tithes? {NAME} asked: Did we not state about him who “stole, dedicated it, and afterwards slaughtered or sold”? As you say there, the one who dedicates is not like a seller, so one who redeems is not like a buyer. The word of {NAME} implies that selling is like redeeming. They said, he has the choice of redeeming and eating it.
[Bava Kamma 7:4.4] {NAME} said: If they saw him slaughtering a black ox in a forest, it is prima facie evidence that it was stolen. Could you not assume that it was lying down? Explain it if they saw him dragging it.
[Bava Kamma 7:4.5] There is a rule about the slaughterer which does not apply to the seller and to the seller which does not apply to the slaughterer, for he who slaughters on the Sabbath is criminally liable but he who sells on the Sabbath cannot be prosecuted. {NAME} said, we find a case of sale for which one is criminally liable on the Sabbath. Think of it, if somebody said to another: tear something off from this ground to acquire, did he not acquire? {NAME} said, the tearing makes him liable, not the sale.
[Bava Kamma 7:5.1] MISHNAH: One who sold it except for a one percent interest in it, or had a partnership interest in it, one who slaughtered and it became a carcass in his hand, or one who stabs or tears out, pays double restitution but not quadruple or quintuple. He who stole on the owner’s property but slaughtered or sold off their property, or stole off their property and slaughtered or sold on their property, or stole and slaughtered or sold off their property has to pay quadruple or quintuple restitution. But if he stole and slaughtered or sold on their property, he is not liable.
[Bava Kamma 7:5.2] HALAKHAH: “One who sold it except for a one percent interest in it,” etc. “He who stole on the owner’s property,” etc. {NAME} asked: It he sold it in halves, what is the rule? If he sold half of it to one person and the other half to another, what is the rule? Let us hear from the following: “If he sold it except for its forefoot, except for its hindfoot, except for its horn, except for its shearings, he pays quadruple or quintuple restitution. {NAME} says, except for its horn he pays double restitution, except for its shearings he pays quadruple or quintuple restitution. Rebbi says, except for a vital organ he pays quadruple or quintuple restitution; except for a non-vital organ he is not liable.”
[Bava Kamma 7:6.1] MISHNAH: If he was drawing it to lead it out but it died on the owner’s property, he is not liable. If he lifted it or had led it outside the owner’s property when it died, he is liable. If he gave it for his first-born son, to his creditor, to an unpaid guardian or a borrower, to a paid guardian or a renter, and that person was drawing it to lead it out but it died on the owner’s property, he is not liable. If he lifted it or had led it outside the owner’s property when it died, he is liable.
[Bava Kamma 7:6.2] HALAKHAH: “If he was drawing it to lead it out but it died,” etc.; “If he gave it for his first-born son,” etc. {NAME} said, if somebody would explain to me the following, I would carry his בנרייה: What means “is not liable”? Is he not liable for his obligation or not liable for theft?
[Bava Kamma 7:7.1] MISHNAH: One does not raise sheep and goats in the Land of Israel but one raises them in Syria and in the non-arable tracts in the Land of Israel. One does not raise chickens in Jerusalem because of the sacrifices, nor may Cohanim in the Land of Israel do so because of purities. A Jew may not raise pigs, and a person should not raise a dog unless it is tied by a chain. One does not set traps for pigeons unless thirty stadia distant from any settlement.
[Bava Kamma 7:7.2] HALAKHAH: “One does not raise sheep and goats in the Land of Israel,” etc. {NAME} said, for example Mahir which is sixteen by sixteen mil .
[Bava Kamma 7:7.3] It was stated: “One does not raise chickens in Jerusalem because of the sacrifices, nor may Cohanim in the Land of Israel because of purities.” I could think also in Jerusalem in this way, but it might follow what {NAME} said, “Jerusalem the built-up” etc., the city which joins Israel one to the other.
[Bava Kamma 7:7.4] It is written: “They are impure for you”. Why does it say “they shall be impure for you”? One is for the prohibition of eating, the other for the prohibition of usufruct. Anything forbidden [by the Torah is forbidden for trade, but everything whose prohibition] is rabbinical is permitted for trade. But is there not the donkey? It is raised for work. Is there not the camel? It is raised for work.
[Bava Kamma 7:7.5] “A person should not raise a dog unless it is tied by a chain.” {NAME} said: About anybody who raises a biting dog the verse says: “He who refuses kindness to his neighbor,” etc.
[Bava Kamma 7:7.6] “One does not set traps for pigeons unless distant thirty stadia from any settlement.” [Here, you say thirty stadia.] But there, you say 50 cubits. {NAME} said, they feed within fifty cubits; they fly even four mil .
[Bava Kamma 8:1.1] MISHNAH: One who injures another person owes him under five categories: Damages, suffering, medical costs, loss of earnings, and embarrassment. How are damages determined? If he blinded his eye, or cut off his hand, or broke his leg, one considers it as if he were sold as a slave; how much was he worth and how much is he worth now. Suffering: If he burned him with a spit, or with a nail, even on his fingernails where it does not cause a wound, one estimates how much a person in his state would ask to be paid in order to be willing to suffer such pain.
[Bava Kamma 8:1.2] HALAKHAH: “One who injures another person,” etc. It was stated: “One who injures another person in five [respects] pays him for five categories, in four he pays him four, in three he pays him three, in two he pays him two, in one he pays him one.” How? If he hit him on his hand and severed it, he pays him five times: Damages, suffering, medical costs, loss of earnings, and embarassment. If he hit him on his hand and it became swollen, he pays four times: Suffering, medical costs, loss of earnings, and embarassment. If he hit him on his head which became swollen, he pays three times, suffering, medical costs, loss of earnings. At a place where it is not visible he pays twice, suffering and medical costs. With a tome in his hand he pays only once, for embarrassment.
[Bava Kamma 8:1.3] {NAME} asked: If he severed his hand and returned and severed the arm, does he have to pay additionally for the pain inflicted the first time?
[Bava Kamma 8:1.4] It is written: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.” At another place, He says: “Do not be softhearted.” One refers to inadvertent acts, the other to intentional ones. He could mention the inadvertent but not mention the intentional. But if the inadvertent had been mentioned but not the intentional, I would have said that for the inadvertent act he shall pay money, for the intentional [have his hand cut off. Therefore it was necessary to mention the intentional. Or if the intentional had been mentioned but not the inadvertent, I would have said that for the intentional act he shall pay money, for the inadvertent] he should not pay at all. Therefore it was necessary to mention both inadvertent and intentional. And if he blinded a blind man or cut off the arm of an amputee, how could one fulfill: “Do to him as he intended to do to his brother”? This indicates that he only pays money.
[Bava Kamma 8:1.5] “Suffering: If he burned him with a spit, or with a nail, even on his fingernails where it does not cause a wound.” How is this? If he wounded him so that he lost blood, it already is written: “A wound for a wound.” Why does the verse say “a contusion”? To tell you that if he burned him with a spit on the palm of his hand and it swelled, on the sole of his foot and it swelled, or he put snow or ice on him at a place which is not visible, he has to pay his medical expenses.
[Bava Kamma 8:1.6] “One estimates how much a person in his state would ask to be paid in order to be willing to suffer such pain.” {NAME} said, one sees a person and asks him, how much would you give that such pain would not be inflicted on you? And what he says, he has to give. {NAME} said, the Mishnah is “how much a person would ask to be paid,” and you say so? But one sees a person and asks him, how much would you ask that such pain not be inflicted on you? And what he says, he has to give. {NAME} said, one gives food invalidity. What is food invalidity? Before that, I was eating lentils and vegetables but now I can only eat eggs and chicken. What he asks one gives him. {NAME} said, a Roman who was sick would not go into battle until he could eat all he had been missing those days.
[Bava Kamma 8:2.1] MISHNAH: Medical costs. If he hit a person, he has to pay that person’s medical costs. In case a growth on that person’s body developed, if it was a consequence of the injury, he has to pay medical costs. If it started to heal but regressed several times, he has to pay medical costs. After it was healed completely he no longer has to pay medical costs.
[Bava Kamma 8:2.2] HALAKHAH: “Medical costs. If he hit a person, he has to pay that person’s medical costs,” etc. {NAME} asked: If there was a growth around the wound and complications ensued because of the wound, what is the rule? Since it is written: “And healing he shall heal,” if [the patient] did not follow the doctor’s instructions, he is [not liable]. It was stated in another baraita : If [the wound] was covered with scab, he must pay for medical treatment. It was stated: “{NAME} says, if there was a growth around the wound, even if complications ensued because of the wound, he must pay for medical treatment but he is not liable to pay for his loss of earnings. {NAME} says, in this paragraph Scripture introduced a novelty stating that he has to pay for loss of earnings together with medical treatment: ‘Only his loss of earnings he shall compensate and healing he shall heal.’ ”
[Bava Kamma 8:3.1] MISHNAH: Loss of earnings. One considers him as if he were a watchman of pumpkins since he already compensated him for the loss of his hand or loss of his foot. Embarrassment. Everything depends on the person embarrassing and the one embarrassed. One who embarrassed a naked person, or embarrassed a blind person, or embarrassed a sleeping person is liable, but the sleeper who embarrassed is not liable. If a person fell from a roof and caused damage and embarrassed, he is liable for the damage but not liable for the embarrassment since is was said: “She reached out with her hand and grabbed him at his private parts;” one is not liable for embarrassment unless if was intended.
[Bava Kamma 8:3.2] HALAKHAH: “Loss of earnings. One considers him,” etc. Here you say, “one considers him as if he were a watchman of pumpkins.” But there, you say, “if he was earning a mina per day, he pays him a mina; a tetradrachma, he gives him a tetradrachma.” {NAME} said, there are two kinds of inability to work. If he hit him on his hand and cut it off, one does not consider him as if he earned a mina a day but one considers him as if he were a lame person watching pumpkins, because he already compensated him for the loss of his hand or loss of his foot. But if he burned him on the palm of his hand and it swelled, on the flat of his head and it swelled, or he put on him snow or cold water at a place which is not visible, then he has to pay his medical expenses.
[Bava Kamma 8:3.3] It was stated: “She reached out with her hand,” but not the court marshal’s wife. Another Tanna stated, “she reached out with her hand,” including the court marshal’s wife. He who said, “she reached out with her hand,” but not the court marshal’s wife, if he whipped with permission. He who said, “she reached out with her hand,” including the court marshal’s wife, if he whipped without permission. It was stated: Not the wife of two men.
[Bava Kamma 8:4.1] MISHNAH: This is more severe regarding a human than an ox since a human pays damages and pays for unborn children, but the ox pays only damages and does not pay for unborn children. A person who hits his father or mother without causing a concussion or who causes injury on the Day of Atonement is liable for everything. He who injures a Hebrew slave is liable for everything except for lost earnings if he is his own. He who injures another person’s Canaanite slave is liable for everything. {NAME} says, slaves have no claim for embarrassment.
[Bava Kamma 8:4.2] HALAKHAH: “This is more severe regarding a human than an ox,” etc. “A person who hits his father or mother,” etc. It was stated: If the witnesses said, we testify that X blinded both of his eyes simultanously, or that he knocked out two of his teeth simultaneously, he does not have to pay anything. One after the other, he gains his freedom by the first and he pays him damages for the second. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: This implies that one estimates embarrassment for slaves. {NAME} in the name of {NAME}: If a person dedicates his earnings, he dedicates everything. If he dedicates the earnings of his slave, he can take from there his upkeep and the remainder is dedicated. Here you say, the remainder is dedicated, but there you say, everything is holy. {NAME} said, Jews are more obligated to support free people than slaves. But did not {NAME} say: If somebody cuts off the hands of somebody else’s slave, his master collects damages, suffering, medical costs, loss of earnings, and embarrassment, and that one should be supported by welfare. {NAME} said, Jews are more obligated to support amputated slaves than unimpaired ones. But did not {NAME} also give to his slave when he ate meat? Give also to his slave when he drank wine? And recited for himself the verse: “Did not His maker make me in the womb”? They said, there a rule of law, here a rule of mercy.
[Bava Kamma 8:5.1] MISHNAH: It is bad to meet a deaf-mute, an insane, or an underage person: Anybody who injures them is liable but they who cause injury are not liable. It is bad to meet a woman or a slave: Anybody who injures them is liable but they who cause injury are not liable, but they might have to pay later. If the woman was divorced or the slave manumitted, they have to pay. A person who hits his father or mother causing a concussion or who causes injury to a fellow man on the Sabbath is not liable for anything since he is tried for his life. One who injures his own Canaanite slave is not liable for anything.
[Bava Kamma 8:5.2] HALAKHAH: “It is bad to meet a deaf-mute, an insane, or an underage person,” etc. It was stated: If the witnesses said, we testify that X blinded the eye of his slave and broke his tooth, for that is what the master said, and they are found to be perjured, they pay to the slave. How can they say this about the case? {NAME} said, those might say the following: We testify about X that [the slave] came to his hand unimpaired and left with two injuries. Then he gains his freedom with the first and he has to pay him for the second.
[Bava Kamma 8:6.1] MISHNAH: He who hits another pays him a tetradrachma; {NAME} says in the name of {NAME}, a mina . If he hurt him on his earlobe, tore out some of his hair, spat on him and the spit touched him, removed his stole, uncovered a woman’s hair, he pays 400 zuz; everything corresponding to his honor. {NAME} said, even the poorest in Israel are treated as aristocrats who lost their property, for they are descendents of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He told him, you did not say anything since a person who injures himself, while he is not allowed to do that, is not liable, but others who injure him are liable; a person who cuts down his fruit trees, while he is not allowed to do that, is not liable, but others who cut down his fruit trees are.
[Bava Kamma 8:6.2] HALAKHAH: “He who hits another pays him a tetradrachma.” “{NAME} said, even the poorest in Israel,” etc. {NAME} stated: For a kick, one. For an elbow, three. For sqlvnqyt fifteen. Somebody said in the name of {NAME}: He who puts an Elder to shame has fully to pay for his shame. A person insulted {NAME}. The case came before {NAME} who fined him a pound of gold.
[Bava Kamma 8:6.3] “If one spat on him and the spit touched him.” How far does the spit have to reach? On his body, on his garments? But what is the rule if he spat and the spittle did not reach him? {NAME} said, this implies that somebody who insults another person verbally is not liable.
[Bava Kamma 8:6.4] {NAME} stated before {NAME}: “You killed my ox, you cut down my fruit trees,” and the other says, I do not know, he is liable.
